# Introduction

> Tabsdata overview covering Python functions as workflows, Polars expression transforms, automatic DAG orchestration, data versioning, the tdk coding agent skill, and built-in connectors for Snowflake, S3, Postgres, MySQL, and Databricks.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/introduction

Tabsdata is an open-source, distributed, horizontally scalable data integration platform that allows users to turn their Python functions into automated, AI-friendly workflows that move and transform data between a variety of different systems.

Built atop [Kubernetes](https://kubernetes.io/) and the [Polars](https://pola.rs/) DataFrame API, Tabsdata can be deployed on almost any machine that runs Python, requires no admin permissions or Docker dependency, and allows users to move and transform tabular data through an expression-based Pythonic interface.

With the Tabsdata skill installed, a coding agent can also build and analyze workflows through `tdk`.

_Video: Leads data pipeline animation_

# Install Tabsdata

> Installs the Tabsdata Python package with pip or uv, creates a virtual environment, sets the Anthropic or OpenAI LLM key, runs tdkserver quickstart with the kminus provider, and logs in.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/install

Deploy a Tabsdata Server on your Machine in under 5 minutes.

Tabsdata is published as a python package, installable with `pip`

Requirements

-   Machine with a supported OS
    -   Linux (x86)
    -   macOS (Apple Silicon/ARM64)
    -   Windows (x86)
-   **Python 3.12.13 or later**
-   An LLM API key from **Anthropic** or **OpenAI (Required for AI features)**

### Create a Python virtual environment

Using a virtual environment provides a layer of isolation and prevents interference from other python environments on your machine.

-   macOS / Linux
-   Windows (PowerShell)

-   conda
-   uv
-   pyenv
-   venv

```bash
conda create -n tabsdata python=3.12 -y
conda activate tabsdata
```

```bash
uv venv --python 3.12.13 .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
```

```bash
pyenv install 3.12.13
pyenv local 3.12.13
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
```

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
```

-   uv
-   pyenv
-   venv


### Install Tabsdata

After installing, add the Tabsdata skill for your coding agent; see [Configure Your AI Agent](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connect-agent).

-   uv
-   pip

```bash
uv pip install "tabsdata[all]"
```

```bash
pip install "tabsdata[all]"
```

### Set LLM key as environment variable in terminal

-   macOS / Linux
-   Windows (PowerShell)

-   Anthropic
-   OpenAI

```bash
export ANTHROPIC_KEY="sk-ant-..."
```

```bash
export OPENAI_KEY="sk-..."
```

-   Anthropic
-   OpenAI

```powershell
$env:ANTHROPIC_KEY = "sk-ant-..."
```

```powershell
$env:OPENAI_KEY = "sk-..."
```

### Start the Tabsdata server

`tdkserver quickstart` initializes and deploys a Tabsdata Instance. The command should take around 30 seconds to fully execute.

-   Anthropic
-   OpenAI

```bash
tdkserver quickstart --config anthropic-key=env:ANTHROPIC_KEY
```

```bash
tdkserver quickstart --config openai-key=env:OPENAI_KEY
```

Some Notes on Tabsdata Server Providers

Tabsdata runs on Kubernetes, and this install uses `kminus`: a lightweight provider that runs pods as native processes in your Python environment instead of Docker containers, so it needs no root or administrator access. See [Deploy a Server on k-minus](https://docs.tabsdata.com/server-admin/kminus) for the full lifecycle. Tabsdata can also be deployed on [AWS EKS](https://docs.tabsdata.com/server-admin/eks-install), [Azure AKS](https://docs.tabsdata.com/server-admin/aks-install), or [Google GKE](https://docs.tabsdata.com/server-admin/gke-install).

Installing Third-party Database Drivers

If you plan to use the PostgreSQL connectors, they need a database driver that Tabsdata cannot redistribute. Please review [Installing Third-Party Database Drivers](https://docs.tabsdata.com/server-admin/third-party-database-drivers) for more information.

### Log in

```bash
tdk login --server localhost --user admin --password tabsdata
```

Or access the UI at [http://localhost:2457/login](http://localhost:2457/login)

Next: [Configure Your AI Agent](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connect-agent). Install the Tabsdata skill for your coding agent, then run your first pipeline.

## Upgrade Tabsdata

To upgrade Tabsdata, install the new version in a clean virtual environment and run `tdkserver upgrade` from it. The upgrade keeps the instance's custom configuration, for example additional virtual environment requirements.

### Create a new virtual environment

Create a new, clean virtual environment for the new version, as in [Create a Python virtual environment](#create-a-python-virtual-environment), with a new name such as `tabsdata-new` or `.venv-new`. Do not install the new version in the environment of the version you are upgrading from.

### Install the new version

In the new virtual environment, install Tabsdata as in [Install Tabsdata](#install-tabsdata).

### Upgrade the server

From the new virtual environment, run:

```bash
tdkserver upgrade
```

The upgrade stops the Tabsdata Server and leaves it stopped. To start it again as soon as the upgrade completes, pass `--apply true`:

```bash
tdkserver upgrade --apply true
```

Without `--apply true`, start the server with `tdkserver start` when you are ready. `tdkserver upgrade` upgrades the instance named `tabsdata` unless `--instance` names another; see [tdkserver upgrade](https://docs.tabsdata.com/cli/tdkserver/upgrade) for every option.

### Remove the previous virtual environment

Once the upgrade is complete, the virtual environment of the previous version is no longer used and can be deleted.

### Upgrade the clients

Every machine that runs `tdk` needs the new version too. On each one, create a new virtual environment and install the new version, as in the first two steps.

Then run the AI agent configuration again from the new virtual environment, starting with `tdk ai agents install`. See [Configure Your AI Agent](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connect-agent).

# Configure Your AI Agent

> Install the Tabsdata skill so a coding agent works with Tabsdata through tdk in its own shell, then log in so the agent acts through your session.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connect-agent

Tabsdata provides a skill that enables your AI agent to use the `tdk` CLI for development. Supported agents are Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, VS Code, Gemini CLI and Antigravity. Your AI Agent can use Tabsdata's CLI without the skill installation, but the skill file provides the available commands for an easier experience.

Step 1Install the Tabsdata skill

After installing `tabsdata[all]` from [Install Tabsdata](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/install), install the Tabsdata skill files into your shared agents folder. You can also just ask your agent to do this step for you:

```bash
tdk ai agents install
```

The skill is installed for every supported agent on the machine. See [tdk ai agents install](https://docs.tabsdata.com/cli/tdk/ai/agents-install) for its options.

note

Upgrading from an earlier version of Tabsdata? Remove the old MCP connection with `claude mcp remove tabsdata` or `codex mcp remove tabsdata`, then follow this step.

Step 2Log in to the Tabsdata Server

Use the password you have configured for the `--password` flag

```bash
tdk login --server http://127.0.0.1:2457 --user admin --password tabsdata
```

Step 3Use you AI Agent for building Tabsdata Workflows

Start your agent and describe what you need.

```bash
claude
```

Next: [Run Your First Data Integration](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/run-your-first-data-integration)

Registering the publisher that produces **persons**.

```python
@publisher(
  source=LocalFileSrc(paths=["persons.csv"], format=SrcFileFormat.CSV),
  output_tables=["persons"],
)
def ingest_persons(rows: TableFramesSpec) -> TableFrameSpec:
  return rows[0] if rows else None
```

Called tabsdata 2 times (ctrl+o to expand)

⏺

Registered and committed. Now the transformer — full\_name from first\_name and last\_name, age dropped.

```python
@transformer(
  input_tables=["persons"],
  output_tables=["people"],
)
def build_people(persons: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec:
  return persons.with_columns(
      (col("first_name") + " " + col("last_name")).alias("full_name"),
  ).drop("first_name", "last_name", "age")
```

Called tabsdata 2 times (ctrl+o to expand)

⏺

Registered and committed. Last, the subscriber writing people out as .jsonl. Getting the connection and subscriber guides.

Called tabsdata 3 times (ctrl+o to expand)

⏺

Writing , then a destination collection pointed at output-data.

Called tabsdata 2 times (ctrl+o to expand)

⏺

Registering the subscriber.

```python
@subscriber(
  input_tables=["people"],
  destination=LocalFileDest(paths=["people.jsonl"], format=DestFileFormat.JSON),
)
def export_people(people: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec:
  return people
```

Called tabsdata 3 times (ctrl+o to expand)

⏺

Registered. The publisher's commit triggered the transformer, which triggered the subscriber, all in one execution plan — committed, 0 failures.

⏺

**people.jsonl** is live in `qs-example/output-data/`:


# Architecture Overview

> Tabsdata system architecture: resource layer (Functions, Tables) and execution layer (Execution Plans, Transactions, Function Runs), plus scalability, security, deployment providers, and AI integration.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/architecture

## System architecture

Tabsdata is a distributed, horizontally scalable system that runs on **Kubernetes** and can be deployed across a variety of Kubernetes providers. Tabsdata is organized into two conceptual layers: a **resource layer** and an **execution layer**.

The **resource layer** consists of objects that users create to establish the structure of a Tabsdata workflow. These include objects like Tables and Functions, which determine when a workflow runs, what data flows through it, and what work is applied to that data.

The **execution layer** consists of objects that Tabsdata creates when it reads and acts on resources from the resource layer. These objects make up the running workflow that performs work on data. This includes objects like Execution Plans, Transactions, and Function Runs.

[Server](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/server)

[Projects](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/projects)

Resource layer

-   [Groups](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/groups)
    
    -   [Collections](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/collections)
        
        -   [Functions](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/functions)
            
        -   [Connections](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connections)
            
        -   [Tables](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/tables)

# Resource Layer

### Functions

Functions are Tabsdata's unit of work. A function performs a single discrete step of moving data between external systems and internal Tabsdata Tables. There are three types of Tabsdata Functions:

A **publisher** reads from an external system and writes into Tabsdata tables.

A **transformer** reads from Tabsdata tables and writes into new Tabsdata tables.

A **subscriber** reads from Tabsdata tables and writes out to an external system.

Data enters and leaves the server through functions

Database

postgres

Publisher

Tabsdata Server

Table

customers

Transformer

Warehouse

snowflake

### Tables

A unique feature of Tabsdata is that it has its own internal storage for all data produced by functions.

Tabsdata tables persistently store the data produced by functions. Every successful function run that returns data creates a new table version that sits alongside all previous versions of the table.

persons

Tabsdata›Collections›input›persons

### Schema

Table schema defines the structure of a table by listing its columns and their data types.

| Object | Type |
| --- | --- |
| first\_name | str |
| last\_name | str |
| age | i64 |
| nationality | str |
| city | str |

version

While Tabsdata tables share some similarities to database tables, they also have some key differences. Rather than requiring a predefined schema, each version inside a table carries its own, allowing a table's schema to evolve across versions. This not only makes Tabsdata resilient to schema drift, but also stores a lineage of the table's evolution for observability and debugging.

Table version history is available not only to users for viewing, but also to functions for ingestion. Functions can read historical table versions for use cases that require comparing historical data with incoming data.

## Execution Layer

Functions and tables declare how data should be moved. Tabsdata's reads these and builds the actual workflow that ingests, transforms, and loads your data.

### Execution Plans

Traditionally, as more steps are added to a data integration workflow, the more complex it is to orchestrate it.

Tabsdata does not have this issue. Function are declarative and declare their own dependencies. Any functions that write to tables used by other functions are upstream dependent to them. Any functions that use tables produced by other functions are downstream dependent to them.

When a Function is triggered, Tabsdata identifies its downstream dependencies and automatically builds an **Execution Plan**, a DAG (directed acytclic graph) that finds and executes all downstream dependencies.

Click any node to trace its dependencies

In addition to automatically orchestrating workflows, Execution plans record everything that occurs during execution, capturing metadata such as:

-   Execution start and stop time
-   Functions executed
-   Function code used
-   Tables read and written
-   Execution status
-   Execution logs

## Horizontal Scalability

Compute and storage are independently scalable. Each Function runs as an isolated process within the Server's Kubernetes cluster. Storage can be distributed across local file storage or cloud storage providers such as Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage, and Google Cloud Storage.

## Security

Authorization uses a direct permission model, where permissions are assigned directly to users rather than through roles.

Credentials are stored separately from Functions in a secure credential store. This includes both Tabsdata's internal credentials and the credentials used by Connections to authenticate with external systems.

note

Even when credentials are provided inline through the CLI, Tabsdata automatically extracts and stores them in the credential store.

## Deployment

Tabsdata runs on **Linux** for production and **macOS** or **Windows** for development. The underlying Kubernetes can be deployed across several providers

-   **`kminus`**: A lightweight Kubernetes implementation that runs pods as native Python processes instead of Docker containers. The default provider for local development.
-   **`eks`**: Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS).
-   **`aks`:** Azure Kubernetes Service
-   **`gke`**: Google Kubernetes Engine

## AI integration

Coding agents use your Tabsdata Server through the **`tdk` CLI**, in their own shell. The **Tabsdata skill** tells an agent when Tabsdata fits a task and how to use it, and before any work against a Server the agent loads that Server's own skills, so its instructions always match the Server it works on. See [Configure Your AI Agent](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connect-agent) to get started.

There are two ways to use AI in Tabsdata:

-   A **built-in agent** called Tabby for operational tasks within Tabsdata.
-   External coding agents, such as **Claude Code** and **Codex**, working through `tdk` with the Tabsdata skill.

# Server

> What a Tabsdata server contains, how it runs workflows, and how clients connect to it.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/server

A **Tabsdata Server** is the top-level Tabsdata process deployed on a machine. It stores and manages Tabsdata resources, executes workflows, stores tabular data, and isolates Tabsdata processes from other processes running on the machine.

You can interact with a Server through the Tabsdata UI, the `tdk` CLI, or the Python API, and coding agents work with it through `tdk`.

## Resources in a Server

The main units of work within Tabsdata are **Functions**, which perform work on data, and **Tables**, which store data produced by Functions.

As the the top-level process Tabsdata, Servers store Functions and Tables as well as several organizational layers that nest functions and tables:

1.  **Projects** are the top-level workspaces within a Server. Projects isolate their resources and workflows from those in other Projects, allowing multiple teams or workflows to share a single Server without interfering with one another.
2.  **Groups** organize resources according to their role in a workflow. For example, a Project might have separate Groups for ingesting source data, cleaning data, and loading processed data.
3.  **Collections** define transaction boundaries for their Tables, determining how data is committed or rolled back during an execution. Collections are also credential stores that can provide Functions inside them with the credentials needed to connect to external systems.

[Server](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/server)

[Projects](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/projects)

[Groups](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/groups)

[Collections](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/collections)

[Functions](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/functions)[Connections](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connections)[Tables](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/tables)

## Connecting to a Server

A Tabsdata server uses three dedicated endpoints when running:

-   A **public endpoint** runs on port `2457` by default. The Tabsdata UI, `tdk` CLI, and Python API use this endpoint to communicate with the Server.
-   A **private endpoint** runs on port `2458` by default. Tabsdata services use this endpoint for internal communication.
-   An **AI agent endpoint** runs on port `2459` by default. The Tabsdata Conversational agent, Tabby, uses this endpoint.

Using default port configuration, the default local URI for the public endpoint is:

`http://localhost:2457`

You can connect to a Server using several interfaces:

-   The **Tabsdata UI** provides a browser-based interface for managing resources, running workflows, and inspecting results.
-   The **`tdk` CLI** provides command-line access to the Server.
-   The **Python API** provides programmatic access from Python applications.
-   **Coding agents** work with the Server through `tdk`, guided by the Tabsdata skill.

## Managing a Server

The `tdkserver` CLI manages the Server lifecycle, including initializing, creating, starting, and stopping a Server.

See [Deploy Tabsdata on k-minus](https://docs.tabsdata.com/server-admin/kminus) for Quickstart and the complete local Server lifecycle. For a managed Kubernetes deployment, choose [AWS EKS](https://docs.tabsdata.com/server-admin/eks-install), [Azure AKS](https://docs.tabsdata.com/server-admin/aks-install), or [Google GKE](https://docs.tabsdata.com/server-admin/gke-install).

To connect an AI agent, see [Configure Your AI Agent](https://docs.tabsdata.com/server-admin/connect-agent).

# Projects

> How Projects organize and isolate resources within a Tabsdata Server.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/projects

A **Project** is the top-level workspace inside a Tabsdata Server. Projects organize related workflows and their resources while isolating them from other Projects on the same Server.

This allows multiple teams to share a single Server without interfering with each other's work.

## Working in a Project

Most Tabsdata operations are performed within the context of a Project. You can set a default Project for the `tdk` CLI using:

```bash
tdk set --proj sales_analytics
```

The selected Project remains the default for subsequent commands. Commands that support the `--proj` option can target a different Project without changing the default.

## Managing Projects

Creating a Project establishes an empty workspace within an existing Server. Groups and Collections can then be created to organize the Functions and Tables that make up your workflows.

Deleting a Project removes the Project and its resources without affecting other Projects on the Server.

See [Create a Project](https://docs.tabsdata.com/tutorials/managing-projects/create), [Update a Project](https://docs.tabsdata.com/tutorials/managing-projects/update), and [Delete a Project](https://docs.tabsdata.com/tutorials/managing-projects/delete) for step-by-step instructions.

## Project Secrets

A Project can hold secrets: named groups of keys and values, such as the credentials of an API that its Functions call. Every Function of the Project can read them while it runs.

Project secrets are for values your own function code needs. Credentials that a connector uses to read from or write to an external system stay in [Connections](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connections).

### Defining secrets

Write the secrets in a YAML file. Each top-level entry is a secret, and each secret maps its keys to their values:

```yaml
weather_api:
  token: abc123                     # the value itself
  account: $secret:WEATHER_ACCOUNT  # read from the WEATHER_ACCOUNT environment variable
  region:                           # no value: keep the value already stored
```

A value written as `$secret:<VARIABLE>` is read from that environment variable in the shell that runs `tdk`, so the value never has to be written in the file. A key with no value keeps the value already stored, or is empty if there is none; write `""` to store an empty value.

NOTE: Only project admins can manage project secrets.

Pass the file when you create or update the Project:

```bash
tdk project create --name sales_analytics --secrets-file secrets.yaml
tdk project update --name sales_analytics --secrets-file secrets.yaml
```

warning

Each update replaces all the secrets of the Project. A secret or key left out of the file is removed.

To see which secrets a Project holds, run:

```bash
tdk project secrets --name sales_analytics
```

It lists each secret and its keys. Values are never shown, and there is no way to read them back out of Tabsdata.

### Reading secrets in a Function

Give the Function a final `ctx: FunctionCtx` parameter and read a value by secret and key:

```python
from tabsdatak.api import FunctionCtx, TableFrame, transformer

@transformer(input_tables=["cities"], output_tables=["forecast"])
def forecast(cities: TableFrame, ctx: FunctionCtx) -> TableFrame:
    token = ctx.secret("weather_api", "token")
    # or, in one string: ctx.secret("weather_api.token")
    ...
```

Secret and key names are not case-sensitive. `ctx.secret_names` lists the secrets of the Project, and `ctx.secret_keys("weather_api")` the keys of one of them. Reading a secret or key that does not exist raises `KeyError`.

note

Only Function code receives Project secrets. Connector plugins do not, and the values are not placed in the Function's environment variables.

# Groups

> How Groups organize Collections by data direction and transformation stage.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/groups

A **Group** is an organizational layer inside a tabsdata project that organizes workflow steps according to their role in the workflow. By default, all tabsdata projects come with three groups: **sources, default, and destinations**

1.  the **sources** group stores everything related to ingesting data from external systems
    
2.  the **default** group stores everything related to transforming data inside tabsdata
    
3.  the **destinations** group stores everything related to loading data into external systems
    

Groups separate workflow resources based on type of data movement

Database

postgres

Tabsdata Server

Table

`default`

rank\_users

Table

`destinations`

Warehouse

## System Groups

The **sources, default,** and **destinations** groups are special groups that must exist in your workflow. They are dedicated spaces for registering publisher and subscriber functions and cannot be modified, duplicated, or removed from your project.

Outside these three system groups, users can create any number of groups to organize their transformer functions.

## Use Cases for Groups

Groups are useful for separating workflow steps that happen across tabsdata server boundaries (ingestion, load) from workflow steps that happen inside the tabsdata server (transform).

Groups are also useful for separating data transformation workflow steps by the type of data transformation being done.

For example, a popular data design pattern is the [Medallion Architecture](https://www.databricks.com/blog/what-is-medallion-architecture) for Data Integration, which breaks data transformation into three layers:

-   **Bronze:** Layer that ingests raw source data from external systems with the goal of having as close of a representation to data in the external system
-   **Silver:** Layer that cleans, dedupes, normalizes, and joins related entities
-   **Gold:** Layer that applies granular, business-specific transformations and creates "consumer-ready" tables.

Users looking to implement this design pattern in tabsdata can do so with five groups within Tabsdata: two built-in groups (sources, destinations) and three custom groups (bronze, silver, gold).

External systems

Group`sources`Publishers

Ingest from external systems.

Built in

Group`bronze`Transformers

Raw data, kept as close to the external system as possible.

User created

Group`silver`Transformers

Cleaned, deduped, normalized, and joined.

User created

Group`gold`Transformers

Business-specific transformations, consumer-ready tables.

User created

Group`destinations`Subscribers

Write out to external systems.

Built in

External systems

## Visualizing Groups

The Projects view in the Tabsdata UI shows how data moves between Groups, including the number of Tables, rows, and bytes moving through each stage.

## Managing Groups

The `sources`, `default`, and `destinations` Groups are created with every Project. These system Groups cannot be renamed or deleted.

Custom Groups can be created, renamed, and deleted within a Project.

See [Create a Group](https://docs.tabsdata.com/tutorials/managing-groups/create), [Update a Group](https://docs.tabsdata.com/tutorials/managing-groups/update), and [Delete a Group](https://docs.tabsdata.com/tutorials/managing-groups/delete) for step-by-step instructions.

# Collections

> How Collections contain Functions, Tables, and Connections and define transaction boundaries.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/collections

A **Collection** is an organizational layer inside of a group that stores tables and functions. Collections help manage credentials for functions and define transaction boundaries for tables.

### Collections for Credential Storage

A Function is responsible for moving, and sometimes transforming, data from one place to another. Publishers and Subscribers that read from or write data to external systems also need a way to securely access sensitive credentials for those systems.

Instead of hardcoding credentials directly into Function logic, Tabsdata abstracts credential management into a separate resource called a **Connection**. A Connection is defined in a `.yaml` file and bound to a **Collection**. Any Function registered to the same Collection can access those credentials at runtime.

This allows users to store their credentials once and then securely provision those credentials to as many functions that need them. [Learn more about connections here](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connections).

### Collections as Transaction Boundaries

Triggering a Tabsdata Function creates an Execution Plan that executes the triggering Function along with any functions downstream dependent to it. Because an Execution Plan can span multiple Functions, Tabsdata needs to determine which data should be committed or rolled back if the Execution Plan fails partway through.

Collections act as transaction boundaries within an Execution Plan. Tabsdata treats each participating Collection as a separate transaction and commits data to its Tables only when all participating Functions within that Collection complete successfully. If a Function within the transaction fails, Tabsdata rolls back all changes made to Tables within that transaction.

## Managing Collections

After creating a Collection, users can register Functions into that collection. If a collection is created inside the **sources** or **destinations** group, it can only store publisher or subscriber functions respectively and requires a **connection** to be bound

Deleting a Collection removes the Collection and the resources it contains without affecting other Collections in the Project.

See [Create a Collection](https://docs.tabsdata.com/tutorials/managing-collections/create), [Update a Collection](https://docs.tabsdata.com/tutorials/managing-collections/update), and [Delete a Collection](https://docs.tabsdata.com/tutorials/managing-collections/delete) for step-by-step instructions.

---

# Connections

> How Connections provide Publisher and Subscriber Functions with access to external systems.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connections

A **Connection** is a resource that stores the credentials required to access an external system.

Publisher and Subscriber Functions need credentials to connect to external systems to read and write data, but they do not store these sensitive credentials directly in their code.

Instead, that configuration is defined in a Connection. Connections are `.yaml` files that contain relevant credentials and are attached to Collections, allowing all functions within that collection to access the required credentials during execution.

## Connection Structure

Connections are defined using `.yaml` files. The fields in a Connection depend on the external system and Connection type.

For example, an S3 Connection stores the bucket, region, and credentials needed to access files in an S3 bucket.

conn-s3.yaml

```yaml
kind: connectionDef
apiVersion: '1.0'
type: tabsdatak.conn.s3:S3SrcConn
spec:
  bucket: 'acme-ingest'
  region: 'us-east-1'
  credentials:
    kind: awsAccessSecretKeyCredentials
    apiVersion: '1.0'
    type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:AwsAccessSecretKey
    spec:
      access_key_id: '$secret:AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID'
      secret_access_key: '$secret:AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY'
```

-   required
    
-   required
    
-   required
    
-   optional
    

## Connections and Collections

Connections are bound to Publisher and Subscriber Collections.

A **Publisher Collection** binds a Publisher to an input Connection. The Publisher defines what data to read from the external system and what Tables to create in Tabsdata, while the Connection provides the configuration and credentials needed to access that system during the Publisher's execution.

A **Subscriber Collection** binds a Subscriber to an output Connection. The Subscriber defines which Tabsdata Tables to read and what data to write, while the Connection provides the configuration and credentials needed to access the destination system during the Subscriber's execution.

## Credential Security

When configuring a connection , a credential can be passed directly as `secret:<value>`, or as a reference to an environment variable, written as `$secret:<VARIABLE NAME>`.

Regardless of the method used, when the connection file is registered into Tabsdata, Tabsdata **dehydrates** the document by extracting any secrets into a separate secret store and storing a reference to the secret in the file.

note

For security, once credentials are stored in Tabsdata, they can only be accessed by a Tabsdata Function at runtime.

---

# Functions

> How Tabsdata Functions define, connect, and execute the steps in a data workflow.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/functions/

A Tabsdata **Function** is Tabsdata's operational unit of work and defines a single step that reads data from or writes data to a Tabsdata Table.

Tabsdata Functions build on the familiar model of a regular Python function, where data comes in through a parameter, the function performs work on that parameter, and the result is returned through the return statement.

Tabsdata extends this model to data integration by abstracting data sources and destinations into the simple parameters and return statement of a Python function.

Users define their inputs, which can be a SQL query against a database, a file in object storage, or a Tabsdata Table. They then define where they want the output data to be written, whether that is a database table, a file in object storage, or another Tabsdata Table.

Tabsdata handles retrieving, converting, and moving the data between those systems. While the data is being passed through the Function, Tabsdata materializes it as a DataFrame object that users can transform through an expression-based API.

This allows users to work with tabular data independently of where it is physically stored or how it needs to be moved between systems.

## Function types

There are three types of Tabsdata functions:

1.  **publishers:** read data from external systems and _publish_ data into Tabsdata Tables
2.  **transformers:** read data from Tabsdata Tables and write data into Tabsdata Tables
3.  **subscribers:** read data from Tabsdata Tables and _subscribe_ data into Tabsdata Tables

Publishers

External SystemTabsdata Table

Reads an external system and writes Tabsdata Tables.

Transformers

Tabsdata TableTabsdata Table

Reads Tabsdata Tables and writes new Tabsdata Tables.

Subscribers

Tabsdata TableExternal System

Reads Tabsdata Tables and writes an external system.

## Inputs and outputs

The decorator maps declared inputs to the Python callable's parameters. It also maps returned values to output Tables or to destination slots in an external system. The number and order of parameters and returned values must match the corresponding declarations.

Publishers and Subscribers use a Connector for the system-specific read or write operation. The Collection's [Connection](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connections) supplies the configuration and credentials used by that Connector. Transformers work entirely with Tabsdata Tables and do not use an external Connection.

Output Tables belong to the Collection where the Function is registered. Input Table references can identify Tables in other Collections within the same Project, allowing Functions to connect into a larger workflow.

## `None` inputs and outputs

A parameter or a returned value is `None` when there is no data at that position. `None` is not the same as a `TableFrame` with zero rows: an empty `TableFrame` is data and replaces the previous data, while `None` keeps it. `None` never invalidates data already in Tabsdata.

A `None` parameter has a different meaning for each Function type:

| Function | A parameter is `None` when |
| --- | --- |
| Publisher | The external system has no new data for that source slot. A slot that takes a list of frames receives `None`, not an empty list. The Publisher still runs, and can return data anyway. |
| Transformer, Subscriber | The requested input version does not exist, the input Table has never been produced, or the Table had no data up to that version. The value alone does not tell these cases apart. |

A version range, such as `orders@HEAD~3..HEAD`, reaches a Transformer or Subscriber as a list with one element per version, oldest first. A `None` element is a version that does not exist or that has no data yet. A range of a fixed size, such as `HEAD~3..HEAD`, always has that many elements, and its `None` elements are always at the oldest end, because once a Table has data every later version has data too. A range from `INITIAL`, such as `INITIAL..HEAD`, has one element per existing version and can be empty.

A returned `None` has a different meaning for each Function type:

| Function | Returning `None` for an output |
| --- | --- |
| Publisher, Transformer | Commits a new version of the output Table that holds the same data as the previous version. If the Table has never had data, the new version has no data either. |
| Subscriber | Sends no new data to that destination slot. The Connector still runs and decides what `None` does to the external system; each Connector page describes it under **Write behavior**. |

Any returned `TableFrame` is new data, including an input `TableFrame` returned unchanged; only `None` keeps the previous data. A Transformer or Subscriber that reads a version committed from a `None` receives the previous data as a `TableFrame`, not `None`. Such a version also triggers dependent Transformers and Subscribers like any other commit, so a Subscriber runs for it too: return `None` to leave the external system as it is, or the frame to write the data again.

When a Table version has no data, the UI and `tdk` say so, and say whether the version does not exist or has no data, instead of showing an empty table. `tdk` writes that message to stderr and exits with a non-zero code.

## Triggers

A [Trigger](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/execution-and-triggers) determines when a Function starts. A Transformer or Subscriber without `trigger_by` runs whenever one of its input Tables commits a new version. A Publisher has no input Tables, so without `trigger_by` it runs only when triggered manually. Set `trigger_by` to a schedule, or to one or more Table references, to control what starts the Function.

## Registration

Registration sends the Function definition, source code, and required bundle metadata to the Server. A Function name must be unique within its Collection.

Register a decorated callable from a Python file with:

```bash
tdk fn register --coll <collection_name> --path <path_to_python_file>::<function_name>
```

Pass `--update` when the same command should update an existing Function with that name. Registration records the definition; it does not execute the Function.

See [Register a Function](https://docs.tabsdata.com/tutorials/managing-functions/register) for the full procedure.

## Execution

A manual Trigger can start any registered Function:

```bash
tdk fn trigger --coll <collection_name> --name <function_name>
```

The Server evaluates the Function's dependencies and creates an Execution Plan. Each Function included in that plan gets a Function Run, and a [Worker](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/execution/workers) executes each attempt. A successful run that produces Tables creates new [Table Versions](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/tables); the Server keeps the registered Function definition after the Worker exits.

Function code does not run in the CLI process that sends the command. The CLI requests the Trigger, while the Server coordinates and records the execution.

---

# Publishers

> How @publisher reads an external system, maps source slots to function parameters, and writes versioned Tabsdata tables.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/functions/publishers

A publisher reads data from an external system and publishes it to Tabsdata tables. Each run reads the source, calls the function, and commits the returned tables together.

Unlike a stream publisher, a regular publisher does not keep reading. It reads the source only when it runs. The publisher must be registered in a source collection whose connection matches the source.

## In Action

Tabsdata server

collection · world

Database

PostgreSQL

PostgreSQL · external

Reachable

Connection

conn-postgres.yaml

Publisher

read\_world

Table

country

//world

No versions yet

Table

city

//world

No versions yet

## Parameters

```python
publisher(
    source,
    output_tables,
    trigger_by=None,
    on_tables=None,
)
```

| Parameter | Type |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `source` | `Src` | required |
| `output_tables` | `list[str]` | required |
| `trigger_by` | `CronTrigger \| TablesTrigger` | optional |
| `on_tables` | `list[OnTablesAction]` | optional |

#### `source`

The source to read. The source class decides what is read and how many slots are passed to the function. A SQL source has one slot per query. A file source can read several files into one slot.

The source does not contain the server address or credentials. Those come from the connection of the collection where the publisher is registered. The page for each connector lists its source classes and settings.

#### `output_tables`

A non-empty list of local table names, one for each value the function returns. A name must start with a letter, use only letters, numbers, and underscores, and be no longer than 64 characters.

The source slot count and output table count do not have to match. A publisher can combine several source slots into one table or derive several tables from one slot.

#### `trigger_by`

The trigger that starts the publisher automatically: a `CronTrigger` or `TablesTrigger`. Without `trigger_by`, the publisher runs only when triggered manually. See [Execution & Triggers](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/execution-and-triggers).

#### `on_tables`

Actions to run on the output tables after the publisher succeeds, such as [data quality](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/data-quality) checks.

## Publisher Code Anatomy

read\_world.py

```
1from tabsdatak.api import publisher, TableFrameSpec2from tabsdatak.conn.postgres import PostgresSrc3 4 1@publisher(2    source=PostgresSrc(3        queries=[8            "SELECT * FROM country",9            "SELECT * FROM city",10        ],11    ),4    output_tables=["country", "city"],13)56def read_world(country: TableFrameSpec, city: TableFrameSpec) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec, TableFrameSpec]:7    return (country, city)
```

-   Defines the source and output Tables for the Publisher.
    
    -   Reads data from the external system. The Collection's Connection provides the address and credentials.
        
    -   SQL queries that read the country and city data from Postgres.
        
    -   Tabsdata Tables where the returned data is written.
        
-   Receives the query results and returns the data to write to the output Tables.
    
    -   The `country` and `city` arguments receive the query results in the order listed in `queries`.
        
    -   The returned data is written to the Tables listed in `output_tables`, in that order. Returning `None` for a Table leaves its current version unchanged.
        

## The function

A publisher function has one parameter per source slot and returns one frame per output table.

-   **Parameters.** Source slots are passed to the function in source order. Annotate a parameter as `TableFrameSpec` for one frame or `TableFramesSpec` for a list of frames. A slot is `None` when the external system has no new data for it; see [`None` inputs and outputs](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/functions/#none-inputs-and-outputs).
-   **Context.** The function can have a final `ctx: TransactionCtx` parameter. Use `ctx` to keep values between successful runs. For example, an incremental SQL publisher can save its last processed ID with `ctx.set_attr()` and use it in the next query. Type it `FunctionCtx` to also read the run's identifiers and the project's secrets.
-   **Return value.** Return values map to `output_tables` in order. One output can be returned on its own; several outputs are returned as a tuple. Returning `None` for one output commits a new version that keeps that table's previous data.
-   **Slot counts.** The number of source slots does not have to match the number of output tables. The function can combine several inputs into one table or create several tables from one input.

Tabsdata checks the slot counts and function signature when the publisher is registered.

## Connections and collections

All publishers in a source collection use the same connection. Each publisher has its own source settings, code, and output tables.

The connection is created with the collection. Updating a connection changes how every publisher in that collection reaches the external system.

## Lifecycle

-   **Register.** `tdk fn register` uploads the publisher. Its collection and connection must already exist.
-   **Run.** A manual, cron, or table trigger starts a transaction. The source is read before the function runs.
-   **Commit.** A successful run commits the output tables together. Each commit adds a table version.
-   **Update.** `tdk fn update` replaces the code and decorator settings.
-   **Delete.** Deleting the function stops future runs but does not delete its output tables or their versions.

For step-by-step guides on building a publisher for a specific external system, see [Publishers](https://docs.tabsdata.com/tutorials/publishers/) under How-to Guides.

---

# Stream Publishers

> How @stream_publisher reads a CDC log or a Kafka topic continuously, and how the batch parameters decide when the function runs.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/functions/stream-publishers

A stream publisher reads data continuously from a stream source, such as a CDC log or a Kafka topic, and publishes it into Tabsdata tables in batches.

A regular publisher runs when it is triggered and reads what is in the source at that moment. A stream publisher has no trigger. Registering it starts a worker that keeps reading the source, collects what it reads, and runs the function once per batch. The `batch_*` parameters of `@stream_publisher` decide when a batch is complete.

These sources work with `@stream_publisher`:

| Source | Reads | Page |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `PostgresCdcStreamSrc` | Postgres changes, from the WAL | [Postgres CDC](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connectors/postgres-cdc) |
| `MySQLCdcStreamSrc` | MySQL changes, from the binlog | [MySQL CDC](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connectors/mysql-cdc) |
| `Db2CdcStreamSrc` | Db2 changes, from the SQL Replication CD tables | [Db2 CDC](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connectors/db2-cdc) |
| `KafkaStreamSrc` | Messages from Kafka topics | [Kafka](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connectors/kafka) |

All of them use the batch parameters described on this page.

## In Action

Tabsdata server

collection · events

Kafka topic

Kafka

Kafka · external

Reachable

Connection

conn-kafka.yaml

Stream Publisher

stream\_page\_views

Table

page\_views

//events

No versions yet

## Example

stream\_sales\_changes.py

```python
from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, TableFramesSpec, stream_publisher
from tabsdatak.conn.postgres import PostgresCdcStreamSrc
from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import concat

@stream_publisher(
    source=PostgresCdcStreamSrc(
        tables=["public.orders", "public.customers"],
        replication_slot="tabsdata_sales",
        start_from="full",
    ),
    output_tables=["orders_changes", "customers_changes"],
    batch_max_secs=300,
    batch_max_rows=50_000,
)
def stream_sales_changes(
    orders: TableFramesSpec,
    customers: TableFramesSpec,
) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec, TableFrameSpec]:
    return concat(orders), concat(customers)
```

-   `source` is the stream source. Its connection comes from the collection the function is registered in, as for any publisher.
-   `output_tables` are the Tabsdata tables the function writes, in the order the function returns them.
-   `batch_max_secs` and `batch_max_rows` decide when a batch is handed to the function: here, every 5 minutes, or sooner once 50,000 changes are waiting, but never more often than once a minute.
-   The function receives one parameter per source slot. Each parameter is a list of frames: the data read for that slot since the previous batch. `concat` combines them into one frame.

## Parameters

```python
stream_publisher(
    source,
    output_tables,
    *,
    batch_min_secs=None,
    batch_max_secs=None,
    batch_max_rows=None,
    batch_max_bytes=None,
    batch_idle_secs=None,
    on_tables=None,
    flush_interval_mins=None,
)
```

| Parameter | Type |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `source` | `StreamSrc` | required |
| `output_tables` | `list[str]` | required |
| `batch_min_secs` | `int` | optional |
| `batch_max_secs` | `int` | optional |
| `batch_max_rows` | `int` | optional |
| `batch_max_bytes` | `int` | optional |
| `batch_idle_secs` | `int` | optional |
| `on_tables` | `list[OnTablesAction]` | optional |
| `flush_interval_mins` | `int` | deprecated |

`source` and `output_tables` can be given by position or by name. The other parameters must be given by name.

#### `source`

The stream source to read: one of the sources in the table above.

#### `output_tables`

The tables the function writes, as a non-empty list of table names. The number of output tables does not have to match the number of source slots.

#### `on_tables`

Actions to run on the output tables, such as [data quality](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/data-quality) checks, as for a regular publisher.

## Batch parameters

A batch is everything the worker has read since the previous batch. Each batch runs the function once, and the function's output tables are committed together: every batch adds one version to each output table.

| Parameter | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `batch_min_secs` | `60` | The shortest time between two batches, in seconds. Never less than 60. |
| `batch_max_secs` | none | Seconds after the previous batch at which data that is waiting is handed to the function. |
| `batch_max_rows` | none | Rows waiting that make a batch due. |
| `batch_max_bytes` | none | Bytes waiting that make a batch due. |
| `batch_idle_secs` | none | Seconds after the previous batch at which, if no data is waiting, the function runs with an empty batch. |

At least one of `batch_max_secs`, `batch_max_rows` and `batch_max_bytes` is required.

### When a batch is handed to the function

The worker checks after every read from the source. Counting from the previous batch (or from when the worker started):

-   **When data is waiting**, a batch is due once `batch_min_secs` have passed **and** any of these is true:
    -   `batch_max_secs` have passed,
    -   at least `batch_max_rows` rows are waiting,
    -   at least `batch_max_bytes` bytes are waiting.
-   **When no data is waiting**, nothing happens, unless `batch_idle_secs` is set. Once `batch_idle_secs` have passed, the function runs with an empty batch.

As a result:

-   `batch_min_secs` is a floor for every other setting. If 50,000 rows arrive 10 seconds after a batch, they wait until `batch_min_secs` have passed, and more rows keep joining them in the meantime.
-   `batch_max_rows` and `batch_max_bytes` make a batch due; they do not cap its size. A batch holds everything that is waiting when it closes, which can be more than the threshold.
-   Rows and bytes are counted over all the slots of the source together, not per table. For a CDC source, one row is one change. Bytes are approximate: the size of the data files already written plus an estimate of what is still in memory.
-   `batch_max_secs` counts from the previous batch, not from when the data arrived. After a quiet period longer than `batch_max_secs`, the first data to arrive is handed over right away.

Batches are processed one at a time, in order. Tabsdata looks for new batches about every 30 seconds, so a batch can start up to that long after it is due. If the function takes longer than the batch interval, batches queue up and are processed in turn.

### Validation

The batch parameters are checked when the function is decorated. A violation raises error `API_29`:

-   `batch_min_secs`, `batch_max_secs` and `batch_idle_secs` must be whole numbers of seconds, at least `60`.
-   `batch_max_rows` and `batch_max_bytes` must be whole numbers, at least `1`.
-   `batch_max_secs` must be at least `batch_min_secs`.
-   `batch_idle_secs` must be at least `batch_max_secs`, or, without `batch_max_secs`, at least `batch_min_secs`.
-   At least one of `batch_max_secs`, `batch_max_rows` and `batch_max_bytes` must be set.

### Choosing the parameters

| Goal | Parameters | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Steady, bounded latency | `batch_max_secs=120` | A batch every 2 minutes while data arrives. |
| Size first, with a time bound | `batch_max_rows=100_000, batch_max_secs=900` | A batch as soon as 100,000 rows are waiting, and at least every 15 minutes. |
| Large batches, few runs | `batch_min_secs=600, batch_max_secs=3600` | At most one batch every 10 minutes, and at least one an hour while data arrives. |
| Runs even when the source is quiet | `batch_max_secs=300, batch_idle_secs=3600` | A batch every 5 minutes while data arrives, and an empty run every hour when nothing arrives, for example to keep downstream functions on a schedule. |

### Buffer settings and batch parameters

Stream sources also have buffer settings in their `src_cfg`, such as `tabsdata.cdc.buffer.max_rows` or `tabsdata.kafka.buffer.max_rows`. Buffer settings and batch parameters work at different levels:

-   **Buffer settings** decide when the worker writes what it has read from memory to a data file. They bound the worker's memory.
-   **Batch parameters** decide when the files written so far, and anything still in memory, are handed to the function as one batch.

Most streams only need the batch parameters. The buffer settings of each source are listed on its connector page.

## Stream Publisher Code Anatomy

stream\_sales\_changes.py

```
1from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, TableFramesSpec, stream_publisher2from tabsdatak.conn.postgres import PostgresCdcStreamSrc3from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import concat4 5 1@stream_publisher(2    source=PostgresCdcStreamSrc(3        tables=["public.orders", "public.customers"],9        replication_slot="tabsdata_sales",10        start_from="full",11    ),4    output_tables=["orders_changes", "customers_changes"],5    batch_max_secs=300,14    batch_max_rows=50_000,15)67def stream_sales_changes(17    orders: TableFramesSpec,18    customers: TableFramesSpec,19) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec, TableFrameSpec]:8    return concat(orders), concat(customers)
```

-   Defines the stream source, output Tables, and the conditions that make a batch due.
    
    -   Reads changes continuously from Postgres. The Collection's Connection provides the server address and credentials.
        
    -   Each tracked table is one source slot, in the order listed.
        
    -   Tabsdata Tables that receive the values returned by the function.
        
    -   A batch is due after five minutes or when 50,000 rows are waiting, whichever happens first after the minimum interval.
        
-   Receives one list of frames per source slot and returns one frame per output Table.
    
    -   The arguments receive the frames collected for each source slot since the previous batch.
        
    -   `concat` combines each slot's frames. The returned values map to `output_tables` in order.
        

## The function

A stream publisher function has one parameter per source slot, annotated `TableFramesSpec`, and returns one `TableFrameSpec` per output table.

-   **Slots.** A CDC source has one slot per entry in its `tables`, in the same order. A Kafka source has a single slot.
-   **Parameters.** Each parameter receives a list of frames with the data read for that slot since the previous batch. For a CDC source, the list holds at most one frame. For Kafka, it can hold several, possibly with different schemas; combine them with `concat(frames, how="diagonal_relaxed")` if their columns can differ.
-   **Empty batches.** A slot with no new data receives an empty list. `concat` of an empty list returns `None`.
-   **Return value.** A tuple with one element per output table, in the order of `output_tables`. With a single output table, the frame can be returned on its own. Returning `None` for a table means no new data: it commits a new version that holds the same data as the previous version.
-   **No other parameters.** A stream publisher cannot declare a `ctx` parameter or any parameter beyond its slots.

`concat` is imported from `tabsdatak.tableframe.functions`.

## Lifecycle

-   **Register.** `tdk fn register` starts the worker. The function must be registered in a source collection whose connection matches the source; see the source's connector page.
-   **Disable and enable.** `tdk stream disable` stops the worker; `tdk stream enable` starts it again, from where it stopped. `tdk stream list` shows the stream publishers and their state.
-   **Update.** `tdk fn update` restarts the worker with the new code and settings. It resumes from where it stopped.
-   **Delete.** Deleting the function stops the worker. Check the source's connector page for anything left on the source system, such as a Postgres replication slot.
-   **Failures.** If the worker fails, Tabsdata restarts it, waiting one minute after the first failure and doubling the wait after each further failure, up to 30 minutes.
-   **Start over.** `tdk fn update --reset-stage` discards the stream's recorded position. The stream starts again as if it were new: from the source's starting position, or with a new full load for a CDC source with `start_from="full"`.

On a restart, the stream reads again whatever it had not yet handed to the function. A CDC stream publishes every change once, even across restarts. A Kafka stream is at least once: after a restart, some messages may be published again.

### CDC full load

The full load of a CDC source (`start_from="full"`) is not subject to the batch parameters. It is handed to the function as one batch, covering every tracked table, as soon as it has been read. If the load fails or is interrupted, it is discarded and runs again from the start. The batch parameters apply to the changes that follow.

## `flush_interval_mins` (deprecated)

`flush_interval_mins` was the only batch setting before 2.2.0. It is deprecated, and is converted to `batch_max_secs = flush_interval_mins * 60`, so it must be at least `1`.

-   It cannot be combined with any `batch_*` parameter. Doing so raises error `API_30`.
-   It raises a Python `DeprecationWarning` when the function is decorated, and the worker logs a warning when it starts. Python hides `DeprecationWarning` by default, so the worker log is where the warning shows.

To migrate, replace `flush_interval_mins=N` with `batch_max_secs=N * 60`.

---

# Transformers

> How @transformer reads Tabsdata tables, maps versions to function parameters, and commits transformed output tables.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/functions/transformers

A transformer reads Tabsdata tables, transforms their data, and writes the result back to Tabsdata. It does not read or write an external system, so it does not use a connection.

## In Action

collection · world

collection · insights · data product

Table

country

//world

Committed

Table

//world

Committed

Transformer

find\_big\_cities

Table

big\_cities

//insights

## Parameters

```python
transformer(
    input_tables,
    output_tables,
    trigger_by=None,
    on_tables=None,
)
```

| Parameter | Type |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `input_tables` | `list[str]` | required |
| `output_tables` | `list[str]` | required |
| `trigger_by` | `CronTrigger \| TablesTrigger \| AllTablesTrigger` | optional |
| `on_tables` | `list[OnTablesAction]` | optional |

#### `input_tables`

A non-empty list of table references in the form `[collection/]table[@versions]`. Omit the collection for a table in the transformer's collection. Use `@versions` to select a version, a version range, a comma-separated list, or `NEW`.

Each entry maps to one function parameter. A single-version reference receives a `TableFrameSpec`; a reference that selects several versions receives a `TableFramesSpec`.

#### `output_tables`

A non-empty list of local table names, one for each value returned by the function. The output tables belong to the transformer's collection. Each name must start with a letter, contain only letters, numbers, and underscores, and be no longer than 64 characters.

#### `trigger_by`

The trigger that starts the transformer automatically: a `CronTrigger`, `TablesTrigger`, or `AllTablesTrigger`. Without `trigger_by`, a commit to any input table triggers the transformer. A transformer can also be run manually.

The trigger decides when the function runs. The version selector in `input_tables` decides which versions it reads. See [Execution & Triggers](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/execution-and-triggers).

#### `on_tables`

Actions to run on the output tables after the transformer succeeds, such as [data quality](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/data-quality) checks.

## Transformer Code Anatomy

find\_big\_cities.py

```
1from tabsdatak.api import transformer, TableFrameSpec2import tabsdatak.api.tableframe as tdf3 4 1@transformer(2    input_tables=["world/country", "world/city"],3    output_tables=["big_cities"],8)45def find_big_cities(country: TableFrameSpec, city: TableFrameSpec) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec]:6    countries = country.rename({"name": "country_name"}).drop(11        ["population", "continent"]12    )13    joined = city.join(countries, left_on="country_code", right_on="code")7    return (joined.filter(tdf.col("population") > 3_000_000),)
```

-   Defines the input and output Tables for the Transformer.
    
    -   Tabsdata Tables to read. Use `collection/table` to reference a Table in another Collection.
        
    -   Tables where the transformed data is written. These belong to the Transformer's Collection.
        
-   Reads the country and city data, joins it, and returns cities with a population above three million.
    
    -   The arguments receive the data from `input_tables` in the order listed. An argument is `None` if the requested Table version does not exist.
        
    -   Renames the country name column, removes unused columns, and joins the country and city data.
        
    -   The returned data is written to the Tables listed in `output_tables`, in that order. Returning `None` for a Table leaves its current version unchanged.
        

## The function

A transformer function has one parameter per input table and returns one frame per output table.

-   **Parameters.** Inputs are passed to the function in `input_tables` order. Annotate a parameter as `TableFrameSpec` for one frame or `TableFramesSpec` for a list of frames. An input read at `@NEW`, a `v..v` range or a `v,v` list must be typed `TableFramesSpec`; `TableFrameSpec` is refused at registration. An input is `None` when the requested version does not exist or has no data; see [`None` inputs and outputs](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/functions/#none-inputs-and-outputs).
-   **Context.** The function can have a final `ctx: TransactionCtx` parameter to keep values between successful runs. Type it `FunctionCtx` to also read the run's identifiers and the project's secrets.
-   **Return value.** Return values map to `output_tables` in order. One output can be returned on its own; several outputs are returned as a tuple. Returning `None` for one output commits a new version that keeps that table's previous data.

Tabsdata checks the input count, output count, and function signature when the transformer is registered.

## Collections and table versions

A transformer can read tables from its own collection or another collection. Its output tables are always local to the collection where the transformer is registered.

Table references are resolved when a run starts. When a trigger starts a larger execution plan, Tabsdata passes the versions produced for that transaction through the plan so downstream transformers read a consistent set of data.

## Lifecycle

-   **Register.** `tdk fn register` uploads the transformer to its collection. No connection is required.
-   **Run.** A manual, scheduled, or table trigger starts a transaction and resolves the requested input versions.
-   **Commit.** A successful run commits the output tables together. Each commit adds a table version.
-   **Update.** `tdk fn update` replaces the code and decorator settings.
-   **Delete.** Deleting the function stops future runs but does not delete its output tables or their versions.

For step-by-step guidance on building a transformer, see [Transformers](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/transformers) under How-to Guides.

---

# Subscribers

> How @subscriber reads Tabsdata tables, maps function returns to destination slots, and writes to an external system.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/functions/subscribers

A subscriber reads Tabsdata tables and writes to an external system. The function can filter, rename, or otherwise prepare the data before it is written.

A subscriber belongs to a destination collection. That collection's connection provides the address and credentials for the destination.

## In Action

## Parameters

```python
subscriber(
    destination,
    input_tables,
    trigger_by=None,
)
```

| Parameter | Type |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `destination` | `Dest` | required |
| `input_tables` | `list[str]` | required |
| `trigger_by` | `CronTrigger \| TablesTrigger \| AllTablesTrigger` | optional |

#### `destination`

The destination to write to. The destination class decides where the data is written and how many slots the function must return.

The destination uses the connection of the collection where the subscriber is registered. The page for each connector lists its destination classes and settings.

#### `input_tables`

A non-empty list of table references in the form `[collection/]table[@versions]`. Omit the collection for a table in the subscriber's collection. Use `@versions` to select a version, a version range, a comma-separated list, or `NEW`.

Each entry maps to one function parameter, in list order.

#### `trigger_by`

The trigger that starts the subscriber automatically: a `CronTrigger`, `TablesTrigger`, or `AllTablesTrigger`. Without `trigger_by`, a commit to any input table triggers the subscriber. A subscriber can also be run manually.

The trigger decides when the function runs. The version selector in `input_tables` decides which data it sends. See [Execution & Triggers](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/execution-and-triggers).

## Subscriber Code Anatomy

sales-sub.py

```
1from tabsdatak.api import subscriber, TableFrameSpec2import tabsdatak.api.tableframe as tdf3from tabsdatak.conn.mysql import MySQLDest4 5 1@subscriber(2    destination=MySQLDest(8        tables=["vendors", "items"],9        if_table_exists="replace",10    ),3    input_tables=["sales/vendors", "sales/items"],12)45def write_sales(vendors: TableFrameSpec, items: TableFrameSpec):6    vendors = vendors.filter(tdf.col("active") == 1)7    return (vendors, items)
```

-   Defines the input Tables and destination for the Subscriber.
    
    -   Writes data to the external system. The Collection's Connection provides the address and credentials.
        
    -   Tabsdata Tables to read. This Subscriber reads `vendors` and `items` from the `sales` Collection.
        
-   Receives the input data and returns the data to write to MySQL.
    
    -   The `vendors` and `items` arguments receive the data from `input_tables` in the order listed.
        
    -   Filters the vendors to include only active vendors.
        
    -   The returned data is written to the destination Tables in the order listed in `tables`. Returning `None` for a Table skips the write.
        

## The function

A subscriber function has one parameter per input table and returns one frame per destination slot.

-   **Parameters.** Inputs are passed to the function in `input_tables` order. Annotate a parameter as `TableFrameSpec` for one frame or `TableFramesSpec` for a list of frames. An input read at `@NEW`, a `v..v` range or a `v,v` list must be typed `TableFramesSpec`; `TableFrameSpec` is refused at registration. An input is `None` when the requested version does not exist or has no data; see [`None` inputs and outputs](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/functions/#none-inputs-and-outputs).
-   **Context.** The function can have a final `ctx: TransactionCtx` parameter to keep values between successful runs. Type it `FunctionCtx` to also read the run's identifiers and the project's secrets.
-   **Return value.** Return values map to the destination slots in destination order. One slot can be returned on its own; several slots are returned as a tuple. Returning `None` for a slot sends no new data to it, and the Connector decides what that does to the external system.
-   **Slot counts.** The number of input tables does not have to match the number of destination slots. The function can combine several inputs into one write or create several destination tables from one input.

Tabsdata checks the slot counts and function signature when the subscriber is registered.

## Connections and collections

All subscribers in a destination collection use the same connection. Each subscriber has its own input tables, destination settings, and code.

Input tables can come from the subscriber's collection or another collection. Updating the collection's connection changes how every subscriber in that collection reaches the external system.

## Lifecycle

-   **Register.** `tdk fn register` uploads the subscriber. Its collection and connection must already exist.
-   **Run.** A manual, scheduled, or table trigger starts a transaction and resolves the requested input versions.
-   **Write.** The function's returned frames are handed to the destination. The transaction succeeds only after the destination write succeeds.
-   **Update.** `tdk fn update` replaces the code and decorator settings.
-   **Delete.** Deleting the function stops future writes. It does not remove data already written to the external system.

For step-by-step guides on building a subscriber for a specific external system, see [Subscribers](https://docs.tabsdata.com/tutorials/subscribers/) under How-to Guides.

For inserts, updates, and deletes into Snowflake, BigQuery, or Databricks, see [Merging into SQL destinations](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/functions/sql-merge).

# Tables

> Covers Tabsdata Tables as persistent, versioned stores of function output: version history, the table reference format (`collection/table@version` with HEAD, INITIAL, and ranges), private `_` tables, and commit-based triggers.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/tables

Tables are a unique feature of Tabsdata. Unlike other data integration tools that discard intermediate data after execution, Tabsdata stores the data produced by functions in persistent, versioned Tables.

Tables make it easier to monitor and debug workflows, inspect data from previous executions, track schema changes over time, and understand how data moves through a Project.

Because Tables persist between executions, they can also be used as inputs by other functions and allow Tabsdata to automatically orchestrate workflows based on new data being committed.

## Table Versions

Every Table maintains a complete version history. Each successful function execution that writes data to a Table creates a new **version** containing its own data and schema.

Previous versions remain available, allowing users and functions to access the state of a Table from a specific execution. Each version also includes metadata about the execution that produced it and the function code used during that execution.

persons

Tabsdata›Collections›input›persons

### Schema

Table schema defines the structure of a table by listing its columns and their data types.

| Object | Type |
| --- | --- |
| first\_name | str |
| last\_name | str |
| age | i64 |
| nationality | str |
| city | str |

version

Because each Table version maintains its own schema, schema changes between executions do not cause previous versions of the Table to become invalid.

## Tables in Action

Tables store the data that moves through a Tabsdata workflow. Functions read from and write to Tables depending on their role in the workflow.

Publisher functions ingest data from external systems and write it to Tabsdata Tables.

## Referring to a Table

Functions refer to their input Tables using the following format:

`[collection/]table[@version]`

If the Collection is omitted, Tabsdata looks for the Table within the Function's own Collection.

For example:

```text
persons
input/persons
input/persons@HEAD
```

The version can be used to select a specific version or set of versions of the Table:

-   `HEAD` selects the latest version.
-   `HEAD^` selects the version immediately before `HEAD`.
-   `HEAD~N` selects a version relative to `HEAD`.
-   `INITIAL` selects the first version.
-   A specific version ID selects that version.
-   Comma-separated version IDs select multiple versions.
-   `a..b` selects a range of versions.

If no version is specified, the Function reads from `HEAD`.

Tables can also be referenced across Collections within the same Project. Tables in another Project cannot be referenced.

## Private Tables

Tables whose names begin with `_` are **private Tables**.

Private Tables can only be read by Functions within their own Collection. This makes them useful for intermediate data that needs to move between Functions in a Collection without being accessible to the rest of the Project.

For example:

```text
_cleaned_customers
```

A Function in the same Collection can use `_cleaned_customers` as an input, while Functions in other Collections cannot access it.

## Tables and Triggers

A new Table commit can also trigger downstream Functions.

Transformers and Subscribers are automatically triggered when a new commit is made to one of their input Tables. This allows data to continue moving through a workflow as upstream Functions complete.

A commit does not necessarily mean that the data itself changed. When a Publisher writes multiple Tables, it creates a new commit for each Table on every successful execution, even if the rows in a Table are identical to its previous version.

Each commit can trigger Functions that use that Table as an input.

See [Working with Triggers](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/triggers) to control which input Tables trigger a Function.
