# Execution Plans

> Explains the execution plan DAG Tabsdata builds when a Function is triggered, how Functions pass data through Tables, determinism, and the tdk plan, trx, fnrun, and worker commands.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/execution/execution-plans

An **execution plan** is the Directed Acyclic Graph that Tabsdata automatically builds and executes whenever a function is triggered.

Tabsdata Functions are self describing, allowing Tabsdata to infer a Function's dependencies and automatically fire it when needed.

## How Tabsdata Automates Orchestration

In other systems, DAG nodes need to be manually wired together, with explicit declaration of what data one node passes to the other.

In Tabsdata, Functions never directly pass data to other Functions. Instead, Functions write tabular data into Tables and other Functions use those tables as input. When a Table gets new data, all functions that use it as input get triggered.

tip

Your Functions are also your data flow. Click on a Publisher, Transformer, or Subscriber to see the Execution Plan that is created if that Function is triggered.

Click any node to trace its dependencies

## Determinism

Execution plans are idempotent and deterministic. When an execution plan is generated, it contains a full snapshot of metadata and configurations used for the plan; such as start and stop timestamps, function code used for the plan, source data ingested, Table data generated, and data written out of Tabsdata

## Execution Plan Architecture

An Execution Plan is a DAG of all Functions Tabsdata intends to execute. A plan contains transactions, function runs, and workers. Click into each resource to learn more about what they do.

A function is triggered

creates

[Execution plan](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/execution/execution-plans)One per function triggered

[Transactions](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/execution/transactions)One per collection in the execution plan

[Function runs](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/execution/function-runs)One per function in the transaction

[Workers](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/execution/workers)One per attempted code execution (max 3)

## Inspecting a plan

Four commands cover the four levels: `tdk plan`, `tdk trx`, `tdk fnrun`, and `tdk worker`. See the [CLI Guide](https://docs.tabsdata.com/cli/tdk/#execution) for what each one accepts.

[Execution & Triggers](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/execution-and-triggers) covers what fires a plan in the first place, along with the pristine-state guarantee it carries.

---

# Transactions

> Explains how transactions group Table changes within a Collection so they commit together, preserve pristine state on failure, and make execution plans multi-transactional across Collections.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/execution/transactions

A **transaction** groups together changes made to Tables within a Collection during an [execution plan](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/execution/execution-plans). These changes are committed together, meaning they become available at the same time.

Transactions help Tabsdata maintain **pristine state**. If an execution plan fails before a transaction is committed, its output is not published and the affected Tables remain in their previous state. This prevents incomplete or partially processed data from becoming available to users or downstream Functions.

See [Execution & Triggers](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/execution-and-triggers) for more information about pristine state.

## Collection Transactions

In Tabsdata, a Collection acts as a transaction boundary.

When an execution plan processes Functions within a Collection, changes made to that Collection's Tables are grouped into a transaction. Once the transaction is successfully committed, all of those changes become available together.

This ensures that users and other Functions do not read a Collection while only some of its Tables have been updated.

## Transactions Across Collections

A single execution plan can process Functions across multiple Collections. Because each Collection has its own transaction, an execution plan may contain multiple transactions.

For example, if an execution plan processes Functions across three Collections, each Collection handles and commits its Table changes through its own transaction.

This is why execution plans in Tabsdata are **multi-transactional**.

---

# Function Runs

> Function Runs cover how each Function execution in an Execution Plan is tracked, including status, logs, Worker assignment, recovery, and replay, with CLI commands linked.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/execution/function-runs

A **Function Run** represents a single execution of a Function in Tabsdata.

Whenever a Function is executed as part of an [Execution Plan](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/execution/execution-plans), Tabsdata creates a Function Run to track that individual execution. If an Execution Plan contains multiple Functions, each Function gets its own Function Run.

Function Runs allow Tabsdata to track the execution of each Function independently, including its status, logs, inputs, outputs, and the Worker responsible for executing it.

## Function Runs in an Execution Plan

An Execution Plan describes the set of Functions that need to run and the order in which they need to run. Function Runs represent the individual executions that take place within that plan.

For example, an Execution Plan containing a Publisher, Transformer, and Subscriber would create a separate Function Run for each Function:

```text
Execution Plan
├── Publisher Function Run
├── Transformer Function Run
└── Subscriber Function Run
```

This makes it possible to see the status of each individual Function rather than only whether the Execution Plan as a whole succeeded or failed.

## Function Runs and Workers

Function Runs are executed by [Workers](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/execution/workers).

When a Function is ready to run, Tabsdata assigns its Function Run to a Worker. The Worker performs the actual processing required by the Function and reports the status of the Function Run back to Tabsdata.

This separation allows multiple Function Runs to be processed independently and, when possible, in parallel. Runs of the same function run one at a time, in trigger order (best effort). In case of failures, function runs can be assigned to new workers and retried.

## Function Runs and Transactions

The data produced by a Function Run is written as part of a [Transaction](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/execution/transactions).

A successful Function Run can produce changes to one or more Tables, but those changes do not become available simply because the Function Run finished. They become available when the Transaction containing those changes is committed.

This allows Tabsdata to keep the execution of an individual Function separate from the process of publishing its output.

## Function Run Status

Each Function Run has its own status throughout its execution.

This makes Function Runs useful for understanding where an Execution Plan is currently running or where a failure occurred. If one Function fails in a plan containing several Functions, you can identify the specific Function Run that failed and inspect its logs without treating the Execution Plan as a single unit.

## Recovery and Replay

Because each Function execution is tracked as its own Function Run, Tabsdata can operate on individual runs after they have been created.

A failed Function Run can be **recovered**, allowing Tabsdata to retry that execution without starting the entire workflow again.

A completed Function Run can also be **replayed**, allowing the Function to execute again using the same inputs. Functions can be replayed even if the source data the function relies on has changed.

## Inspecting Function Runs

Function Runs can be inspected through an AI agent connected to Tabsdata, to view their status, logs, and other execution information.

AI agent session

❯Show me the logs for function run fr-3f9a2c1e

Called tabsdata 1 time (ctrl+o to expand)

⏺

Here's fr-3f9a2c1e's log.

❯What's its status?

Called tabsdata 1 time (ctrl+o to expand)

⏺

fr-3f9a2c1e is a Transformer run and finished successfully.

See the [CLI Guide](https://docs.tabsdata.com/cli/tdk/#execution) for the complete set of commands for inspecting, recovering, and replaying Function Runs.

---

# Workers

> Explains what a Tabsdata worker is, how retries work (three attempts by default), and the tdk worker logs, recover, and list commands with their filters.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/execution/workers

A **worker** is the process that executes the code defined in a Tabsdata 

Each worker runs as an isolated process on the Tabsdata server's Kubernetes cluster. Performance optimizations such as Polars Streaming and Lazy Evaluation allow workers to process datasets incrementally, allowing them to handle datasets larger than the memory available on the machine's hardware.

## Retries

Tabsdata deploys one worker for each execution attempt of the function code. If a worker fails, Tabsdata snapshots the worker's execution log and spins up a new worker to retry the execution. By default, a function run will attempt three executions before stalling.

A function is triggered

Function runGenerated by the trigger

Worker 1Failed

Worker 2Failed

Worker 3Succeeded

Three workers is the default limit. Had the third one failed as well, the function run would stall instead of starting a fourth.

## Logs

A worker is where a function's output ends up, so its logs are the first place to look when a function run fails:

```bash
$ tdk worker logs --worker WID
```

Pass `--file -` to write the log to stdout.

## Recovery

You can retry a single worker without re-running the whole plan:

```bash
$ tdk worker recover --worker WID
```

## Finding a worker

`tdk worker list` filters down from any level of the plan, so you can start from whichever identifier you already have:

```bash
$ tdk worker list [--status R] [--coll C] [--fn F] [--plan P] [--trx T] [--fnrun FR]
```

See the [CLI Guide](https://docs.tabsdata.com/cli/tdk/#execution) for the full set of commands and the status codes each accepts.

---

# Connectors

> The connectors built into Tabsdata, and the source and destination classes each one provides.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connectors/

A **connector** is the set of Python classes Tabsdata uses to read from or write to one external system. Every built-in connector is part of the `tabsdatak.conn` package and provides a source class, a destination class, or both, along with the connection types that hold the system's address and credentials.

A publisher uses a connector's source class to read from the external system and write into Tabsdata tables. A subscriber uses a connector's destination class to read from Tabsdata tables and write out to the external system. Neither class stores credentials. The address and credentials live on the [connection](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connections) of the collection the function is registered in, so the same connection is shared by every publisher or subscriber in that collection.

Kafka and the three CDC connectors provide a stream source class instead of a source class. A [stream publisher](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/functions/stream-publishers) uses a stream source to consume the external system continuously, and runs each time a batch of messages or changes rolls over instead of on a manual, cron, or table trigger.

## Built-in connectors

Each connector's page covers its connection fields and the options of its classes, and links to a full walkthrough in Tutorials.

# Schema Evolution

> What strict and update do when a write brings a new column or a wider type, per table destination: the write behavior matrix, type widening, native and Iceberg schema evolution, and the permissions update needs.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connectors/schema-evolution

Every table destination takes a `schema_evolution` setting that decides what happens when a write brings a column the destination table does not have, or a value type wider than the column's. The table destinations are Databricks, Snowflake, BigQuery, ClickHouse, StarRocks, Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB, Microsoft SQL Server, Oracle and Db2. The same two values apply to append, replace and merge on all of them, but what each one does differs by destination. Druid cannot enforce a schema, so `"update"` is its only value and its default.

## Policies

`schema_evolution` takes one of two values:

| Value | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `"strict"` | Refuses a new column, and refuses a wider type unless its values fit the column, with error `SQL_COMMON_10`, before any data is loaded. |
| `"update"` | Adds new columns, widens types and makes columns nullable. It never drops or reorders columns. |

Under either value, a column the batch lacks is written as NULL on append and keeps its stored value on merge.

Renamed in 2.3.0

ClickHouse and StarRocks called `update` `"iceberg"` before 2.3.0. A function that still sets `schema_evolution="iceberg"` fails validation after the upgrade; change it to `"update"`.

## Behavior per destination

What each destination does with a new or wider column, and how it carries out `replace`:

| Destination | `strict` append | `strict` replace | `strict` merge | `update` | `replace` mechanism | `replace` atomic |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Databricks | Fails in `COPY INTO` (`DATABRICKS_9`) | Schema follows the batch | Refused before the `MERGE` (`SQL_COMMON_10`) | Append: `mergeSchema` and `delta.enableTypeWidening`. Merge: `MERGE WITH SCHEMA EVOLUTION` and widening | `CREATE OR REPLACE … read_files() LIMIT 0`, then `COPY INTO` | No |
| Snowflake | Refused before `COPY` | Refused: the schema check runs before the `TRUNCATE` | Refused | Append and replace: native `ENABLE_SCHEMA_EVOLUTION`, adds columns and makes columns nullable. Merge: Iceberg engine, set in `dest_cfg`; `ALTER` adds columns and widens `VARCHAR` length and `NUMBER` precision | `TRUNCATE`, then `COPY INTO`; the table definition is kept | No |
| BigQuery | Fails in the load job (`BIGQUERY_7`) | Schema replaced | Refused | Append and replace: native, adds columns and relaxes `REQUIRED`, never widens. Merge: Iceberg engine, set in `dest_cfg`; `ALTER` adds and widens, and `REQUIRED` stays `REQUIRED` | `WRITE_TRUNCATE` load job | Yes |
| ClickHouse | Refused before the load on a new column, a wider type whose values do not fit, or a NULL into a non-`Nullable` column. Column order is ignored, a narrower type fits, a missing column is NULL | Schema follows the batch | Not supported | Adds `Nullable` columns, makes columns nullable, widens `Int8` up to `Int64`, `UInt` likewise, and `Float32` to `Float64` | Stage, `DROP TABLE IF EXISTS`, `CREATE … MergeTree() ORDER BY tuple()`, `INSERT` by name | No |
| StarRocks | Refused before the load on a new column, or a wider type whose values do not fit. A missing column gets its default or NULL | Same check, then `TRUNCATE` and `INSERT`; the table must exist | Not supported | `ADD COLUMN … NULL`; `MODIFY COLUMN` widens integers, `FLOAT` to `DOUBLE`, `VARCHAR` and `DECIMAL`, waiting up to 30 minutes for the `ALTER` job | `TRUNCATE`, then `INSERT … SELECT FROM FILES()` | No |
| Druid | Refused at registration | Refused at registration | Not supported | The default and only value: schema discovery adds columns, and a missing column reads as NULL | `index_parallel` with `dropExisting` over 1970 to 2100 | Per datasource |
| Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server, Oracle, Db2 | Refused on a new column, or a wider type whose values do not fit (`SQL_COMMON_10`) | Schema follows the batch | Not supported | `ALTER TABLE … ADD`; widens integers, decimals and floats by digits or width. Db2 then runs `REORG`. No drops, and no retyping of non-number columns | `DROP TABLE IF EXISTS`, then the table is created on write | Postgres, SQL Server and Db2: inside `transactional`. MySQL, MariaDB and Oracle: no, and their `update` `ALTER`s commit implicitly |

A write to several tables runs one table after another and is not atomic across tables, except on the relational destinations with `transactional=True`. The Databricks and BigQuery merge staging tables are real tables named `<target>_<8 hex characters>`, created next to the target; only Snowflake's is `TEMPORARY`.

## Type widening under `update`

Each destination widens only these types:

| Destination | Widens |
| --- | --- |
| Snowflake | `VARCHAR` length and `NUMBER` precision, on merge |
| BigQuery | `INT64` to `BIGNUMERIC` to `FLOAT64`, on merge |
| ClickHouse | Integers up to 64 bits, signed and unsigned, and `Float32` to `Float64` |
| StarRocks | Integers, `FLOAT` to `DOUBLE`, `VARCHAR` and `DECIMAL` |
| Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server, Oracle, Db2 | Integers, decimals and floats, by digits or width |

A change outside these rules fails the write.

## Native and Iceberg schema evolution

Under `"update"`, a destination changes the table in one of two ways. Native schema evolution is the destination's own: the load or merge statement adds the columns. Iceberg schema evolution is applied by the connector: it compares the incoming and destination schemas following Apache Iceberg's evolution rules, and runs the `ALTER TABLE` statements before the write. It does not convert the destination into an Apache Iceberg table.

| Destination | `append` and `replace` | `merge` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Databricks | Native | Native |
| Snowflake, BigQuery | Native | Iceberg, set in `dest_cfg` |
| ClickHouse, StarRocks, Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server, Oracle, Db2 | Iceberg | Not supported |
| Druid | Native | Not supported |

Snowflake's and BigQuery's native schema evolution adds columns and makes columns nullable, but never widens a type, and does not apply to `MERGE`. A Snowflake or BigQuery merge under `"update"` needs the Iceberg engine set in `dest_cfg`:

```python
dest_cfg={"snowflake.schema_evolution_engine": "iceberg"}
dest_cfg={"bigquery.schema_evolution_engine": "iceberg"}
```

Without it, the merge is refused at registration. The engine setting is accepted only on a Snowflake or BigQuery merge under `"update"`; on any other write mode or destination, and under `"strict"`, registration refuses `<database>.schema_evolution_engine`.

## Permissions

`update` needs permission to `ALTER` the destination table. Db2 also runs `REORG` through `ADMIN_CMD` after an `ALTER`, and BigQuery creates and deletes a temporary external table. On the relational destinations, `replace` drops and recreates the table, so it needs `DROP` and `CREATE`.

See [Merge into SQL destinations](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/functions/sql-merge) for merge, and each destination's page for its other settings.

# Object Store Options

> The obstore.* keys that configure the object store behind the file connectors and the staging locations: which keys each provider takes, where they are set, and what they override.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connectors/object-store-options

Several connectors read or write cloud object storage through an object store client. Keys that start with `obstore.` configure that client. Set them where the connector takes its other settings: `conn_cfg` on the connection for the file connectors, and `cfg` on the `staging` location for ClickHouse, StarRocks and Druid.

## Where the keys apply

| Connector | Set with | What the keys configure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob Storage | `conn_cfg` on the connection | Reads and writes |
| ClickHouse | `cfg` on the `staging` location | The staging upload, the address ClickHouse reads the files from, and the cleanup |
| StarRocks | `cfg` on the `staging` location | The staging upload. StarRocks reads the files through its own path, which the keys do not change |
| Druid | `cfg` on the `staging` location | The staging upload. The ingestion input source does not use them |

On the file connectors, a key in `conn_cfg` overrides the matching credential in the connection. The explorer ignores these keys.

## Keys by provider

| Provider | Keys |
| --- | --- |
| Amazon S3 | `access_key_id`, `secret_access_key`, `session_token`, `region`, `endpoint`, `virtual_hosted_style_request`, `allow_http`, `anonymous`, `skip_signature` |
| Azure Blob Storage | `account_name`, `account_key`, `sas_token`, `endpoint`, `allow_http` |
| Google Cloud Storage | `service_account_key`, `service_account`, `allow_http` |

`service_account` is the path to a key file on the Tabsdata server. Raw option names with the `aws_`, `azure_` or `google_` prefix are accepted as well.

For example, to point an S3 connection at a MinIO server:

```yaml
conn_cfg:
  obstore.endpoint: 'http://minio.internal:9000'
```

On ClickHouse, an unknown `obstore.*` key fails the write.

# Merging into SQL destinations

> How Subscriber Functions apply inserts, updates, and deletes to Snowflake, BigQuery, and Databricks tables.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/functions/sql-merge

When Subscribing data, you may need to dynamically update, delete, and insert records within a single function.

Tabsdata supports **sql merge** writes. Users can specify key columns to match records and an operation column that tells Tabsdata whether to insert, update, or delete each row. The Subscriber returns the changes, and the connector applies them to the destination table.

Merge writes are supported by the [Snowflake](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connectors/snowflake), [BigQuery](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connectors/bigquery), and [Databricks](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connectors/databricks) connectors.

## Merge configuration

To configure a merge, set `if_table_exists="merge"` on the destination and pass a `merge_cfg` list containing the key and operation columns for each table.

For example, this Subscriber reads order changes from Tabsdata and applies them to `ORDERS` in Snowflake:

```python
from tabsdatak.api import subscriber, TableFrameSpec
from tabsdatak.conn.snowflake import MergeCfg, SnowflakeDest


@subscriber(
    destination=SnowflakeDest(
        tables=["ORDERS"],
        if_table_exists="merge",
        merge_cfg=[MergeCfg(on=["order_id"], op_column="op")],
        schema_evolution="update",
        dest_cfg={"snowflake.schema_evolution_engine": "iceberg"},
    ),
    input_tables=["capture/order_changes"],
)
def load_orders(changes: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec:
    return changes
```

Here, `on=["order_id"]` matches records by order ID, while `op_column="op"` identifies the column containing the operation. The Function returns the changes from `capture/order_changes` for the connector to write.

Because a Subscriber can write to several tables, the `MergeCfg` entries must follow the order of `tables`, and both lists must have the same length. Use a list even for a single table. The `merge_cfg` setting is required for merge writes and cannot be used with other write modes.

The `on` setting requires at least one key column, and those columns must exist in both the incoming data and the destination when the merge runs. If several columns form the key, all their values must match.

`MergeCfg` is imported from the same connector module as the destination. On Snowflake and BigQuery, a merge under `schema_evolution="update"` needs `"iceberg"` set as the schema evolution engine in `dest_cfg`. See [Schema evolution](#schema-evolution).

## Row operations

After matching records by key, Tabsdata uses the operation column to decide what to write. In the example above, `op` accepts these values:

| Marker | Operation |
| --- | --- |
| `i` | Insert the row if its key does not exist in the destination. |
| `u` | Update the row matching its key. |
| `d` | Delete the row matching its key. |
| `l` | Load: the row comes from an initial load. The destination is emptied before the load's rows are inserted. |
| `t` | Truncate: the destination is emptied. |

An insert leaves an existing record unchanged, while an update or delete does nothing if the record is missing.

Uppercase `I`, `U`, `D`, `L` and `T` are also accepted, but spaces are not removed, so `" d "` is invalid. Tabsdata removes rows with invalid or null operations before processing the batch.

Because the operation column is used to control the write, Tabsdata excludes it when creating the destination table or updating its schema.

### Load and truncate markers

`l` and `t` reset the table. When a batch contains one, the changes before the last reset are discarded, and the destination's rows are replaced in one statement by what follows it. A CDC stream that uses `start_from="full"` or captures table truncates sends these markers.

## Multiple changes to one record

A record may change several times within the same batch. Tabsdata combines changes with the same key before writing them, using the first and last valid operations to determine the result.

These operations follow the row order in the materialized batch, so the order returned by the Function matters:

| First operation | Last operation | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Insert | Insert or update | Insert using the latest row. |
| Insert | Delete | No destination write for this key. |
| Update or delete | Insert or update | Update using the latest row. |
| Update or delete | Delete | Delete the matching record. |

For example, `i → u → d → i` inserts the latest row because the final change adds the record again. With `i → u → d`, nothing is written because the record was created and deleted in the same batch.

For a delete, Tabsdata keeps the data from the last insert or update for that key, or the first row if all operations are deletes. This allows delete records to contain just the key columns and operation.

The destination therefore receives the combined change, without storing the intermediate changes as history.

## Destination tables and columns

If the destination table does not exist, all three connectors can create it from the staged data's schema, excluding the operation column. The database and schema or dataset must already exist, and the Connection must have the required permissions.

For existing tables, Snowflake and BigQuery write columns shared by the incoming data and the destination. Updates leave the keys unchanged, while inserts include them.

Columns found only in the destination are left unchanged on updates and omitted from inserts, where the destination's defaults and constraints apply.

A batch with a column the destination lacks is refused under `schema_evolution="strict"`, with `SQL_COMMON_10`, before the merge runs; under `update` the column is added. Values written to shared columns must still satisfy the destination's types and constraints.

Databricks handles column matching through Delta's merge rules, and `update` uses `MERGE WITH SCHEMA EVOLUTION`, which excludes the operation column. The operation marker should therefore use a separate column from the data being written.

## Schema evolution

Incoming data may contain new columns or values too large for the destination's current column types. **Schema evolution** controls whether Tabsdata can change the table to accept that data.

Set `schema_evolution` on the destination to choose the behavior. All three destinations default to `"strict"`:

| Setting | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `"strict"` | Refuses a new column, and a wider type unless its values fit the column, with `SQL_COMMON_10`, before the merge runs. A configured watermark column is an exception. |
| `"update"` | Allows new data columns and supported type widening. |

`strict` accepts a wider type when its values fit the column, and an incoming type narrower than the column's. Making a column nullable counts as widening and is refused. A column the batch lacks keeps its stored value. [Schema Evolution](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connectors/schema-evolution) has the same policy for every table destination and write mode.

Snowflake's and BigQuery's native schema evolution does not apply to `MERGE`. A Snowflake or BigQuery merge under `"update"` needs the `iceberg` engine set in `dest_cfg`, and is refused at registration without it:

```python
# SnowflakeDest
dest_cfg={"snowflake.schema_evolution_engine": "iceberg"}

# BigQueryDest
dest_cfg={"bigquery.schema_evolution_engine": "iceberg"}
```

The `iceberg` engine compares the incoming and destination schemas and applies supported changes through `ALTER TABLE`. It controls how schemas are compared; it does not convert the destination into an Apache Iceberg table. Under `"strict"`, a merge that sets the engine is refused at registration.

Databricks uses Delta's `MERGE WITH SCHEMA EVOLUTION` for `schema_evolution="update"`, so it does not require a `schema_evolution_engine` setting. On each merge, Tabsdata also sets the destination table's `delta.enableTypeWidening` property to `true` for `update` or `false` for `strict`.

### Type widening

Type widening allows a column to store larger values, such as longer strings or numbers with greater precision. The supported changes depend on the destination:

| Destination | Supported widening |
| --- | --- |
| Snowflake | Wider `VARCHAR` lengths and greater `NUMBER` precision at the same scale. The connector does not widen between different base types. |
| BigQuery | Supported numeric promotions, including `INT64 → NUMERIC → BIGNUMERIC → FLOAT64`, and wider type parameters. |
| Databricks | Type changes supported by Delta type widening. |

Setting `schema_evolution="update"` allows these supported changes. If the incoming data requires a conversion outside these rules, the write can still fail.

## Retrying a write

A Subscriber may retry a write after data has already reached the destination. To recognize these retries, Tabsdata can store the Transaction ID in a **watermark column**. If that ID is already in the table, Tabsdata skips the write.

Set `watermark_column` on the destination to enable this check:

```python
SnowflakeDest(
    tables=["ORDERS"],
    if_table_exists="merge",
    merge_cfg=[MergeCfg(on=["order_id"], op_column="op")],
    watermark_column="wm",
)
```

The configured name applies to all tables listed in the destination. If the column is missing, Tabsdata adds it even when `schema_evolution="strict"`. Existing rows have `NULL` in the new column, while inserted and updated rows receive the current Transaction ID.

The watermark name must differ from the key columns and operation column, following the destination's rules for uppercase and lowercase names. Watermarks work with `append` and `merge`, but not with `replace`.

Retries use the same Transaction ID, while new Transactions have different IDs and write normally. The check depends on a matching ID remaining in the destination. A batch containing only deletes leaves no new watermark value.

## Connector differences

The connectors differ in how they stage data, change schemas, and match column names:

| Behavior | Snowflake | BigQuery | Databricks |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Staging | Snowflake stage, then a `TEMPORARY` table | GCS, then a staging table `<target>_<8 hex characters>` beside the target | Unity Catalog volume, then a staging table `<target>_<8 hex characters>` beside the target |
| Schema changes under `update` | Connector applies `ALTER TABLE` using Iceberg schema comparison | Connector applies `ALTER TABLE` using Iceberg schema comparison | Delta merge schema evolution |
| Engine for merge | `iceberg`, required under `update` | `iceberg`, required under `update` | No engine setting |
| Column names | Unquoted names resolve as uppercase; double quotes preserve case | Case-insensitive; backticks quote names | Case-insensitive; backticks quote names |

The BigQuery and Databricks staging tables are real tables, so the Connection needs permission to create and drop them, and a run that is killed can leave one behind.

For example, Snowflake resolves an unquoted `order_id` as uppercase, so `on=["order_id"]` matches a stored `ORDER_ID` column. BigQuery and Databricks match column names without considering case, including when those names are quoted.

BigQuery also requires destination table names to be enclosed in backticks, as in ``tables=["`orders`"]``.

## Errors

Tabsdata checks the configuration before writing and validates the incoming data during execution. The following conditions can cause the merge to fail:

| Condition | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Merge mode without `merge_cfg`, or `merge_cfg` without merge mode | Configuration error. |
| `merge_cfg` is not a list, or its length differs from `tables` | Configuration error. |
| Empty `on`, or an operation column that matches a key | Configuration error. |
| Snowflake or BigQuery merge under `update` without `schema_evolution_engine="iceberg"`, or under `strict` with an engine set | Refused at registration. |
| The same table listed twice in `tables` | Refused at registration (`CONN_37`). Databricks compares names ignoring case, Snowflake folds unquoted parts to uppercase, and BigQuery compares them verbatim. |
| A watermark with `replace`, or a watermark name that matches a key or operation column | Configuration error. |
| Missing operation or key columns in the incoming batch | Runtime error. |
| A new column, or a wider type whose values do not fit, under `strict` | Refused before the merge (`SQL_COMMON_10`). |
| No shared data columns between the batch and destination | Runtime error. |
| Several incoming columns match the same configured column name | Runtime error. |

For field definitions, see the `MergeCfg` API reference for [Snowflake](https://docs.tabsdata.com/api/category/connectors/destination/mergecfg-snowflake), [BigQuery](https://docs.tabsdata.com/api/category/connectors/destination/mergecfg-bigquery), and [Databricks](https://docs.tabsdata.com/api/category/connectors/destination/mergecfg-databricks).

# Amazon S3

> Reference for the Tabsdata Amazon S3 connector.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connectors/amazon-s3

The Amazon S3 connector lets Tabsdata read files from and write files to Amazon S3.

The `S3Src` connector can be used by a publisher function to read data from Amazon S3 into a Tabsdata table.

The `S3Dest` connector can be used by a subscriber function to write data from a Tabsdata table into Amazon S3.

## Supported formats

| Format | Publish | Subscribe |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `AUTO` | Yes | Yes |
| `CSV` | Yes | Yes |
| `JSON` | Yes | Yes |
| `AVRO` | Yes | Yes |
| `PARQUET` | Yes | Yes |
| `LOG` | Yes | No |
| `EXCEL` | Yes | No |

## Publisher

The `S3Src` connector can be used by a publisher function to read data from Amazon S3 into a Tabsdata table. [See the full publisher walkthrough](https://docs.tabsdata.com/tutorials/publishers/amazon-s3)

The publisher is registered in a collection created with a `AwsAccessSecretKey` connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in [Publisher connection](#publisher-connection), at the end of this page.

### Prerequisites

-   The bucket exists and is reachable from the Tabsdata server.
-   The AWS principal can list the bucket and read every object matched by `paths`.
-   Compressed objects need `include_compressed=True`; see [`include_compressed`](#include_compressed).

### Publisher

Configure `S3Src` as the `source` of a publisher function to select the files that Tabsdata reads from S3.

publish\_orders.py

```python
from tabsdatak.api import publisher
from tabsdatak.conn.s3 import S3Src, SrcFileFormat

@publisher(
    source=S3Src(
        paths=[
            "incoming/orders.parquet",
        ],
    ),
    output_tables=["orders"],
)
def publish_orders(orders):
    return orders
```

-   required
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    

### Function Config Parameters

#### `paths`

Defines the files that the publisher reads from S3.

Each path is relative to the `base_path` configured in `S3SrcConn`. Source paths:

-   cannot begin or end with `/`
-   cannot contain empty path segments
-   cannot be `.` or `..`, or contain a `${...}` token
-   can contain a `*` glob in the final path segment. `*` matches any run of characters and `?` matches one character; in directory segments, both are literal.

For example:

```python
S3Src(
    paths=[
        "orders/2026/*.parquet",
        "customers/customers.csv",
    ]
)
```

Each element in `paths` represents one source slot and maps positionally to an argument in the publisher function.

When a path uses a glob to match multiple files, the matching files are provided through the corresponding publisher input.

#### `format`

Sets the format used to read the source files.

Supported formats are `AUTO`, `CSV`, `JSON`, `AVRO`, `PARQUET`, `LOG`, and `EXCEL`. The default is `AUTO`, which determines the format from the file extension. `AUTO` resolves the format for each file from its own extension. For a compressed file, that is the extension before the compression extension. A file whose extension names no format fails the run. A source whose files resolve to different formats also fails the run. `EXCEL` reads `.xlsx` workbooks only. Pick a sheet with a `#n` suffix on the path, such as `paths=["book.xlsx#2"]`; the sheet number starts at 1 and counts hidden sheets, and `#0` is refused. Its `format_cfg` takes `has_header`.

#### `format_cfg`

Sets format-specific reader options. Configuration is keyed by `SrcFileFormat`.

For `CSV`, `has_header=False` reads the first row as data. The columns are then named `column_0`, `column_1`, ... `skip_lines` skips that many lines at the start of each file before the header is read. A `""` field is read as an empty string.

#### `include_compressed`

When `True`, the publisher reads compressed objects. A path that ends in a compression extension fails validation without it. The compression extensions are `.gz`, `.zlib`, `.zst`, `.zstd`, `.bz2`, `.xz`, `.lz4` and `.br`, plus single-entry `.zip` and `.tar` archives. The format comes from the name before the compression extension, so `orders.csv.gz` is read as CSV. An archive must hold one file, and a name can have only one compression extension.

#### `purge`

When `True`, the publisher deletes each matched object that the cursor skipped, if its modification time is at or after `initial_last_modified`. `purge` requires `initial_last_modified`; without it the run fails with `FILE_COMMON_35`. Deletion runs for each slot after that slot's frames are read.

warning

`purge` deletes data, including a late object that the cursor skipped before the publisher ever read it. It needs delete permission on the source objects.

#### `initial_last_modified`

Sets the initial cutoff for incremental ingestion.

On the first run, Tabsdata imports files modified at or after the specified timestamp. The cutoff then advances so subsequent runs only import newer files. The value must be timezone-aware, for example `datetime(2026, 1, 1, tzinfo=timezone.utc)`.

#### `src_cfg`

Sets additional source configuration.

The following options are supported:

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `tabsdata.src_metadata.drop` | When `True`, excludes the `@td.file.path` metadata column. |

By default, rows read from S3 include a `@td.file.path` metadata column containing the `s3://` URI of the file the row was read from.

## Subscriber

The `S3Dest` connector can be used by a subscriber function to write data from a Tabsdata table into Amazon S3. [See the full subscriber walkthrough](https://docs.tabsdata.com/tutorials/subscribers/amazon-s3)

The subscriber is registered in a collection created with a `AwsAccessSecretKey` connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in [Subscriber connection](#subscriber-connection), at the end of this page.

### Prerequisites

-   The bucket exists and is reachable from the Tabsdata server.
-   The AWS principal can write objects under the configured `base_path`.
-   The destination path is relative and does not contain a glob.

### Subscriber

Configure `S3Dest` as the `destination` of a subscriber function to define where Tabsdata writes files in S3.

write\_orders.py

```python
from tabsdatak.api import subscriber
from tabsdatak.conn.s3 import S3Dest, DestFileFormat

@subscriber(
    destination=S3Dest(
        paths=[
            "exports/orders.parquet",
        ],
    ),
    input_tables=["orders"],
)
def write_orders(orders):
    return orders
```

-   required
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    

### Function Config Parameters

#### `paths`

Defines where the subscriber writes files in S3.

Each path is relative to the `base_path` configured in `S3DestConn`. Destination paths:

-   cannot begin or end with `/`
-   cannot contain empty path segments
-   cannot contain globs

Each element in `paths` represents one destination slot and maps positionally to a value returned by the subscriber function.

Destination paths can contain variables that Tabsdata substitutes when the subscriber runs:

| Variable | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `${EXEC_PLAN_ID}` | Current execution plan ID. |
| `${TRX_ID}` | Current transaction ID. |
| `${TRIGGERED_ON}` | Timestamp in file-safe form, such as `20260604T083428.376Z`. Replaces `${EXEC_PLAN_TS}`. |
| `${EXEC_PLAN_TS}` | Timestamp when the execution plan started. Deprecated since 2.3.0; use `${TRIGGERED_ON}`. |

For example:

```python
S3Dest(
    paths=[
        "exports/${EXEC_PLAN_ID}/orders.parquet",
    ]
)
```

Dynamic paths can be used to create a new S3 object for each execution instead of overwriting an existing object.

#### `format`

Sets the format used to write the destination file.

Supported formats are `AUTO`, `CSV`, `JSON`, `AVRO`, and `PARQUET`. The default is `AUTO`, which determines the format from the destination file extension.

#### `format_cfg`

Sets format-specific writer options. Configuration is keyed by `DestFileFormat`.

#### `dest_cfg`

Sets additional destination configuration.

## File behavior

Each entry in a publisher's `paths` is one source slot. A literal path reads one object; a final-segment `*` glob can read several. The slots map by position to the publisher function arguments and then to `output_tables`. Each slot receives one frame per matched object, oldest object first by modification time and then by name. A slot with no matches receives an empty list. Subdirectories are not searched.

`initial_last_modified` sets the cutoff for the first run. After a successful run, Tabsdata advances the cutoff so the same unchanged objects are not published again. Without `initial_last_modified`, every run reads every matched object. The cutoff is kept for each slot position and pattern, so reordering `paths` resets it. A late object whose modification time is older than the newest object already taken is skipped. An object that shares a modification time with another is taken once, and overlapping globs import the same object twice.

Each entry in a subscriber's `paths` is one destination slot and maps by position to a returned value. Use `${EXEC_PLAN_ID}`, `${TRX_ID}`, or `${TRIGGERED_ON}` in a path when every run needs a new object. `${TRIGGERED_ON}` is a timestamp in file-safe form, such as `20260604T083428.376Z`. `${EXEC_PLAN_TS}` still works, but it is deprecated since 2.3.0 and logs a warning. A fixed path writes to the same location again.

## Operational notes

-   Without `trigger_by`, a publisher runs only when triggered manually, while a subscriber runs when any input table commits. Set `trigger_by` to change when the function runs.
-   Tabsdata validates the connection document when the collection is created, but it does not contact Amazon S3 then. A bad path, credential, or permission fails when the function runs.
-   Globs are allowed only for publisher source paths, and only in the final path segment. Subscriber destination paths cannot contain globs.
-   All configured paths are relative to the connection's `base_path`.

## Publisher connection

Amazon S3 publishers use `S3SrcConn` to define the S3 bucket and credentials used by the publisher.

conn-s3-in.yaml

```yaml
kind: connectionDef
apiVersion: '1.0'
type: tabsdatak.conn.s3:S3SrcConn
spec:
  bucket: 'acme-ingest'
  region: 'us-east-1'
  credentials:
    kind: awsAccessSecretKeyCredentials
    apiVersion: '1.0'
    type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:AwsAccessSecretKey
    spec:
      access_key_id: 'secret:AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE'
      secret_access_key: 'secret:wJalrXUtnFEMI0EXAMPLEKEY'
```

-   required
    
-   required
    
-   required
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    

### Create the collection

A publisher is registered in a source collection, and a source collection is created with its connection. Every function registered in the collection uses that connection.

Generate a connection template, which lists all the connection fields:

```bash
tdk connection template --type s3-file-in --file conn-s3-in.yaml
```

Edit the template file with the Amazon S3 connection information, check it, and create the collection with it:

```bash
tdk connection validate --file conn-s3-in.yaml
```

```bash
tdk collection create --name s3_in --conn-file conn-s3-in.yaml
```

Then register the publisher in the collection:

```bash
tdk fn register --coll s3_in --path publish_orders.py::publish_orders
```

-   The collection goes in the `sources` group, because the connection is a source connection. `--group` can be left out; if it is given, it must be `sources`.
-   `secret:<value>` gives a secret value in the file itself. `$secret:<ENV_VAR>` reads it from an environment variable when the collection is created, so the value never appears in the file. Either way, Tabsdata stores the secret separately, and the stored connection only shows a placeholder.
-   Functions in the collection must use the connector of its connection: `S3Src` for a collection created with `S3SrcConn`. Transformers go in a collection of their own.
-   To change the connection later, for example to rotate a password, run `tdk collection update --name s3_in --conn-file conn-s3-in.yaml`. The connector cannot change; to use another one, create another collection.
-   Creating a source or destination collection requires permission to manage the project.

### Connection Config Parameters

#### `bucket`

The name of the S3 bucket that contains the files to publish.

#### `region`

The AWS region where the S3 bucket is located, such as `us-east-1`.

#### `credentials`

The AWS credentials used to access the bucket. `AwsAccessSecretKey` requires an `access_key_id` and `secret_access_key`.

#### `base_path`

Sets the base path within the S3 bucket. All paths configured in `S3Src` are relative to this path.

`base_path` starts with `/`, cannot end with `/`, and cannot contain empty path segments. The default is `/`.

For example, with:

```yaml
base_path: /hr
```

the source path:

```text
employees/2026.csv
```

refers to:

```text
/hr/employees/2026.csv
```

within the configured S3 bucket.

#### `conn_cfg`

Optional connector configuration overrides. Keys that start with `obstore.` configure the object store; see [Object Store Options](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connectors/object-store-options).

# Apache Druid

> Reference for the Tabsdata Apache Druid destination connector, cloud staging, and subscriber configuration.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connectors/druid

The Apache Druid connector lets Tabsdata subscribers write data from Tabsdata tables into Druid datasources.

The connector stages the data as Parquet files in cloud storage, then submits a Druid ingestion task that loads it from there.

[See the full subscriber walkthrough](https://docs.tabsdata.com/tutorials/subscribers/druid)

The subscriber is registered in a collection created with a `DruidDestConn` connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in [Connection](#connection), at the end of this page.

### Prerequisites

-   The Druid Overlord API is reachable from the Tabsdata server.
-   The Overlord credentials can submit and inspect ingestion tasks.
-   Tabsdata can write to the S3 or Azure staging location and Druid can read the staged Parquet files.
-   The Druid cluster has the `druid-parquet-extensions` extension loaded, plus the S3 or Azure extension for the staging location.

### Subscriber

Configure `DruidDest` as the `destination` of a subscriber function to define which datasources Tabsdata writes in Druid.

write\_events.py

```python
from tabsdatak.api import subscriber, TableFrameSpec
from tabsdatak.conn.druid import DruidDest

@subscriber(
    destination=DruidDest(
        tables=[
            "events",
        ],
    ),
    input_tables=["events"],
)
def write_events(events: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec:
    return events
```

-   required
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    

### Function Config Parameters

#### `tables`

Defines the Druid datasources the subscriber writes to. Each name is 1 to 128 characters, does not start with `.` or `_`, and contains no `/`, backslash or NUL.

Each element in `tables` represents one destination slot and maps positionally to a value returned by the subscriber function.

#### `if_table_exists`

`"append"` (the default) adds rows to the datasource. `"replace"` overwrites it.

#### `time_column`

The column Druid uses as its primary `__time` field. Druid requires a time column on every datasource. Without one, every row gets the fixed timestamp `2000-01-01T00:00:00Z`, so set `time_column` to a column that holds a timestamp for every row.

#### `segment_granularity`

The time span of each Druid segment: `ALL` (the default), `NONE`, `SECOND`, `MINUTE`, `FIFTEEN_MINUTE`, `THIRTY_MINUTE`, `HOUR`, `SIX_HOUR`, `DAY`, `WEEK`, `MONTH`, `QUARTER` or `YEAR`.

#### `max_concurrent_subtasks`, `max_rows_per_segment`, `max_rows_in_memory` and `http_timeout_sec`

Tuning for the ingestion task: its concurrency (default `1`), the row cap per segment (default `5000000`), the in-memory row cap per task (default `1000000`), and the HTTP request timeout in seconds (default `300`).

#### `dest_cfg`

Sets additional destination configuration. The only accepted key is `druid.logging_level`. The keys `druid.poll_interval_seconds`, `druid.retry_attempts` and `druid.retry_backoff_seconds` are accepted but have no effect. The connector polls the task every 2 seconds and makes 3 attempts, with 2-second exponential backoff, on 429, 502, 503 and 504 responses and on connection or timeout errors.

## Write behavior

Each entry in `tables` is one destination slot and maps by position to a value returned by the subscriber function. Returning `None` for a slot skips that write.

`if_table_exists="append"` adds data to the datasource. `"replace"` overwrites it: the ingestion task drops the existing segments in the range 1970-01-01 to 2100-01-01, and rows outside that range are discarded. Datasources are written one after another. `time_column` selects the row timestamp used as Druid `__time`; without it, every row gets `__time` set to `2000-01-01T00:00:00Z`.

### Schema evolution

Druid cannot enforce a schema, so `"update"` is its only `schema_evolution` value and its default; `"strict"` is refused at registration. On `"append"` and `"replace"`, Druid's native schema discovery adds a new column to the datasource, and a column the batch lacks reads as NULL. Druid has no keyed upsert, so `"merge"` is not supported.

## Operational notes

-   The connection is to the Overlord API, not a SQL endpoint.
-   A write finishes only after the submitted ingestion task finishes. The task is polled with no overall timeout. `http_timeout_sec` limits each HTTP request, not the whole wait.
-   Staged files are deleted when the ingestion task ends, whether it succeeds or fails with `DRUID_9`. If the outcome is unknown, the files are kept, so a lifecycle rule on the staging prefix can clear them. The staging credentials need delete permission.
-   `segment_granularity` and the row limits change the ingestion task, not the Tabsdata input table.
-   Tabsdata does not contact Druid or the staging service when the collection is created. Those checks happen when the subscriber runs.

## Connection

Druid subscribers use `DruidDestConn` to define the Overlord, the credentials, and the cloud storage the data is staged in.

conn-druid.yaml

```yaml
kind: connectionDef
apiVersion: '1.0'
type: tabsdatak.conn.druid:DruidDestConn
spec:
  overlord_url: 'http://druid-overlord.internal:8081'
  credentials:
    kind: userPasswordCredentials
    apiVersion: '1.0'
    type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:UserPassword
    spec:
      user: 'secret:tabsdata_writer'
      password: 'secret:example-password'
  staging:
    kind: druidS3Location
    apiVersion: '1.0'
    type: tabsdatak.conn.druid:S3Location
    spec:
      bucket: 'acme-staging'
      region: 'us-east-1'
      credentials:
        kind: awsAccessSecretKeyCredentials
        apiVersion: '1.0'
        type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:AwsAccessSecretKey
        spec:
          access_key_id: 'secret:example-access-key'
          secret_access_key: 'secret:example-secret-key'
      base_path: '/druid'
```

-   required
    
-   required
    
-   required
    
-   optional
    

### Create the collection

A subscriber is registered in a destination collection, and a destination collection is created with its connection. Every function registered in the collection uses that connection.

Generate a connection template, which lists all the connection fields:

```bash
tdk connection template --type druid-bulk-out --file conn-druid.yaml
```

Edit the template file with the Druid connection information, check it, and create the collection with it:

```bash
tdk connection validate --file conn-druid.yaml
```

```bash
tdk collection create --name druid_out --conn-file conn-druid.yaml
```

Then register the subscriber in the collection:

```bash
tdk fn register --coll druid_out --path write_events.py::write_events
```

-   The collection goes in the `destinations` group, because the connection is a destination connection. `--group` can be left out; if it is given, it must be `destinations`.
-   `secret:<value>` gives a secret value in the file itself. `$secret:<ENV_VAR>` reads it from an environment variable when the collection is created, so the value never appears in the file. Either way, Tabsdata stores the secret separately, and the stored connection only shows a placeholder.
-   Functions in the collection must use the connector of its connection: `DruidDest` for a collection created with `DruidDestConn`. Transformers go in a collection of their own.
-   To change the connection later, for example to rotate a password, run `tdk collection update --name druid_out --conn-file conn-druid.yaml`. The connector cannot change; to use another one, create another collection.
-   Creating a source or destination collection requires permission to manage the project.

### Connection Config Parameters

#### `overlord_url`

The `http://` or `https://` URL of the Druid Overlord, for example `http://druid.example:8081`. Accepts `secret:` too.

#### `credentials`

A `UserPassword` used for HTTP basic authentication with the Overlord. Cloud storage credentials are configured separately under `staging`.

#### `staging`

An `S3Location` or an `AzBlobLocation` from `tabsdatak.conn.druid`, where the Parquet files are staged before ingestion. Tabsdata must be able to upload the staged files, and Druid must be able to read them. Keys under `cfg` on the location configure the upload; see [Object Store Options](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connectors/object-store-options).

#### `conn_cfg`

Optional connector configuration. It affects only the explorer, not writes.

# Azure Blob Storage

> Reference for the Tabsdata Azure Blob Storage connector.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connectors/azure

The Azure Blob Storage connector lets Tabsdata read files from and write files to Azure Blob Storage.

The `AzureBlobSrc` connector can be used by a publisher function to read data from Azure Blob Storage into a Tabsdata table.

## Supported formats

| `AVRO` | Yes | Yes |
| `PARQUET` | Yes | Yes |
| `LOG` | Yes | No |

## Publisher

The `AzureBlobSrc` connector can be used by a publisher function to read data from Azure Blob Storage into a Tabsdata table. [See the full publisher walkthrough](https://docs.tabsdata.com/tutorials/publishers/azure)

-   optional
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    

### Function Config Parameters

#### `paths`

Defines the files that the publisher reads from Azure Blob Storage.

Each path is relative to the `base_path` configured in `AzureBlobSrcConn`. Source paths:

-   cannot begin or end with `/`
-   cannot contain empty path segments
-   cannot be `.` or `..`, or contain a `${...}` token
-   can contain a `*` glob in the final path segment. `*` matches any run of characters and `?` matches one character; in directory segments, both are literal.

For example:

```python
AzureBlobSrc(
    paths=[
        "orders/2026/*.parquet",
        "customers/customers.csv",

```

Each element in `paths` represents one source slot and maps positionally to an argument in the publisher function.

When a path uses a glob to match multiple files, the matching files are provided through the corresponding publisher input.

#### `format`

Sets the format used to read the source files.

Supported formats are `AUTO`, `CSV`, `JSON`, `AVRO`, `PARQUET`, `LOG`, and `EXCEL`. The default is `AUTO`, which determines the format from the file extension. `AUTO` resolves the format for each file from its own extension. For a compressed file, that is the extension before the compression extension. A file whose extension names no format fails the run. A source whose files resolve to different formats also fails the run. `EXCEL` reads `.xlsx` workbooks only. Pick a sheet with a `#n` suffix on the path, such as `paths=["book.xlsx#2"]`; the sheet number starts at 1 and counts hidden sheets, and `#0` is refused. Its `format_cfg` takes `has_header`.

#### `format_cfg`

Sets format-specific reader options. Configuration is keyed by `SrcFileFormat`.

For `CSV`, `has_header=False` reads the first row as data. The columns are then named `column_0`, `column_1`, ... `skip_lines` skips that many lines at the start of each file before the header is read. A `""` field is read as an empty string.

#### `include_compressed`

When `True`, the publisher reads compressed blobs. A path that ends in a compression extension fails validation without it. The compression extensions are `.gz`, `.zlib`, `.zst`, `.zstd`, `.bz2`, `.xz`, `.lz4` and `.br`, plus single-entry `.zip` and `.tar` archives. The format comes from the name before the compression extension, so `orders.csv.gz` is read as CSV. An archive must hold one file, and a name can have only one compression extension.

#### `purge`

When `True`, the publisher deletes each matched blob that the cursor skipped, if its modification time is at or after `initial_last_modified`. `purge` requires `initial_last_modified`; without it the run fails with `FILE_COMMON_35`. Deletion runs for each slot after that slot's frames are read.

warning

`purge` deletes data, including a late blob that the cursor skipped before the publisher ever read it. It needs delete permission on the source blobs.

#### `initial_last_modified`

Sets the initial cutoff for incremental ingestion.

On the first run, Tabsdata imports files modified at or after the specified timestamp. The cutoff then advances so subsequent runs only import newer files. The value must be timezone-aware, for example `datetime(2026, 1, 1, tzinfo=timezone.utc)`.

#### `src_cfg`

Sets additional source configuration.

The following options are supported:

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `tabsdata.src_metadata.drop` | When `True`, excludes the `@td.file.path` metadata column. |

By default, rows read from Azure Blob Storage include a `@td.file.path` metadata column containing the source file's URI.

## Subscriber

The `AzureBlobDest` connector can be used by a subscriber function to write data from a Tabsdata table into Azure Blob Storage. [See the full subscriber walkthrough](https://docs.tabsdata.com/tutorials/subscribers/azure)

The subscriber is registered in a collection created with a `AzureBlobDestConn` connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in [Subscriber connection](#subscriber-connection), at the end of this page.

### Prerequisites

-   The container exists and is reachable from the Tabsdata server.
-   The storage account can create and write blobs under the configured `base_path`.
-   The destination path is relative and does not contain a glob.

### Subscriber

Configure `AzureBlobDest` as the `destination` of a subscriber function to define where Tabsdata writes files in Azure Blob Storage.

write\_orders.py

```python
from tabsdatak.api import subscriber
from tabsdatak.conn.azureblob import AzureBlobDest, DestFileFormat

@subscriber(
    destination=AzureBlobDest(
        paths=[
            "exports/orders.parquet",
        ],
    ),
    input_tables=["orders"],
)
def write_orders(orders):
    return orders
```

-   required
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    

### Function Config Parameters

#### `paths`

Defines where the subscriber writes files in Azure Blob Storage.

Each path is relative to the `base_path` configured in `AzureBlobDestConn`. Destination paths:

-   cannot begin or end with `/`
-   cannot contain empty path segments
-   cannot contain globs

Each element in `paths` represents one destination slot and maps positionally to a value returned by the subscriber function.

Destination paths can contain variables that Tabsdata substitutes when the subscriber runs:

| Variable | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `${EXEC_PLAN_ID}` | Current execution plan ID. |
| `${TRX_ID}` | Current transaction ID. |
| `${TRIGGERED_ON}` | Timestamp in file-safe form, such as `20260604T083428.376Z`. Replaces `${EXEC_PLAN_TS}`. |
| `${EXEC_PLAN_TS}` | Timestamp when the execution plan started. Deprecated since 2.3.0; use `${TRIGGERED_ON}`. |

For example:

```python
AzureBlobDest(
    paths=[
        "exports/${EXEC_PLAN_ID}/orders.parquet",
    ]
)
```

Dynamic paths can be used to create a new object for each execution instead of overwriting an existing object.

#### `format`

Sets the format used to write the destination file.

Supported formats are `AUTO`, `CSV`, `JSON`, `AVRO`, and `PARQUET`. The default is `AUTO`, which determines the format from the destination file extension.

#### `format_cfg`

Sets format-specific writer options. Configuration is keyed by `DestFileFormat`.

#### `dest_cfg`

Sets additional destination configuration.

## File behavior

Each entry in a publisher's `paths` is one source slot. A literal path reads one blob; a final-segment `*` glob can read several. The slots map by position to the publisher function arguments and then to `output_tables`. Each slot receives one frame per matched blob, oldest blob first by modification time and then by name. A slot with no matches receives an empty list. Subdirectories are not searched.

`initial_last_modified` sets the cutoff for the first run. After a successful run, Tabsdata advances the cutoff so the same unchanged blobs are not published again. Without `initial_last_modified`, every run reads every matched blob. The cutoff is kept for each slot position and pattern, so reordering `paths` resets it. A late blob whose modification time is older than the newest blob already taken is skipped. An blob that shares a modification time with another is taken once, and overlapping globs import the same blob twice.

Each entry in a subscriber's `paths` is one destination slot and maps by position to a returned value. Use `${EXEC_PLAN_ID}`, `${TRX_ID}`, or `${TRIGGERED_ON}` in a path when every run needs a new blob. `${TRIGGERED_ON}` is a timestamp in file-safe form, such as `20260604T083428.376Z`. `${EXEC_PLAN_TS}` still works, but it is deprecated since 2.3.0 and logs a warning. A fixed path writes to the same location again.

## Operational notes

-   Without `trigger_by`, a publisher runs only when triggered manually, while a subscriber runs when any input table commits. Set `trigger_by` to change when the function runs.
-   Tabsdata validates the connection document when the collection is created, but it does not contact Azure Blob Storage then. A bad path, credential, or permission fails when the function runs.
-   Globs are allowed only for publisher source paths, and only in the final path segment. Subscriber destination paths cannot contain globs.
-   All configured paths are relative to the connection's `base_path`.

## Publisher connection

Azure Blob Storage publishers use `AzureBlobSrcConn` to define the container and credentials used by the publisher.

conn-azure-in.yaml

```yaml
kind: connectionDef
apiVersion: '1.0'
type: tabsdatak.conn.azureblob:AzureBlobSrcConn
spec:
  container: 'acme-ingest'
  credentials:
    kind: azureAccountKeyCredentials
    apiVersion: '1.0'
    type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:AzureAccountKey
    spec:
      account_name: 'secret:mystorageaccount'
      account_key: 'secret:8Zs0RExAmPlEkEy0000=='
```

-   required
    
-   required
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    

### Create the collection

A publisher is registered in a source collection, and a source collection is created with its connection. Every function registered in the collection uses that connection.

Generate a connection template, which lists all the connection fields:

```bash
tdk connection template --type az-file-in --file conn-azure-in.yaml
```

Edit the template file with the Azure Blob Storage connection information, check it, and create the collection with it:

```bash
tdk connection validate --file conn-azure-in.yaml
```

```bash
tdk collection create --name azure_in --conn-file conn-azure-in.yaml
```

Then register the publisher in the collection:

```bash
tdk fn register --coll azure_in --path publish_orders.py::publish_orders
```

-   The collection goes in the `sources` group, because the connection is a source connection. `--group` can be left out; if it is given, it must be `sources`.
-   `secret:<value>` gives a secret value in the file itself. `$secret:<ENV_VAR>` reads it from an environment variable when the collection is created, so the value never appears in the file. Either way, Tabsdata stores the secret separately, and the stored connection only shows a placeholder.
-   Functions in the collection must use the connector of its connection: `AzureBlobSrc` for a collection created with `AzureBlobSrcConn`. Transformers go in a collection of their own.
-   To change the connection later, for example to rotate a password, run `tdk collection update --name azure_in --conn-file conn-azure-in.yaml`. The connector cannot change; to use another one, create another collection.
-   Creating a source or destination collection requires permission to manage the project.

### Connection Config Parameters

#### `container`

The name of the Azure Blob container that contains the files to publish.

#### `credentials`

The Azure storage-account credentials used to access the container. `AzureAccountKey` requires an `account_name` and `account_key`.

#### `base_path`

Sets the base path within the container. All paths configured in `AzureBlobSrc` are relative to this path.

`base_path` starts with `/`, cannot end with `/`, and cannot contain empty path segments. The default is `/`.

#### `conn_cfg`

Optional connector configuration overrides. Keys that start with `obstore.` configure the object store; see [Object Store Options](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connectors/object-store-options).

# BigQuery

> Reference for the Tabsdata BigQuery connector.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connectors/bigquery

The BigQuery connector lets Tabsdata write tables into BigQuery. BigQuery is destination-only: there is no publisher-side connector for reading from BigQuery.

The `BigQueryDest` connector can be used by a subscriber function to write data from a Tabsdata table into BigQuery. [See the full subscriber walkthrough](https://docs.tabsdata.com/tutorials/subscribers/bigquery)

The subscriber is registered in a collection created with a `BigQueryDestConn` connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in [Connection](#connection), at the end of this page.

### Prerequisites

-   The BigQuery project and dataset exist, and the service account can create and load tables in them.
-   The GCS staging bucket exists. The service account can write staged Parquet files there and BigQuery can load them.
-   The project and dataset are set either in each table name or as connection defaults.

### Subscriber

For merge writes, schema evolution, and retry watermarks, see [Merging into SQL destinations](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/functions/sql-merge).

Configure `BigQueryDest` as the `destination` of a subscriber function to define which tables Tabsdata writes in BigQuery.

write\_orders.py

```python
from tabsdatak.api import subscriber
from tabsdatak.conn.bigquery import BigQueryDest

@subscriber(
    destination=BigQueryDest(
        tables=[
            "orders",
        ],
    ),
    input_tables=["orders"],
)
def write_orders(orders):
    return orders
```

-   required
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    

### Function Config Parameters

#### `tables`

Defines the destination tables the subscriber writes to in BigQuery.

Each element in `tables` represents one destination slot and maps positionally to a value returned by the subscriber function. Each name is `[[project.]dataset.]table`; a bare `table` or `dataset.table` is completed from the connection's `project`/`dataset` defaults. BigQuery wraps the whole name in one backtick pair, e.g. `` `my-project.ds.t` ``.

#### `if_table_exists`

`"merge"` applies inserts, updates, and deletes by key and requires a `merge_cfg` list. See [Merge configuration](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/functions/sql-merge#merge-configuration) for a complete example.

Controls what happens when the destination table already exists. `"append"` (the default) adds rows. `"replace"` drops and recreates the table.

#### `schema_evolution`

Controls what happens when the returned frame has a column the table lacks or a wider type. `"update"` adds and widens columns. `"strict"` is the default: an append fails in the load job (`BIGQUERY_7`), and a merge is refused before it runs (`SQL_COMMON_10`). See [Schema Evolution](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connectors/schema-evolution).

#### `dest_cfg`

Sets additional destination configuration. Supported keys include `bigquery.logging_level` and `bigquery.schema_evolution_engine`. The engine key is only for a merge under `schema_evolution="update"`, where it must be `"iceberg"`. See [Schema evolution](#schema-evolution).

## Write behavior

Each entry in `tables` is one destination slot and maps by position to a value returned by the subscriber function. Returning `None` for a slot skips that write.

`if_table_exists="append"` adds rows. `"replace"` drops and recreates the table. `"merge"` applies inserts, updates, and deletes by key and needs `merge_cfg`.

With `schema_evolution="strict"`, a frame with a new column, or a wider type whose values do not fit, fails instead of changing the table. `"update"` adds and widens columns before the load.

### Schema evolution

`schema_evolution` decides what a write does when the returned frame has a column the destination table lacks, or a type wider than the column's. `"strict"`, the default, refuses a new column, and refuses a wider type unless its values fit the column. `"update"` changes the table to fit the frame. On BigQuery, the schema evolution `"update"` uses depends on `if_table_exists`:

| `if_table_exists` | `"update"` uses | Changes to the table |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `"append"`, `"replace"` | BigQuery's native schema evolution | Adds columns and makes columns nullable. It never widens a type. |
| `"merge"` | [Iceberg schema evolution](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connectors/schema-evolution#native-and-iceberg-schema-evolution), applied by the connector through `ALTER TABLE`. Needs `dest_cfg={"bigquery.schema_evolution_engine": "iceberg"}`. | Adds columns and widens types. |

BigQuery's native schema evolution does not apply to `MERGE`, so a merge under `"update"` without the `iceberg` engine is refused at registration. `bigquery.schema_evolution_engine` is accepted only on a merge under `"update"`: setting it on `"append"` or `"replace"`, or on a merge under `"strict"`, is also refused at registration. See [Schema Evolution](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connectors/schema-evolution) for the types each destination widens.

## Operational notes

-   Each write is staged as Parquet in GCS before the BigQuery load job runs. Both the staging write and the BigQuery load must succeed.
-   Bare table names use the connection's `project` and `dataset`. Fully qualified names override those defaults.
-   Tabsdata does not contact GCS or BigQuery when the collection is created. Connection and permission errors appear when the subscriber runs.

## Connection

BigQuery subscribers use `BigQueryDestConn` to define the GCS staging location and credentials used by the subscriber. The connector stages each write as parquet in GCS, then runs a load job against BigQuery referencing that object.

conn-bigquery.yaml

```yaml
kind: connectionDef
apiVersion: '1.0'
type: tabsdatak.conn.bigquery:BigQueryDestConn
spec:
  staging:
    bucket: 'acme-stage'
    credentials:
      kind: gcpJsonCredentials
      apiVersion: '1.0'
      type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:GCPJson
      spec:
        json: 'secret:{"type": "service_account", ...}'
    base_path: '/bigquery'
  credentials:
    kind: gcpJsonCredentials
    apiVersion: '1.0'
    type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:GCPJson
    spec:
      json: 'secret:{"type": "service_account", ...}'
```

-   required
    
-   required
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    

### Create the collection

A subscriber is registered in a destination collection, and a destination collection is created with its connection. Every function registered in the collection uses that connection.

Generate a connection template, which lists all the connection fields:

```bash
tdk connection template --type bigquery-bulk-out --file conn-bigquery.yaml
```

Edit the template file with the BigQuery connection information, check it, and create the collection with it:

```bash
tdk connection validate --file conn-bigquery.yaml
```

```bash
tdk collection create --name bigquery_out --conn-file conn-bigquery.yaml
```

Then register the subscriber in the collection:

```bash
tdk fn register --coll bigquery_out --path write_orders.py::write_orders
```

-   The collection goes in the `destinations` group, because the connection is a destination connection. `--group` can be left out; if it is given, it must be `destinations`.
-   `secret:<value>` gives a secret value in the file itself. `$secret:<ENV_VAR>` reads it from an environment variable when the collection is created, so the value never appears in the file. Either way, Tabsdata stores the secret separately, and the stored connection only shows a placeholder.
-   Functions in the collection must use the connector of its connection: `BigQueryDest` for a collection created with `BigQueryDestConn`. Transformers go in a collection of their own.
-   To change the connection later, for example to rotate a password, run `tdk collection update --name bigquery_out --conn-file conn-bigquery.yaml`. The connector cannot change; to use another one, create another collection.
-   Creating a source or destination collection requires permission to manage the project.

### Connection Config Parameters

#### `staging`

The `GCSLocation` used as the parquet staging bucket for load jobs: a `bucket`, `credentials` (GCP service-account JSON), and `base_path` (defaults to `/`, same rules as other connectors' `base_path`: starts with `/`, cannot end with `/`, cannot contain empty path segments).

#### `credentials`

The GCP service-account JSON credentials (`GCPJson`) used to run the BigQuery load job, separate from the credentials on `staging` used to upload to GCS.

#### `project`

The default GCP project id. Required when `dataset` is set.

#### `dataset`

The default BigQuery dataset id. Requires `project` to be set.

#### `entity_whitelist`

A YAML list of regular expressions, not a comma-separated string. It is checked to be a list of valid regular expressions, but it has no effect yet. Leave it out.

#### `conn_cfg`

Optional connector configuration overrides.
