# Local File System

> Reference for the Tabsdata Local File System connector.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connectors/local-file-system

The Local File System connector lets Tabsdata read files from and write files to the server's own filesystem.

The `LocalFileSrc` connector can be used by a publisher function to read data from local files into a Tabsdata table.

The `LocalFileDest` connector can be used by a subscriber function to write data from a Tabsdata table into local files.

## Supported formats

| Format | Publish | Subscribe |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `AUTO` | Yes | Yes |
| `CSV` | Yes | Yes |
| `JSON` | Yes | Yes |
| `AVRO` | Yes | Yes |
| `PARQUET` | Yes | Yes |
| `LOG` | Yes | No |
| `EXCEL` | Yes | No |

## Publisher

The `LocalFileSrc` connector can be used by a publisher function to read data from local files into a Tabsdata table. [See the full publisher walkthrough](https://docs.tabsdata.com/tutorials/publishers/local-file-system)

The publisher is registered in a collection created with a `LocalFileSrcConn` connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in [Publisher connection](#publisher-connection), at the end of this page.

### Prerequisites

-   The configured `base_path` exists on the Tabsdata server and is readable by the function worker.
-   Every source path stays under `base_path`; parent-directory segments are refused.
-   Compressed files need `include_compressed=True`; see [`include_compressed`](#include_compressed).

### Publisher

Configure `LocalFileSrc` as the `source` of a publisher function to select the files that Tabsdata reads from disk.

publish\_orders.py

```python
from tabsdatak.api import publisher
from tabsdatak.conn.localfile import LocalFileSrc, SrcFileFormat

@publisher(
    source=LocalFileSrc(
        paths=[
            "incoming/orders.parquet",
        ],
    ),
    output_tables=["orders"],
)
def publish_orders(orders):
    return orders
```

-   required
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    

### Function Config Parameters

#### `paths`

Defines the files that the publisher reads from disk.

Each path is relative to the `base_path` configured in `LocalFileSrcConn`. Source paths:

-   cannot begin or end with `/`
-   cannot contain empty path segments
-   cannot be `.` or `..`, or contain a `${...}` token
-   can contain a `*` glob in the final path segment. `*` matches any run of characters and `?` matches one character; in directory segments, both are literal.

For example:

```python
LocalFileSrc(
    paths=[
        "orders/2026/*.parquet",
        "customers/customers.csv",
    ]
)
```

Each element in `paths` represents one source slot and maps positionally to an argument in the publisher function.

When a path uses a glob to match multiple files, the matching files are provided through the corresponding publisher input.

#### `format`

Sets the format used to read the source files.

Supported formats are `AUTO`, `CSV`, `JSON`, `AVRO`, `PARQUET`, `LOG`, and `EXCEL`. The default is `AUTO`, which determines the format from the file extension. `AUTO` resolves the format for each file from its own extension. For a compressed file, that is the extension before the compression extension. A file whose extension names no format fails the run. A source whose files resolve to different formats also fails the run. `EXCEL` reads `.xlsx` workbooks only. Pick a sheet with a `#n` suffix on the path, such as `paths=["book.xlsx#2"]`; the sheet number starts at 1 and counts hidden sheets, and `#0` is refused. Its `format_cfg` takes `has_header`.

#### `format_cfg`

Sets format-specific reader options. Configuration is keyed by `SrcFileFormat`.

For `CSV`, `has_header=False` reads the first row as data. The columns are then named `column_0`, `column_1`, ... `skip_lines` skips that many lines at the start of each file before the header is read. A `""` field is read as an empty string.

#### `include_compressed`

When `True`, the publisher reads compressed files. A path that ends in a compression extension fails validation without it. The compression extensions are `.gz`, `.zlib`, `.zst`, `.zstd`, `.bz2`, `.xz`, `.lz4` and `.br`, plus single-entry `.zip` and `.tar` archives. The format comes from the name before the compression extension, so `orders.csv.gz` is read as CSV. An archive must hold one file, and a name can have only one compression extension.

#### `purge`

When `True`, the publisher deletes each matched file that the cursor skipped, if its modification time is at or after `initial_last_modified`. `purge` requires `initial_last_modified`; without it the run fails with `FILE_COMMON_35`. Deletion runs for each slot after that slot's frames are read.

warning

`purge` deletes data, including a late file that the cursor skipped before the publisher ever read it. It needs delete permission on the source files.

#### `initial_last_modified`

Sets the initial cutoff for incremental ingestion.

On the first run, Tabsdata imports files modified at or after the specified timestamp. The cutoff then advances so subsequent runs only import newer files. The value must be timezone-aware, for example `datetime(2026, 1, 1, tzinfo=timezone.utc)`.

#### `src_cfg`

Sets additional source configuration.

The following options are supported:

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `tabsdata.src_metadata.drop` | When `True`, excludes the `@td.file.path` metadata column. |

By default, rows read from disk include a `@td.file.path` metadata column containing the source file's path.

## Subscriber

The `LocalFileDest` connector can be used by a subscriber function to write data from a Tabsdata table into local files. [See the full subscriber walkthrough](https://docs.tabsdata.com/tutorials/subscribers/local-file-system)

The subscriber is registered in a collection created with a `LocalFileDestConn` connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in [Subscriber connection](#subscriber-connection), at the end of this page.

### Prerequisites

-   The configured `base_path` exists on the Tabsdata server and is writable by the function worker.
-   Every destination path stays under `base_path`; parent-directory segments and globs are refused.
-   Enough disk space is available for the files written by the run.

### Subscriber

Configure `LocalFileDest` as the `destination` of a subscriber function to define where Tabsdata writes files on disk.

write\_orders.py

```python
from tabsdatak.api import subscriber
from tabsdatak.conn.localfile import LocalFileDest, DestFileFormat

@subscriber(
    destination=LocalFileDest(
        paths=[
            "exports/orders.parquet",
        ],
    ),
    input_tables=["orders"],
)
def write_orders(orders):
    return orders
```

-   required
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    

### Function Config Parameters

#### `paths`

Defines where the subscriber writes files on disk.

Each path is relative to the `base_path` configured in `LocalFileDestConn`. Destination paths:

-   cannot begin or end with `/`
-   cannot contain empty path segments
-   cannot contain globs

Each element in `paths` represents one destination slot and maps positionally to a value returned by the subscriber function.

Destination paths can contain variables that Tabsdata substitutes when the subscriber runs:

| Variable | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `${EXEC_PLAN_ID}` | Current execution plan ID. |
| `${TRX_ID}` | Current transaction ID. |
| `${TRIGGERED_ON}` | Timestamp in file-safe form, such as `20260604T083428.376Z`. Replaces `${EXEC_PLAN_TS}`. |
| `${EXEC_PLAN_TS}` | Timestamp when the execution plan started. Deprecated since 2.3.0; use `${TRIGGERED_ON}`. |

For example:

```python
LocalFileDest(
    paths=[
        "exports/${EXEC_PLAN_ID}/orders.parquet",
    ]
)
```

Dynamic paths can be used to create a new file for each execution instead of overwriting an existing one.

#### `format`

Sets the format used to write the destination file.

Supported formats are `AUTO`, `CSV`, `JSON`, `AVRO`, and `PARQUET`. The default is `AUTO`, which determines the format from the destination file extension.

#### `format_cfg`

Sets format-specific writer options. Configuration is keyed by `DestFileFormat`.

#### `dest_cfg`

Sets additional destination configuration.

## File behavior

Each entry in a publisher's `paths` is one source slot. A literal path reads one file; a final-segment `*` glob can read several. The slots map by position to the publisher function arguments and then to `output_tables`. Each slot receives one frame per matched file, oldest file first by modification time and then by name. A slot with no matches receives an empty list. Subdirectories are not searched.

`initial_last_modified` sets the cutoff for the first run. After a successful run, Tabsdata advances the cutoff so the same unchanged files are not published again. Without `initial_last_modified`, every run reads every matched file. The cutoff is kept for each slot position and pattern, so reordering `paths` resets it. A late file whose modification time is older than the newest file already taken is skipped. An file that shares a modification time with another is taken once, and overlapping globs import the same file twice.

Each entry in a subscriber's `paths` is one destination slot and maps by position to a returned value. Use `${EXEC_PLAN_ID}`, `${TRX_ID}`, or `${TRIGGERED_ON}` in a path when every run needs a new file. `${TRIGGERED_ON}` is a timestamp in file-safe form, such as `20260604T083428.376Z`. `${EXEC_PLAN_TS}` still works, but it is deprecated since 2.3.0 and logs a warning. A fixed path writes to the same location again.

## Operational notes

-   Without `trigger_by`, a publisher runs only when triggered manually, while a subscriber runs when any input table commits. Set `trigger_by` to change when the function runs.
-   Tabsdata validates the connection document when the collection is created, but it does not contact local filesystem then. A bad path, credential, or permission fails when the function runs.
-   Globs are allowed only for publisher source paths, and only in the final path segment. Subscriber destination paths cannot contain globs.
-   All configured paths are relative to the connection's `base_path`.

## Publisher connection

Local File System publishers use `LocalFileSrcConn` to define the root filesystem path used by the publisher. Unlike the cloud storage connectors, there is no bucket and no credentials: the connector reads directly off the server's own disk.

conn-local-in.yaml

```yaml
kind: connectionDef
apiVersion: '1.0'
type: tabsdatak.conn.localfile:LocalFileSrcConn
spec:
  base_path: '/data/hr'
```

-   required
    
-   optional
    

### Create the collection

A publisher is registered in a source collection, and a source collection is created with its connection. Every function registered in the collection uses that connection.

Generate a connection template, which lists all the connection fields:

```bash
tdk connection template --type local-file-in --file conn-local-in.yaml
```

Edit the template file with the Local File System connection information, check it, and create the collection with it:

```bash
tdk connection validate --file conn-local-in.yaml
```

```bash
tdk collection create --name local_in --conn-file conn-local-in.yaml
```

Then register the publisher in the collection:

```bash
tdk fn register --coll local_in --path publish_orders.py::publish_orders
```

-   The collection goes in the `sources` group, because the connection is a source connection. `--group` can be left out; if it is given, it must be `sources`.
-   `secret:<value>` gives a secret value in the file itself. `$secret:<ENV_VAR>` reads it from an environment variable when the collection is created, so the value never appears in the file. Either way, Tabsdata stores the secret separately, and the stored connection only shows a placeholder.
-   Functions in the collection must use the connector of its connection: `LocalFileSrc` for a collection created with `LocalFileSrcConn`. Transformers go in a collection of their own.
-   To change the connection later, for example to rotate a password, run `tdk collection update --name local_in --conn-file conn-local-in.yaml`. The connector cannot change; to use another one, create another collection.
-   Creating a source or destination collection requires permission to manage the project.

### Connection Config Parameters

#### `base_path`

The absolute filesystem path that acts as the root for all paths the publisher reads. It is optional and defaults to `/`; set it to confine the connector to one directory.

#### `conn_cfg`

Optional connector configuration overrides.

# MariaDB

> Reference for the Tabsdata MariaDB connector.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connectors/mariadb

The MariaDB connector lets Tabsdata run queries against MariaDB and write tables into MariaDB.

The `MySQLSrc` connector can be used by a publisher function to read data from MariaDB into a Tabsdata table.

The `MySQLDest` connector can be used by a subscriber function to write data from a Tabsdata table into MariaDB.

## Publisher

The `MySQLSrc` connector can be used by a publisher function to read data from MariaDB into a Tabsdata table. [See the full publisher walkthrough](https://docs.tabsdata.com/tutorials/publishers/mariadb)

The publisher is registered in a collection created with a `MySQLSrcConn` connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in [Publisher connection](#publisher-connection), at the end of this page.

### Prerequisites

-   The MariaDB server is reachable from the Tabsdata server.
-   The connection user can run every query in `queries` and read every referenced table or view.

### Publisher

Configure `MySQLSrc` as the `source` of a publisher function to select the queries that Tabsdata runs against MariaDB.

publish\_orders.py

```python
from tabsdatak.api import publisher
from tabsdatak.conn.mysql import MySQLSrc

@publisher(
    source=MySQLSrc(
        queries=[
            "SELECT * FROM orders",
        ],
    ),
    output_tables=["orders"],
)
def publish_orders(orders):
    return orders
```

-   required
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    

### Function Config Parameters

#### `queries`

Defines the SQL queries the publisher runs against MariaDB.

Each element in `queries` represents one source slot and maps positionally to an argument in the publisher function.

For example:

```python
MySQLSrc(
    queries=[
        "SELECT * FROM country",
        "SELECT * FROM city",
    ],
)
```

#### `initial_values`

The first-run values for named parameters in `queries`, written `:name`. On later runs each parameter takes the value the publisher stored with `ctx.set_attr(name, value)`, so a query can read only the rows added since the last run.

Parameters bind values such as IDs and timestamps, not identifiers. Schema and table names have to be written into the query.

For example:

```python
from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, TrxCtx, publisher
from tabsdatak.conn.mysql import MySQLSrc


@publisher(
    source=MySQLSrc(
        queries=["SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id > :last_id ORDER BY id"],
        initial_values={"last_id": 0},
    ),
    output_tables=["orders"],
)
def publish_orders(orders: TableFrameSpec, ctx: TrxCtx) -> TableFrameSpec:
    row = orders.max_for("id")
    if row is not None and row["id"] is not None:
        ctx.set_attr("last_id", int(row["id"]))
    return orders
```

#### `src_cfg`

Sets additional source configuration.

## Subscriber

The `MySQLDest` connector can be used by a subscriber function to write data from a Tabsdata table into MariaDB. [See the full subscriber walkthrough](https://docs.tabsdata.com/tutorials/subscribers/mariadb)

The subscriber is registered in a collection created with a `MySQLDestConn` connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in [Subscriber connection](#subscriber-connection), at the end of this page.

### Prerequisites

-   The MariaDB server is reachable from the Tabsdata server.
-   The connection user can create missing destination tables and insert rows. With `if_table_exists="replace"`, it also needs to drop and create tables, and with `schema_evolution="update"`, to alter them.

### Subscriber

Configure `MySQLDest` as the `destination` of a subscriber function to define which tables Tabsdata writes in MariaDB.

write\_orders.py

```python
from tabsdatak.api import subscriber
from tabsdatak.conn.mysql import MySQLDest

@subscriber(
    destination=MySQLDest(
        tables=[
            "orders",
        ],
    ),
    input_tables=["orders"],
)
def write_orders(orders):
    return orders
```

-   required
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    

### Function Config Parameters

#### `tables`

Defines the destination tables the subscriber writes to in MariaDB.

Each element in `tables` represents one destination slot and maps positionally to a value returned by the subscriber function.

For example:

```python
MySQLDest(
    tables=[
        "vendors",
        "items",
    ],
)
```

#### `if_table_exists`

Controls what happens when the destination table already has rows. `"append"` (the default) keeps inserting into the existing rows. `"replace"` drops the table and creates it again from the returned frame, so the table's schema follows the frame. The drop and the create commit implicitly, so a failed write is not undone. On `"append"`, `schema_evolution` decides what happens to a new or wider column.

#### `schema_evolution`

`"strict"` (the default) or `"update"`. A refused write fails with `SQL_COMMON_10` before anything is written. The `ALTER` statements `"update"` runs commit implicitly, so they are not undone if the write fails. See [Schema evolution](#schema-evolution).

#### `dest_cfg`

Sets additional destination configuration.

## Query results

Each entry in `queries` produces one source slot. The slots map by position to the publisher function arguments and then to `output_tables`. Keep those three lists in the same order.

Queries run when the publisher is triggered. They are not a continuous change feed. To read incrementally, put named parameters such as `:last_id` in the query, set their first values with `initial_values`, and save the next values with `ctx.set_attr()` after each successful run.

## Write behavior

Each entry in `tables` is one destination slot and maps by position to a value returned by the subscriber function. Returning `None` for a slot skips that write.

`if_table_exists="append"` keeps the rows already in the destination and inserts the returned rows. `"replace"` drops the table and creates it again from the returned frame. On `"append"`, `schema_evolution="update"` adds new columns and widens number types; removing a column or changing a non-number type still needs a database migration before the subscriber runs.

### Schema evolution

`schema_evolution` decides what a write does when the returned frame has a column the destination table lacks, or a type wider than the column's. `"strict"`, the default, refuses a new column, and refuses a wider type unless its values fit the column. `"update"` changes the table to fit the frame. On MariaDB, `"update"` uses [Iceberg schema evolution](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connectors/schema-evolution#native-and-iceberg-schema-evolution), applied by the connector, on `"append"` and `"replace"`: `ALTER TABLE … ADD` adds columns, and integers, decimals and floats are widened by digits or width. It never drops a column or changes a non-number type. `"merge"` is not supported.

## Operational notes

-   Without `trigger_by`, a publisher runs only when triggered manually, while a subscriber runs when any input table commits. Set `trigger_by` to change when the function runs.
-   Tabsdata checks the connection document when the collection is created, but it does not connect to MariaDB then. A bad host, credential, query, or permission fails when the function runs.
-   Every function in the collection uses the same connection. Use another collection when functions need another database or another set of credentials.

## Publisher connection

MariaDB publishers use `MySQLSrcConn` to define the database connection and credentials used by the publisher.

conn-mariadb-in.yaml

```yaml

spec:
  uri: 'mariadb://db.internal:3306/world'
  credentials:
    kind: userPasswordCredentials
    apiVersion: '1.0'
    type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:UserPassword
    spec:
      user: 'secret:tabsdata_reader'
      password: 'secret:example-password'
```

-   required
    
-   required
    
-   optional
    
-   optional

```

Then register the publisher in the collection:

```

-   The collection goes in the `sources` group, because the connection is a source connection. `--group` can be left out; if it is given, it must be `sources`.
-   `secret:<value>` gives a secret value in the file itself. `$secret:<ENV_VAR>` reads it from an environment variable when the collection is created, so the value never appears in the file. Either way, Tabsdata stores the secret separately, and the stored connection only shows a placeholder.
-   Functions in the collection must use the connector of its connection: `MySQLSrc` for a collection created with `MySQLSrcConn`. Transformers go in a collection of their own.
-   To change the connection later, for example to rotate a password, run `tdk collection update --name mariadb_in --conn-file conn-mariadb-in.yaml`. The connector cannot change; to use another one, create another collection.

MariaDB uses the MySQL connection types; the `mariadb://` URI scheme is accepted in `uri`.

### Connection Config Parameters

#### `uri`

The SQLAlchemy-style connection URI: `mariadb://host:port/database`. Written as a plain value here, but accepts `secret:` too.

#### `credentials`

The database user and password, spliced into the URI at connect time. `UserPassword` requires a `user` and `password`.

#### `entity_whitelist`

A YAML list of regular expressions, not a comma-separated string. It is checked to be a list of valid regular expressions, but it has no effect yet. Leave it out.

#### `conn_cfg`

Driver-side options forwarded to the connection as SQLAlchemy `connect_args`.

# MongoDB

> Reference for the Tabsdata MongoDB destination connector and subscriber configuration.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connectors/mongodb

The MongoDB connector lets Tabsdata subscribers write data from Tabsdata tables into MongoDB collections, one document per row.

[See the full subscriber walkthrough](https://docs.tabsdata.com/tutorials/subscribers/mongodb)

The subscriber is registered in a collection created with a `MongoDBDestConn` connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in [Connection](#connection), at the end of this page.

### Prerequisites

-   The MongoDB deployment is reachable from the Tabsdata server.
-   The MongoDB user can create and write the target collections, and can drop them when replace mode is used.
-   `use_trxs=True` requires a replica set or sharded cluster that supports transactions.

### Subscriber

Configure `MongoDBDest` as the `destination` of a subscriber function to define which MongoDB collections Tabsdata writes.

write\_orders.py

```python
from tabsdatak.api import subscriber, TableFrameSpec
from tabsdatak.conn.mongodb import MongoDBDest

@subscriber(
    destination=MongoDBDest(
        collections_with_ids=[("sales_db.orders", "order_id")],
    ),
    input_tables=["orders"],
)
def write_orders(orders: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec:
    return orders
```

-   required
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    

### Function Config Parameters

#### `collections_with_ids`

A list of `(collection, id_field)` pairs. `collection` is the target collection, written `<database>.<collection>` or as a bare `<collection>` in the database named in the connection URI. `id_field` is the field used as each document's `_id`; `None` lets MongoDB generate the ids.

Each pair in `collections_with_ids` represents one destination slot and maps positionally to a value returned by the subscriber function.

#### `if_collection_exists`

`"append"` (the default) leaves the existing documents in place. `"replace"` drops the collection before writing, and its indexes and validators go with it.

#### `update_existing`

When `True` (the default), a document whose id already exists is updated (an upsert). When `False`, documents are inserted and an existing id fails the batch. Ignored when `id_field` is `None`, since generated ids never collide.

#### `use_trxs` and `docs_per_trx`

`docs_per_trx` sets the documents per write batch, `1000` by default. With `use_trxs=True`, each batch is written in a MongoDB transaction, which requires a replica set.

#### `maintain_order`

When `True`, documents are inserted in input order. Slower, but the server-side order is deterministic.

#### `fail_on_duplicate_key`

When `True` (the default), a duplicate-key error fails the write. When `False`, the outcome depends on the other settings. With `use_trxs=True`, the transaction is aborted, so the whole batch that holds the duplicate is rolled back and skipped. With `maintain_order=True`, the write stops at the first duplicate, so the rows after it are skipped.

#### `log_intermediate_files`

When `True`, each flushed batch is logged with its document count, for debugging large writes.

#### `dest_cfg`

Sets additional destination configuration. The only accepted key is `mongodb.logging_level`. `pymongo.*` options go in the connection's `conn_cfg`.

## Write behavior

Each `(collection, id_field)` entry in `collections_with_ids` is one destination slot. A named `id_field` becomes the document `_id`; `None` lets MongoDB generate it.

`if_collection_exists="append"` keeps existing documents. `"replace"` drops the collection first. With `update_existing=True`, matching ids are upserted with `$set`, so fields the row lacks keep their stored values; a missing column fails with `MONGODB_21`. With it disabled, the connector inserts and an id collision fails the batch.

## Operational notes

-   `docs_per_trx` is both the write-batch size and, when transactions are enabled, the number of documents per transaction.
-   `maintain_order=True` keeps input order but gives up some write throughput.
-   `fail_on_duplicate_key=False` with `use_trxs=True` drops the whole batch that holds the duplicate, not only the duplicate. Use it only when the other documents in that batch can be skipped.
-   Collections are written one after another in one session. Each `docs_per_trx` batch is its own transaction, so a failure leaves earlier batches committed; nothing rolls back across batches.
-   Tabsdata does not connect to MongoDB when the collection is created. URI, credential, topology, and permission errors appear when the subscriber runs.

## Connection

MongoDB subscribers use `MongoDBDestConn` to define the server and the credentials used by the subscriber.

conn-mongodb.yaml

```yaml
kind: connectionDef
apiVersion: '1.0'
type: tabsdatak.conn.mongodb:MongoDBDestConn
spec:
  uri: 'mongodb://mongo.internal:27017/sales_db'
  credentials:
    kind: userPasswordCredentials
    apiVersion: '1.0'
    type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:UserPassword
    spec:
      user: 'secret:tabsdata_writer'
      password: 'secret:example-password'
```

-   required
    
-   required
    
-   optional
    

### Create the collection

A subscriber is registered in a destination collection, and a destination collection is created with its connection. Every function registered in the collection uses that connection.

Generate a connection template, which lists all the connection fields:

```bash
tdk connection template --type mongodb-out --file conn-mongodb.yaml
```

Edit the template file with the MongoDB connection information, check it, and create the collection with it:

```bash
tdk connection validate --file conn-mongodb.yaml
```

```bash
tdk collection create --name mongodb_out --conn-file conn-mongodb.yaml
```

Then register the subscriber in the collection:

```bash
tdk fn register --coll mongodb_out --path write_orders.py::write_orders
```

-   The collection goes in the `destinations` group, because the connection is a destination connection. `--group` can be left out; if it is given, it must be `destinations`.
-   `secret:<value>` gives a secret value in the file itself. `$secret:<ENV_VAR>` reads it from an environment variable when the collection is created, so the value never appears in the file. Either way, Tabsdata stores the secret separately, and the stored connection only shows a placeholder.
-   Functions in the collection must use the connector of its connection: `MongoDBDest` for a collection created with `MongoDBDestConn`. Transformers go in a collection of their own.
-   To change the connection later, for example to rotate a password, run `tdk collection update --name mongodb_out --conn-file conn-mongodb.yaml`. The connector cannot change; to use another one, create another collection.
-   Creating a source or destination collection requires permission to manage the project.

### Connection Config Parameters

#### `uri`

The MongoDB connection URI without credentials, starting with `mongodb://` or `mongodb+srv://`, for example `mongodb://host:27017/sales_db`. The database in the URI is the one bare collection names are written to. Accepts `secret:` too.

#### `credentials`

A `UserPassword` with the MongoDB user and password, spliced into the URI when the subscriber writes.

#### `conn_cfg`

Options for the MongoDB client. `pymongo.*` keys are forwarded to `pymongo.MongoClient`.

# MSSQL

> Reference for the Tabsdata MSSQL connector.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connectors/mssql

The MSSQL connector lets Tabsdata run queries against MSSQL and write tables into MSSQL.

The `MSSQLSrc` connector can be used by a publisher function to read data from MSSQL into a Tabsdata table.

The `MSSQLDest` connector can be used by a subscriber function to write data from a Tabsdata table into MSSQL.

## Publisher

The `MSSQLSrc` connector can be used by a publisher function to read data from MSSQL into a Tabsdata table. [See the full publisher walkthrough](https://docs.tabsdata.com/tutorials/publishers/mssql)

The publisher is registered in a collection created with a `MSSQLSrcConn` connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in [Publisher connection](#publisher-connection), at the end of this page.

### Prerequisites

-   The MSSQL server is reachable from the Tabsdata server.
-   The Microsoft ODBC Driver 18 for SQL Server is installed on the Tabsdata server. The URI names it with `driver`; see [Installing Third-Party Database Drivers](https://docs.tabsdata.com/server-admin/third-party-database-drivers).
-   The connection user can run every query in `queries` and read every referenced table or view.

### Publisher

Configure `MSSQLSrc` as the `source` of a publisher function to select the queries that Tabsdata runs against MSSQL.

publish\_orders.py

```python
from tabsdatak.api import publisher
from tabsdatak.conn.mssql import MSSQLSrc

@publisher(
    source=MSSQLSrc(
        queries=[
            "SELECT * FROM orders",
        ],
    ),
    output_tables=["orders"],
)
def publish_orders(orders):
    return orders
```

-   required
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    

### Function Config Parameters

#### `queries`

Defines the SQL queries the publisher runs against MSSQL.

Each element in `queries` represents one source slot and maps positionally to an argument in the publisher function.

For example:

```python
MSSQLSrc(
    queries=[
        "SELECT * FROM country",
        "SELECT * FROM city",
    ],
)
```

#### `initial_values`

The first-run values for named parameters in `queries`, written `:name`. On later runs each parameter takes the value the publisher stored with `ctx.set_attr(name, value)`, so a query can read only the rows added since the last run.

Parameters bind values such as IDs and timestamps, not identifiers. Schema and table names have to be written into the query.

For example:

```python
from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, TrxCtx, publisher
from tabsdatak.conn.mssql import MSSQLSrc


@publisher(
    source=MSSQLSrc(
        queries=["SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id > :last_id ORDER BY id"],
        initial_values={"last_id": 0},
    ),
    output_tables=["orders"],
)
def publish_orders(orders: TableFrameSpec, ctx: TrxCtx) -> TableFrameSpec:
    row = orders.max_for("id")
    if row is not None and row["id"] is not None:
        ctx.set_attr("last_id", int(row["id"]))
    return orders
```

#### `src_cfg`

Sets additional source configuration.

## Subscriber

The `MSSQLDest` connector can be used by a subscriber function to write data from a Tabsdata table into MSSQL. [See the full subscriber walkthrough](https://docs.tabsdata.com/tutorials/subscribers/mssql)

The subscriber is registered in a collection created with a `MSSQLDestConn` connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in [Subscriber connection](#subscriber-connection), at the end of this page.

### Prerequisites

-   The MSSQL server is reachable from the Tabsdata server.
-   The Microsoft ODBC Driver 18 for SQL Server is installed on the Tabsdata server. The URI names it with `driver`; see [Installing Third-Party Database Drivers](https://docs.tabsdata.com/server-admin/third-party-database-drivers).
-   The connection user can create missing destination tables and insert rows. With `if_table_exists="replace"`, it also needs to drop and create tables, and with `schema_evolution="update"`, to alter them.

### Subscriber

Configure `MSSQLDest` as the `destination` of a subscriber function to define which tables Tabsdata writes in MSSQL.

write\_orders.py

```python
from tabsdatak.api import subscriber
from tabsdatak.conn.mssql import MSSQLDest

@subscriber(
    destination=MSSQLDest(
        tables=[
            "orders",
        ],
    ),
    input_tables=["orders"],
)
def write_orders(orders):
    return orders
```

-   required
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    

### Function Config Parameters

#### `tables`

Defines the destination tables the subscriber writes to in MSSQL.

Each element in `tables` represents one destination slot and maps positionally to a value returned by the subscriber function.

For example:

```python
MSSQLDest(
    tables=[
        "vendors",
        "items",
    ],
)
```

#### `if_table_exists`

Controls what happens when the destination table already has rows. `"append"` (the default) keeps inserting into the existing rows. `"replace"` drops the table and creates it again from the returned frame, so the table's schema follows the frame. With `transactional=True`, the drop, the create and the insert run in one transaction. On `"append"`, `schema_evolution` decides what happens to a new or wider column.

#### `schema_evolution`

`"strict"` (the default) or `"update"`. A refused write fails with `SQL_COMMON_10` before anything is written. See [Schema evolution](#schema-evolution).

#### `dest_cfg`

Sets additional destination configuration.

## Query results

Each entry in `queries` produces one source slot. The slots map by position to the publisher function arguments and then to `output_tables`. Keep those three lists in the same order.

Queries run when the publisher is triggered. They are not a continuous change feed. To read incrementally, put named parameters such as `:last_id` in the query, set their first values with `initial_values`, and save the next values with `ctx.set_attr()` after each successful run.

## Write behavior

Each entry in `tables` is one destination slot and maps by position to a value returned by the subscriber function. Returning `None` for a slot skips that write.

`if_table_exists="append"` keeps the rows already in the destination and inserts the returned rows. `"replace"` drops the table and creates it again from the returned frame. On `"append"`, `schema_evolution="update"` adds new columns and widens number types; removing a column or changing a non-number type still needs a database migration before the subscriber runs.

### Schema evolution

`schema_evolution` decides what a write does when the returned frame has a column the destination table lacks, or a type wider than the column's. `"strict"`, the default, refuses a new column, and refuses a wider type unless its values fit the column. `"update"` changes the table to fit the frame. On SQL Server, `"update"` uses [Iceberg schema evolution](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connectors/schema-evolution#native-and-iceberg-schema-evolution), applied by the connector, on `"append"` and `"replace"`: `ALTER TABLE … ADD` adds columns, and integers, decimals and floats are widened by digits or width. It never drops a column or changes a non-number type. `"merge"` is not supported.

## Operational notes

-   Without `trigger_by`, a publisher runs only when triggered manually, while a subscriber runs when any input table commits. Set `trigger_by` to change when the function runs.
-   Tabsdata checks the connection document when the collection is created, but it does not connect to MSSQL then. A bad host, credential, query, or permission fails when the function runs.
-   Every function in the collection uses the same connection. Use another collection when functions need another database or another set of credentials.

## Publisher connection

MSSQL publishers use `MSSQLSrcConn` to define the database connection and credentials used by the publisher.

conn-mssql-in.yaml

```yaml
kind: connectionDef
apiVersion: '1.0'
type: tabsdatak.conn.mssql:MSSQLSrcConn
spec:
  uri: 'mssql+pyodbc://db.internal:1433/world?driver=ODBC+Driver+18+for+SQL+Server'
  credentials:
    kind: userPasswordCredentials
    apiVersion: '1.0'
    type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:UserPassword
    spec:
      user: 'secret:tabsdata_reader'
      password: 'secret:example-password'
```

-   required
    
-   required
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    

### Create the collection

A publisher is registered in a source collection, and a source collection is created with its connection. Every function registered in the collection uses that connection.

Generate a connection template, which lists all the connection fields:

```bash
tdk connection template --type mssql-sql-in --file conn-mssql-in.yaml
```

Edit the template file with the MSSQL connection information, check it, and create the collection with it:

```bash
tdk connection validate --file conn-mssql-in.yaml
```

```bash
tdk collection create --name mssql_in --conn-file conn-mssql-in.yaml
```

Then register the publisher in the collection:

```bash
tdk fn register --coll mssql_in --path publish_orders.py::publish_orders
```

-   The collection goes in the `sources` group, because the connection is a source connection. `--group` can be left out; if it is given, it must be `sources`.
-   `secret:<value>` gives a secret value in the file itself. `$secret:<ENV_VAR>` reads it from an environment variable when the collection is created, so the value never appears in the file. Either way, Tabsdata stores the secret separately, and the stored connection only shows a placeholder.
-   Functions in the collection must use the connector of its connection: `MSSQLSrc` for a collection created with `MSSQLSrcConn`. Transformers go in a collection of their own.
-   To change the connection later, for example to rotate a password, run `tdk collection update --name mssql_in --conn-file conn-mssql-in.yaml`. The connector cannot change; to use another one, create another collection.
-   Creating a source or destination collection requires permission to manage the project.

### Connection Config Parameters

#### `uri`

The SQLAlchemy-style connection URI: `mssql+pyodbc://host:port/database?driver=ODBC+Driver+18+for+SQL+Server`. The `driver` value names the ODBC driver installed on the server. Written as a plain value here, but accepts `secret:` too.

#### `credentials`

The database user and password, spliced into the URI at connect time. `UserPassword` requires a `user` and `password`.

#### `entity_whitelist`

A YAML list of regular expressions, not a comma-separated string. It is checked to be a list of valid regular expressions, but it has no effect yet. Leave it out.

#### `conn_cfg`

Driver-side options forwarded to the connection as SQLAlchemy `connect_args`.

## Subscriber connection

MSSQL subscribers use `MSSQLDestConn` to define the database connection and credentials used by the subscriber.

conn-mssql-out.yaml

```yaml
kind: connectionDef
apiVersion: '1.0'
type: tabsdatak.conn.mssql:MSSQLDestConn
spec:
  uri: 'mssql+pyodbc://db.internal:1433/warehouse?driver=ODBC+Driver+18+for+SQL+Server'
  credentials:
    kind: userPasswordCredentials
    apiVersion: '1.0'
    type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:UserPassword
    spec:
      user: 'secret:tabsdata_reader'
      password: 'secret:example-password'
```

-   required
    
-   required
    
-   optional

-   The collection goes in the `destinations` group, because the connection is a destination connection. `--group` can be left out; if it is given, it must be `destinations`.

# MySQL

> Reference for the Tabsdata MySQL connector.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connectors/mysql

The MySQL connector lets Tabsdata run queries against MySQL and write tables into MySQL.

The `MySQLSrc` connector can be used by a publisher function to read data from MySQL into a Tabsdata table.

The `MySQLDest` connector can be used by a subscriber function to write data from a Tabsdata table into MySQL.

note

A connection URI that names the `mysql+mysqlconnector://` driver uses `mysql-connector-python`, which Tabsdata does not redistribute. Install it as described in [Installing Third-Party Database Drivers](https://docs.tabsdata.com/server-admin/third-party-database-drivers).

# MySQL CDC

> Reference for the Tabsdata MySQL CDC stream source: prerequisites, the full load, change rows, and the connection.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connectors/mysql-cdc

The MySQL CDC connector lets Tabsdata capture the changes made to MySQL tables (inserts, updates, deletes and truncates) as they are committed, and publish them into Tabsdata tables.

With `start_from="full"`, the stream starts with a full load: it takes a consistent snapshot of the tracked tables and then switches to change capture from the exact point of that snapshot, with no gaps and no duplicates when the global read lock is taken. Where the server refuses the lock, the limits in [Full load without the global read lock](#full-load-without-the-global-read-lock) apply. The full load and the change capture are one stream publisher, so there is nothing to reconcile between them.

The `MySQLCdcStreamSrc` connector can be used by a [stream publisher](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/functions/stream-publishers) function to follow the MySQL binary log (binlog) as a replica would and write every captured change into a Tabsdata table.

Unlike `MySQLSrc`, which runs queries on a trigger, a CDC source runs continuously: registering the stream publisher starts a long-lived worker that keeps reading the binlog until the function is disabled or deleted.

## Publisher

The `MySQLCdcStreamSrc` connector can be used by a stream publisher function to capture changes from MySQL into Tabsdata tables. [See the full publisher walkthrough](https://docs.tabsdata.com/tutorials/publishers/mysql-cdc)

The stream publisher is registered in a collection created with a `MySQLCdcStreamSrcConn` connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in [Connection](#connection), at the end of this page.

### Prerequisites

-   The server's binlog is set up for row-based capture: `log_bin = ON`, `binlog_format = ROW`, `binlog_row_image = FULL` and `gtid_mode = ON`. The stream checks these at start and refuses a server that does not have them.
-   The connecting user holds the replication privileges a binlog reader needs (`REPLICATION SLAVE` and `REPLICATION CLIENT`).
-   When streaming from a replica, the replica runs with `log_replica_updates = ON`, and with `replica_preserve_commit_order = ON` if it applies transactions in parallel.
-   For `start_from="full"`, the connecting user also holds `SELECT` on every tracked table, and `RELOAD` where the server grants it, for the global read lock. The tracked tables are InnoDB. Managed services such as Amazon RDS and Aurora refuse the global read lock, and the full load still runs there with the same transactional consistency.

### Publisher

Configure `MySQLCdcStreamSrc` as the `source` of a `@stream_publisher` function to select the tables whose changes Tabsdata captures.

stream\_sales\_changes.py

```python
from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, TableFramesSpec, stream_publisher
from tabsdatak.conn.mysql import MySQLCdcStreamSrc
from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import concat

@stream_publisher(
    source=MySQLCdcStreamSrc(
        tables=[
            "sales.orders",
            "sales.customers",
        ],
        start_from="full",
    ),
    batch_max_secs=120,
    output_tables=["orders_changes", "customers_changes"],
)
def stream_sales_changes(
    orders: TableFramesSpec,
    customers: TableFramesSpec,
) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec, TableFrameSpec]:
    return concat(orders), concat(customers)
```

-   required
    
-   required
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    

`batch_max_secs=120` hands the captured changes to the function at least every two minutes. The `batch_*` parameters decide when a batch of changes is handed to the function, and are the same for every stream source. See [Stream Publishers](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/functions/stream-publishers#batch-parameters) for all of them.

A stream publisher differs from a regular publisher in three ways:

-   It has no trigger. Registering it starts the stream worker, which runs until the function is disabled or deleted.
-   Each element of `tables` is one function parameter, and each parameter receives a list of frames: the changes captured for that table since the previous batch. Fold them with `concat`, which also returns `None` when the batch carried nothing for that table.
-   The function must not declare a `ctx` parameter.

### Function Config Parameters

#### `tables`

Defines the MySQL tables whose changes are captured, as qualified `database.table` names.

Each element in `tables` represents one source slot and maps positionally to an argument in the publisher function and to an entry in `output_tables`. A table listed twice is refused with `CONN_37`.

For example:

```python
MySQLCdcStreamSrc(
    tables=[
        "sales.orders",
        "sales.customers",
    ],
    start_from="tail",
)
```

#### `start_from`

Where the stream starts the first time it runs. Later runs resume from the position the stream has recorded.

-   `"full"`: a full load of every tracked table, then the changes committed after it. See [Full load](#full-load).
-   `"tail"`: only changes committed after the stream starts.
-   `"head"`: replay from the oldest change still in binlog retention.
-   `GtidPosition(gtid="<uuid>:<n>")`: after a global transaction id. The given GTIDs count as already read, and the stream starts with the next transaction. A range such as `"<uuid>:1-<n>"` is accepted too.
-   `BinlogPosition(file="mysql-bin.000001", pos=4)`: from a binlog file and byte offset, as `SHOW BINARY LOG STATUS` or `SHOW BINLOG EVENTS` report them. Position `4` is the start of a file.
-   `TimestampPosition(ts=...)`: from the first binlog event at or after a point in time. A naive datetime is read as UTC. A time before the oldest retained binlog is refused.

#### Full load

With `start_from="full"`, the stream first emits every row of each tracked table and then captures the changes from the exact binlog position of that snapshot. The snapshot is consistent across all the tracked tables, and when the global read lock is taken, no change is missed or repeated between the snapshot and the change capture.

-   Each table's snapshot is preceded by one `LOAD` row (`@td.cdc.meta.op = "l"`), and its rows arrive as inserts. A `LOAD` row tells the consumer to empty its copy of the table before applying the rows that follow.
-   The tables are read in one consistent-snapshot transaction. To pin that snapshot to a binlog position, the stream briefly takes the global read lock. The lock is held only while the position is read, not while the tables are scanned. On servers that refuse the lock, such as Amazon RDS and Aurora, the load runs without it; see [Full load without the global read lock](#full-load-without-the-global-read-lock).

To resynchronize a destination later, keep `start_from="full"` and reset the function's stage:

```bash
tdk fn update --reset-stage <other options>
```

The stream then starts again with a new full load and its `LOAD` rows. Resetting the stage with any other `start_from` restarts at that position and sends no `LOAD` row.

#### Full load without the global read lock

Without the lock, the snapshot is not pinned to one binlog position. The connector brackets the load with the binlog position before and after it, and deduplicates the changes that fall inside that window. The lockless load has these limits:

-   A table with a primary key is deduplicated by key. A keyless table cannot be matched row by row, so its changes inside the window arrive twice.
-   A key swap, a `TRUNCATE` or a schema change during the load fails the stream with `CDC_23` to `CDC_25`.
-   The `map` format fails the load with `CDC_26`.
-   A load with more changes in its window than `tabsdata.cdc.initial_load.max_window_changes` fails with `CDC_29`.

#### `columns_format`

How each change row lays out the table's column values: `"columns"` (the default), `"struct"` or `"map"`. See [Change rows](#change-rows).

#### `flatten_columns`

When `True` (the default), the new column values are written as ordinary top-level columns, so each change row reads like a row of the source table. `columns_format` then only shapes the old values. See [Change rows](#change-rows).

#### `src_cfg`

Sets additional source configuration. Only these keys are accepted:

| Key | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `tabsdata.cdc.buffer.max_rows` | `10000` | Rows buffered in the worker before they are written out to a file. |
| `tabsdata.cdc.buffer.max_bytes` | none | Bytes buffered before they are written out. Measuring bytes costs time on every change; prefer bounding by rows. |
| `tabsdata.cdc.buffer.max_secs` | `60` | Longest time a change waits in the buffer. |
| `tabsdata.cdc.poll.max_secs` | `1` | Longest time one read of the binlog waits for changes. |
| `tabsdata.cdc.poll.idle_secs` | `1` | Pause after a read that found no changes. |
| `tabsdata.cdc.max_large_text_length` | `1024` | Longest value, in characters, accepted from an unbounded text column. A longer value fails the stream. |
| `tabsdata.cdc.initial_load.max_window_changes` | `100000` | Most changes the full load can hold in its window when it runs without the global read lock. Above it the load fails with `CDC_29`. |
| `tabsdata.cdc.fetch_size` | `100000` | Rows fetched per round trip while reading the full load. |
| `tabsdata.cdc.chunk_size` | `100000` | Rows per chunk while writing the full load. |
| `mysql.cdc.logging_level` | `40` | Logging verbosity of the connector, as a Python logging level number (`10` debug, `20` info, `30` warning, `40` error). |

The buffer settings control when captured changes are written to files inside the worker. When those files are handed to the function is controlled by the [batch parameters](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/functions/stream-publishers#batch-parameters) of `@stream_publisher`.

## Change rows

Every row the stream emits is one change. Besides the column values, each row carries change metadata:

| Column | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `@td.cdc.meta.op` | `str` | The operation: `"i"` insert, `"u"` update, `"d"` delete, `"t"` truncate, `"l"` load (start of a full load). |
| `@td.cdc.meta.tx` | `str` | The transaction's GTID. Full load rows carry `initial-load`. |
| `@td.cdc.meta.sq` | `int` | The change's sequence within its transaction. |
| `@td.cdc.meta.ts` | `datetime` (UTC) | When the transaction committed. Full load rows carry the time the snapshot was taken. |
| `@td.cdc.meta.seg` | `decimal` | The transaction's number in its GTID. Full load rows carry `-1`. |
| `@td.cdc.meta.ord` | `decimal` | The position of the change within the transaction. Ordering by `seg` and then `ord` gives the order the changes were committed in. |
| `@td.cdc.meta.fmt` | `str` | The `columns_format` the row was produced with. |
| `@td.cdc.meta.flat` | `bool` | The `flatten_columns` setting the row was produced with. |
| `@td.cdc.meta.sch` | `str` | A hash of the source table's schema when the change was captured. It changes when the table's columns change. |

The column values are laid out according to `flatten_columns` and `columns_format`:

|  | New values | Old values |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `flatten_columns=True` (default) | One top-level column per source column, with the source column's name. | Depends on `columns_format`. |
| `columns_format="columns"` (default) | `@td.cdc.data.col.new.<column>` per column, when not flattened. | `@td.cdc.data.col.old.<column>` per column. |
| `columns_format="struct"` | `@td.cdc.data.row.new`, one struct, when not flattened. | `@td.cdc.data.row.old`, one struct. |
| `columns_format="map"` | `@td.cdc.data.map.new`, a JSON object as a string, when not flattened. | `@td.cdc.data.map.old`, a JSON object as a string. |

What each operation carries:

| Operation | New values | Old values |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Insert (`i`) | The inserted row. | Empty. |
| Update (`u`) | The row after the update. | The complete row before the update. |
| Delete (`d`) | The deleted row. | Empty. |
| Truncate (`t`), Load (`l`) | Empty. | Empty. |

Empty values are null columns with `"columns"`, a struct whose fields are all null with `"struct"`, and a JSON object whose values are all null with `"map"`.

A `LOAD` row tells the consumer to empty its copy of the table before applying the rows that follow. A `TRUNCATE` row reports that the source table was truncated.

`BLOB` columns are not captured: they always arrive as null.

`TIMESTAMP` columns are rewritten to the server time zone's wall clock. When that zone is unknown, the connector uses UTC and logs one warning.

Use `"columns"` with `flatten_columns=True` for changes that land in a table and get queried. Use `"struct"` or `"map"` when the source table's schema may change while the stream runs, to carry the values opaquely instead of changing the output table's columns.

## Operational notes

-   MariaDB is not supported. A `mariadb://` URI is accepted, but the server check fails with `MYSQL_27`, because MariaDB has no `gtid_mode`.
-   MySQL has no replication slot, so a stopped stream holds nothing on the server. It resumes from its recorded GTID, provided the server still retains the binlogs from that point. If they were purged, the stream fails and needs a new full load: reset the stage with `start_from="full"`.
-   A stream follows one source server. Switching it to another server (for example after a failover) is not supported: the new server's changes would be dropped as already published. Start a new stream instead.

## Connection

MySQL CDC stream publishers use `MySQLCdcStreamSrcConn` to define the database connection and credentials used by the stream.

conn-mysql-cdc.yaml

```yaml
kind: connectionDef
apiVersion: '1.0'
type: tabsdatak.conn.mysql:MySQLCdcStreamSrcConn
spec:
  uri: 'mysql://db.internal:3306/sales'
  credentials:
    kind: userPasswordCredentials
    apiVersion: '1.0'
    type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:UserPassword
    spec:
      user: 'secret:tabsdata_cdc'
      password: 'secret:example-password'
```

-   required
    
-   required
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    

### Create the collection

A stream publisher is registered in a source collection, and a source collection is created with its connection. Every function registered in the collection uses that connection.

Generate a connection template, which lists all the connection fields:

```bash
tdk connection template --type mysql-cdc --file conn-mysql-cdc.yaml
```

Edit the template file with the MySQL connection information, check it, and create the collection with it:

```bash
tdk connection validate --file conn-mysql-cdc.yaml
```

```bash
tdk collection create --name sales_cdc --conn-file conn-mysql-cdc.yaml
```

Then register the stream publisher in the collection:

```bash
tdk fn register --coll sales_cdc --path stream_sales_changes.py::stream_sales_changes
```

-   The collection goes in the `sources` group, because the connection is a source connection. `--group` can be left out; if it is given, it must be `sources`.
-   `secret:<value>` gives a secret value in the file itself. `$secret:<ENV_VAR>` reads it from an environment variable when the collection is created, so the value never appears in the file. Either way, Tabsdata stores the secret separately, and the stored connection only shows a placeholder.
-   Functions in the collection must use the connector of its connection: `MySQLCdcStreamSrc` for a collection created with `MySQLCdcStreamSrcConn`. Transformers go in a collection of their own.
-   To change the connection later, for example to rotate a password, run `tdk collection update --name sales_cdc --conn-file conn-mysql-cdc.yaml`. The connector cannot change; to use another one, create another collection.
-   Creating a source or destination collection requires permission to manage the project.
-   A batch `MySQLSrc` publisher cannot share this collection, because it uses a different connection (`mysql-sql-in`).

### Connection Config Parameters

#### `uri`

The SQLAlchemy-style connection URI: `mysql://host:port/database`. Written as a plain value here, but accepts `secret:` too.

#### `credentials`

The database user and password, spliced into the URI at connect time. `UserPassword` requires a `user` and `password`.

#### `server_id`

The replica id the stream registers with when it reads the binlog. Defaults to `512`.

MySQL admits one replica per `server_id`: a second stream connecting with the same id disconnects the first. Give every stream publisher reading the same MySQL server its own connection with a distinct `server_id`, and keep them clear of the ids your real replicas use.

#### `entity_whitelist`

A YAML list of regular expressions, not a comma-separated string. It is checked to be a list of valid regular expressions, but it has no effect yet: it does not limit which tables a stream can track. Leave it out.

#### `conn_cfg`

pymysql connection keywords such as `ssl_ca`, `ssl_cert`, `ssl_key`, `ssl_disabled`, `charset` or `connect_timeout`. They apply to every connection the stream opens: catalog reads, the binlog reader, the full load and the server checks.

# Oracle

> Reference for the Tabsdata Oracle connector.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connectors/oracle

The Oracle connector lets Tabsdata run queries against Oracle and write tables into Oracle.

The `OracleSrc` connector can be used by a publisher function to read data from Oracle into a Tabsdata table.

The `OracleDest` connector can be used by a subscriber function to write data from a Tabsdata table into Oracle.

warning

The Oracle connector needs the `oracledb` driver, which Tabsdata does not redistribute. See [Installing Third-Party Database Drivers](https://docs.tabsdata.com/server-admin/third-party-database-drivers) to add it to your Tabsdata server.

## Publisher

The `OracleSrc` connector can be used by a publisher function to read data from Oracle into a Tabsdata table. [See the full publisher walkthrough](https://docs.tabsdata.com/tutorials/publishers/oracle)

The publisher is registered in a collection created with a `OracleSrcConn` connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in [Publisher connection](#publisher-connection), at the end of this page.

### Prerequisites

-   The Oracle server is reachable from the Tabsdata server.
-   The connection user can run every query in `queries` and read every referenced table or view.

### Publisher

Configure `OracleSrc` as the `source` of a publisher function to select the queries that Tabsdata runs against Oracle.

publish\_orders.py

```python
from tabsdatak.api import publisher
from tabsdatak.conn.oracle import OracleSrc

@publisher(
    source=OracleSrc(
        queries=[
            "SELECT * FROM orders",
        ],
    ),
    output_tables=["orders"],
)
def publish_orders(orders):
    return orders
```

-   required
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    

### Function Config Parameters

#### `queries`

Defines the SQL queries the publisher runs against Oracle.

Each element in `queries` represents one source slot and maps positionally to an argument in the publisher function.

For example:

```python
OracleSrc(
    queries=[
        "SELECT * FROM country",
        "SELECT * FROM city",
    ],
)
```

#### `initial_values`

The first-run values for named parameters in `queries`, written `:name`. On later runs each parameter takes the value the publisher stored with `ctx.set_attr(name, value)`, so a query can read only the rows added since the last run.

Parameters bind values such as IDs and timestamps, not identifiers. Schema and table names have to be written into the query.

For example:

```python
from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, TrxCtx, publisher
from tabsdatak.conn.oracle import OracleSrc


@publisher(
    source=OracleSrc(
        queries=["SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id > :last_id ORDER BY id"],
        initial_values={"last_id": 0},
    ),
    output_tables=["orders"],
)
def publish_orders(orders: TableFrameSpec, ctx: TrxCtx) -> TableFrameSpec:
    row = orders.max_for("id")
    if row is not None and row["id"] is not None:
        ctx.set_attr("last_id", int(row["id"]))
    return orders
```

#### `src_cfg`

Sets additional source configuration.

## Subscriber

The `OracleDest` connector can be used by a subscriber function to write data from a Tabsdata table into Oracle. [See the full subscriber walkthrough](https://docs.tabsdata.com/tutorials/subscribers/oracle)

The subscriber is registered in a collection created with a `OracleDestConn` connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in [Subscriber connection](#subscriber-connection), at the end of this page.

### Prerequisites

-   The Oracle server is reachable from the Tabsdata server.
-   The connection user can create missing destination tables and insert rows. With `if_table_exists="replace"`, it also needs to drop and create tables, and with `schema_evolution="update"`, to alter them.

### Subscriber

Configure `OracleDest` as the `destination` of a subscriber function to define which tables Tabsdata writes in Oracle.

write\_orders.py

```python
from tabsdatak.api import subscriber
from tabsdatak.conn.oracle import OracleDest

@subscriber(
    destination=OracleDest(
        tables=[
            "orders",
        ],
    ),
    input_tables=["orders"],
)
def write_orders(orders):
    return orders
```

-   required
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    

### Function Config Parameters

#### `tables`

Defines the destination tables the subscriber writes to in Oracle.

Each element in `tables` represents one destination slot and maps positionally to a value returned by the subscriber function.

For example:

```python
OracleDest(
    tables=[
        "vendors",
        "items",
    ],
)
```

#### `if_table_exists`

Controls what happens when the destination table already has rows. `"append"` (the default) keeps inserting into the existing rows. `"replace"` drops the table and creates it again from the returned frame, so the table's schema follows the frame. The drop and the create commit implicitly, so a failed write is not undone. On `"append"`, `schema_evolution` decides what happens to a new or wider column.

#### `schema_evolution`

`"strict"` (the default) or `"update"`. A refused write fails with `SQL_COMMON_10` before anything is written. The `ALTER` statements `"update"` runs commit implicitly, so they are not undone if the write fails. See [Schema evolution](#schema-evolution).

#### `dest_cfg`

Sets additional destination configuration.

## Query results

Each entry in `queries` produces one source slot. The slots map by position to the publisher function arguments and then to `output_tables`. Keep those three lists in the same order.

Queries run when the publisher is triggered. They are not a continuous change feed. To read incrementally, put named parameters such as `:last_id` in the query, set their first values with `initial_values`, and save the next values with `ctx.set_attr()` after each successful run.

## Write behavior

Each entry in `tables` is one destination slot and maps by position to a value returned by the subscriber function. Returning `None` for a slot skips that write.

`if_table_exists="append"` keeps the rows already in the destination and inserts the returned rows. `"replace"` drops the table and creates it again from the returned frame. On `"append"`, `schema_evolution="update"` adds new columns and widens number types; removing a column or changing a non-number type still needs a database migration before the subscriber runs.

### Schema evolution

`schema_evolution` decides what a write does when the returned frame has a column the destination table lacks, or a type wider than the column's. `"strict"`, the default, refuses a new column, and refuses a wider type unless its values fit the column. `"update"` changes the table to fit the frame. On Oracle, `"update"` uses [Iceberg schema evolution](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connectors/schema-evolution#native-and-iceberg-schema-evolution), applied by the connector, on `"append"` and `"replace"`: `ALTER TABLE … ADD` adds columns, and integers, decimals and floats are widened by digits or width. It never drops a column or changes a non-number type. `"merge"` is not supported.

## Operational notes

-   Without `trigger_by`, a publisher runs only when triggered manually, while a subscriber runs when any input table commits. Set `trigger_by` to change when the function runs.
-   Tabsdata checks the connection document when the collection is created, but it does not connect to Oracle then. A bad host, credential, query, or permission fails when the function runs.
-   Every function in the collection uses the same connection. Use another collection when functions need another database or another set of credentials.

#### `credentials`

# Postgres

> Reference for the Tabsdata Postgres connector.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connectors/postgres

The Postgres connector lets Tabsdata run queries against Postgres and write tables into Postgres.

The `PostgresSrc` connector can be used by a publisher function to read data from Postgres into a Tabsdata table.

The `PostgresDest` connector can be used by a subscriber function to write data from a Tabsdata table into Postgres.

warning

The PostgreSQL connector needs the `psycopg2-binary` driver, which Tabsdata does not redistribute. See [Installing Third-Party Database Drivers](https://docs.tabsdata.com/server-admin/third-party-database-drivers) to add it to your Tabsdata server.

## Publisher

The `PostgresSrc` connector can be used by a publisher function to read data from Postgres into a Tabsdata table. [See the full publisher walkthrough](https://docs.tabsdata.com/tutorials/publishers/postgres)

The publisher is registered in a collection created with a `PostgresSrcConn` connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in [Publisher connection](#publisher-connection), at the end of this page.

### Prerequisites

-   The Postgres server is reachable from the Tabsdata server.
-   The connection user can run every query in `queries` and read every referenced table or view.

### Publisher

Configure `PostgresSrc` as the `source` of a publisher function to select the queries that Tabsdata runs against Postgres.

publish\_orders.py

```python
from tabsdatak.api import publisher
from tabsdatak.conn.postgres import PostgresSrc

@publisher(
    source=PostgresSrc(
        queries=[
            "SELECT * FROM orders",
        ],
    ),
    output_tables=["orders"],
)
def publish_orders(orders):
    return orders
```

-   required
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    

### Function Config Parameters

#### `queries`

Defines the SQL queries the publisher runs against Postgres.

Each element in `queries` represents one source slot and maps positionally to an argument in the publisher function.

For example:

```python
PostgresSrc(
    queries=[
        "SELECT * FROM country",
        "SELECT * FROM city",
    ],
)
```

#### `initial_values`

The first-run values for named parameters in `queries`, written `:name`. On later runs each parameter takes the value the publisher stored with `ctx.set_attr(name, value)`, so a query can read only the rows added since the last run.

Parameters bind values such as IDs and timestamps, not identifiers. Schema and table names have to be written into the query.

For example:

```python
from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, TrxCtx, publisher
from tabsdatak.conn.postgres import PostgresSrc


@publisher(
    source=PostgresSrc(
        queries=["SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id > :last_id ORDER BY id"],
        initial_values={"last_id": 0},
    ),
    output_tables=["orders"],
)
def publish_orders(orders: TableFrameSpec, ctx: TrxCtx) -> TableFrameSpec:
    row = orders.max_for("id")
    if row is not None and row["id"] is not None:
        ctx.set_attr("last_id", int(row["id"]))
    return orders
```

#### `src_cfg`

Sets additional source configuration.

## Subscriber

The `PostgresDest` connector can be used by a subscriber function to write data from a Tabsdata table into Postgres. [See the full subscriber walkthrough](https://docs.tabsdata.com/tutorials/subscribers/postgres)

The subscriber is registered in a collection created with a `PostgresDestConn` connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in [Subscriber connection](#subscriber-connection), at the end of this page.

### Prerequisites

-   The Postgres server is reachable from the Tabsdata server.
-   The connection user can create missing destination tables and insert rows. With `if_table_exists="replace"`, it also needs to drop and create tables, and with `schema_evolution="update"`, to alter them.

### Subscriber

Configure `PostgresDest` as the `destination` of a subscriber function to define which tables Tabsdata writes in Postgres.

write\_orders.py

```python
from tabsdatak.api import subscriber
from tabsdatak.conn.postgres import PostgresDest

@subscriber(
    destination=PostgresDest(
        tables=[
            "orders",
        ],
    ),
    input_tables=["orders"],
)
def write_orders(orders):
    return orders
```

-   required
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    

### Function Config Parameters

#### `tables`

Defines the destination tables the subscriber writes to in Postgres.

Each element in `tables` represents one destination slot and maps positionally to a value returned by the subscriber function.

For example:

```python
PostgresDest(
    tables=[
        "vendors",
        "items",
    ],
)
```

#### `if_table_exists`

Controls what happens when the destination table already has rows. `"append"` (the default) keeps inserting into the existing rows. `"replace"` drops the table and creates it again from the returned frame, so the table's schema follows the frame. With `transactional=True`, the drop, the create and the insert run in one transaction. On `"append"`, `schema_evolution` decides what happens to a new or wider column.

#### `schema_evolution`

`"strict"` (the default) or `"update"`. A refused write fails with `SQL_COMMON_10` before anything is written. See [Schema evolution](#schema-evolution).

#### `dest_cfg`

Sets additional destination configuration.

## Query results

Each entry in `queries` produces one source slot. The slots map by position to the publisher function arguments and then to `output_tables`. Keep those three lists in the same order.

Queries run when the publisher is triggered. They are not a continuous change feed. To read incrementally, put named parameters such as `:last_id` in the query, set their first values with `initial_values`, and save the next values with `ctx.set_attr()` after each successful run.

## Write behavior

Each entry in `tables` is one destination slot and maps by position to a value returned by the subscriber function. Returning `None` for a slot skips that write.

`if_table_exists="append"` keeps the rows already in the destination and inserts the returned rows. `"replace"` drops the table and creates it again from the returned frame. On `"append"`, `schema_evolution="update"` adds new columns and widens number types; removing a column or changing a non-number type still needs a database migration before the subscriber runs.

### Schema evolution

`schema_evolution` decides what a write does when the returned frame has a column the destination table lacks, or a type wider than the column's. `"strict"`, the default, refuses a new column, and refuses a wider type unless its values fit the column. `"update"` changes the table to fit the frame. On Postgres, `"update"` uses [Iceberg schema evolution](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connectors/schema-evolution#native-and-iceberg-schema-evolution), applied by the connector, on `"append"` and `"replace"`: `ALTER TABLE … ADD` adds columns, and integers, decimals and floats are widened by digits or width. It never drops a column or changes a non-number type. `"merge"` is not supported.

## Operational notes

-   Without `trigger_by`, a publisher runs only when triggered manually, while a subscriber runs when any input table commits. Set `trigger_by` to change when the function runs.
-   Tabsdata checks the connection document when the collection is created, but it does not connect to Postgres then. A bad host, credential, query, or permission fails when the function runs.
-   Every function in the collection uses the same connection. Use another collection when functions need another database or another set of credentials.

## Publisher connection

Postgres publishers use `PostgresSrcConn` to define the database connection and credentials used by the publisher.

conn-postgres-in.yaml

```yaml
kind: connectionDef
apiVersion: '1.0'
type: tabsdatak.conn.postgres:PostgresSrcConn
spec:
  uri: 'postgres://db.internal:5432/world'
  credentials:
    kind: userPasswordCredentials
    apiVersion: '1.0'
    type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:UserPassword
    spec:
      user: 'secret:tabsdata_reader'
      password: 'secret:example-password'
```

-   required
    
-   required
    
-   optional
    
-   optional
    

### Create the collection

A publisher is registered in a source collection, and a source collection is created with its connection. Every function registered in the collection uses that connection.

Generate a connection template, which lists all the connection fields:

```bash
tdk connection template --type postgres-sql-in --file conn-postgres-in.yaml
```

Edit the template file with the Postgres connection information, check it, and create the collection with it:

```bash
tdk connection validate --file conn-postgres-in.yaml
```

```bash
tdk collection create --name postgres_in --conn-file conn-postgres-in.yaml
```

Then register the publisher in the collection:

```bash
tdk fn register --coll postgres_in --path publish_orders.py::publish_orders
```

-   The collection goes in the `sources` group, because the connection is a source connection. `--group` can be left out; if it is given, it must be `sources`.
-   `secret:<value>` gives a secret value in the file itself. `$secret:<ENV_VAR>` reads it from an environment variable when the collection is created, so the value never appears in the file. Either way, Tabsdata stores the secret separately, and the stored connection only shows a placeholder.
-   Functions in the collection must use the connector of its connection: `PostgresSrc` for a collection created with `PostgresSrcConn`. Transformers go in a collection of their own.
-   To change the connection later, for example to rotate a password, run `tdk collection update --name postgres_in --conn-file conn-postgres-in.yaml`. The connector cannot change; to use another one, create another collection.
-   Creating a source or destination collection requires permission to manage the project.

### Connection Config Parameters

#### `uri`

The SQLAlchemy-style connection URI: `postgres://host:port/database`. Written as a plain value here, but accepts `secret:` too.

#### `credentials`

The database user and password, spliced into the URI at connect time. `UserPassword` requires a `user` and `password`.

#### `entity_whitelist`

A YAML list of regular expressions, not a comma-separated string. It is checked to be a list of valid regular expressions, but it has no effect yet. Leave it out.

#### `conn_cfg`

Driver-side options forwarded to the connection as SQLAlchemy `connect_args`.
