# Automatic Orchestration

> How Tabsdata determines which functions to run and in what order based on the tables they read and write.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/automatic-orchestration

In Tabsdata, **Automatic Orchestration** handles the order in which Functions run based on the Tables they read and write. Instead of requiring users to manually define a DAG, Tabsdata uses the declared dependencies between Tables and Functions to determine what needs to run. When a Function is triggered, Tabsdata automatically identifies any downstream Functions that depend on its output and executes them in the appropriate order.

_Video: A publisher is triggered from the CLI, Tabsdata builds an execution plan by following the tables each function declares, and each table that gets new data starts the function that reads it, until the plan commits new versions of customers and customers_clean._

## Traditional Orchestration

Traditionally, orchestrating a data pipeline involves manually defining a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) that specifies how each step depends on the others and the order in which they should execute.

As a pipeline grows or changes, the DAG has to be updated to account for any new or modified dependencies. This also means that adding a new step to a pipeline requires updating its orchestration logic, even if the step's inputs and outputs are already known.

## How Tabsdata Orchestrates Functions

In Tabsdata, Functions do not pass data directly to one another. Instead, Functions write their output to Tabsdata Tables, which can then be read by other Functions.

Each Function declares the Tables it reads from and writes to as part of its decorator:

-   **Publishers** declare the Tables they write to using `output_tables`.
-   **Transformers** declare the Tables they read from using `input_tables` and the Tables they write to using `output_tables`.
-   **Subscribers** declare the Tables they read from using `input_tables`.

Because these dependencies are declared ahead of time, Tabsdata already knows which Functions depend on each other. When a Function writes a new version of a Table, Tabsdata can identify every downstream Function that reads from it.

For example, registering a new Transformer that reads from the `customers` Table automatically adds it to the workflow. The next time `customers` receives a new version, Tabsdata knows to execute the Transformer without requiring any changes to an existing DAG.

## Tables as Triggers

In Tabsdata, new Table versions are what trigger downstream Functions to run.

By default, Transformers and Subscribers run whenever one of their input Tables receives a new version, unless a different trigger is specified using `trigger_by`.

Publishers do not have input Tables, so they can be triggered manually, through a cron schedule, or by a Table specified in `trigger_by`. Stream Publishers are triggered whenever a new batch of data is ready from their stream source.

See [Execution and Triggers](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/execution-and-triggers) for more information about the available trigger types.

## Execution Plans

Whenever a Function is triggered, Tabsdata uses the declared Table dependencies to build an [Execution Plan](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/execution/execution-plans) containing all the downstream Functions that need to run.

The Execution Plan determines the order in which Functions execute, including Functions across different Collections, so that each Function runs after the Tables it depends on have been updated.

As the plan executes, each Function reads the data written by the upstream Functions in that same execution. However, Tabsdata does not commit any of the new Table versions until every Function in the Execution Plan has completed successfully.

If any Function fails, none of the new Table versions are committed. This prevents partially completed workflows from leaving Tables in inconsistent states.

Tabsdata also records which Table versions each Function read and wrote during the execution, allowing users to trace how data was produced and how it moved through the workflow. See [Lineage](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/lineage) for more information.

---

# Execution & Triggers

> Covers the four Tabsdata function trigger types (manual via `tdk fn trigger` or the UI, CRON schedule, new-data on input table versions, and stream workers such as SQL CDC and Kafka), plus automatic execution plans and streaming publishers.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/execution-and-triggers

## Triggers

A **trigger** decides _when_ a Function runs. There are four kinds of triggers:

Manually

When you run it

When a function is executed through the `tdk fn trigger` CLI Command or through the `trigger` button in the Tabsdata UI

On a schedule

At set times

When a function is executed on a CRON schedule

On new data

When an input Table receives new data

Execute the Function whenever an input Table receives a new Version.

On a stream batch

When a batch of streamed data is due

Execute the Function each time a stream worker, such as SQL CDC or Kafka, hands over a batch

## Automatic orchestration

No matter which trigger fires a function, Tabsdata doesn't run just that one function. It follows the data dependencies and builds an [execution plan](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/execution/execution-plans): the graph of every function that must run as a result, in the correct order, across collections. There is no orchestration for you to wire up.

## Pristine state

Every table in an execution plan stays in sync, because new data is only committed if every function in the plan succeeds. A partial failure commits nothing.

## Streaming publishers

A normal publisher pulls a batch of data each time it runs. A **streaming publisher** stays running continuously, creating new table versions as data arrives: for change-data-capture feeds, log tails, and message queues like [Kafka](https://docs.tabsdata.com/tutorials/publishers/kafka).

---

# Manual Triggers

> Covers triggering a Tabsdata Function by hand with `tdk fn trigger` from the CLI or the UI, the default for Publishers without `trigger_by`, and how the resulting Execution Plan runs downstream Functions.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/triggers/manual

A manual trigger runs a Function on demand, from the CLI or the UI. Nothing about the Function's definition needs to change to allow it: every Function can be triggered by hand, including one that already has a cron or Table trigger configured.

_Video: A Function triggered from the Tabsdata CLI_

## From the CLI

```bash
tdk fn trigger --coll <collection_name> --name <function_name>
```

`<function_name>` is the name the Function was registered under, not the name of its file.

## The default for Publishers

A Publisher reads no Tabsdata Tables, so there is nothing upstream that could fire it. With no `trigger_by` on the decorator, a Publisher runs only when triggered manually.

Transformers and Subscribers behave differently, because they do have input Tables. Left unconfigured, they run on a commit to any of them. See [Table Commit Triggers](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/triggers/table-commit).

## What a manual trigger actually starts

Triggering one Function does not run only that Function. Tabsdata builds an [Execution Plan](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/execution/execution-plans) covering every downstream Function that has to run as a result, and nothing commits unless all of them succeed.

For the UI walkthrough and the full `trigger_by` reference, see [Working with Triggers](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/triggers).

---

# Cron Triggers

> Cron triggers in Tabsdata: crontab mask syntax with UTC schedules, optional start and end window, and enabling or disabling Functions with tdk fn enable and disable. Wait, that's over-long and has a colon-style fragment. Corrected: Cron Triggers: five-field Unix crontab masks run in UTC, optional start and end windows, and enabling or disabling Functions with tdk fn enable/disable.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/triggers/cron

A scheduled trigger runs a Function at fixed times, whether or not any upstream data has changed. Publishers, Transformers, and Subscribers can all use one.

_Video: A cron schedule triggering a Function run_

Configure it by passing a `CronTrigger` to `trigger_by`.

```python
from tabsdatak.api import CronTrigger, publisher, TableFrameSpec
from tabsdatak.conn.mysql import MySQLSrc


@publisher(
    trigger_by=CronTrigger("0 * * * *"),
    source=MySQLSrc(queries=["SELECT * FROM sales"]),
    output_tables=["sales"],
)
def read_sales(sales: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec:
    return sales
```

## The mask

The first argument is a standard Unix crontab mask with five fields and minute precision:

```text
Minute Hour Day Month Day-of-Week
```

| Mask | Runs |
| --- | --- |
| `0,30 * * * *` | every 30 minutes, on the hour and at minute 30 |
| `0 0 * * *` | daily at 00:00 |
| `0 22 * * FRI` | Fridays at 22:00 |

Non-standard shorthands such as `@hourly` and `@daily` are **not** supported.

note

All crontab schedules are interpreted in **UTC**.

## Limiting the window

`CronTrigger` also takes optional `start` and `end` parameters, each either a timezone-aware Python `datetime` or an ISO 8601 string in UTC (`2026-01-01T12:00:00Z`).

With them set, the mask only fires between those two times. With them omitted, it fires indefinitely from the moment the Function is registered.

## Enabled and disabled Functions

A cron schedule only runs while its Function is enabled. Registration defaults to enabled, and `tdk fn register` takes `--enabled` / `--disabled` explicitly. An already-registered Function is toggled with `tdk fn enable` and `tdk fn disable`.

A disabled Function ignores its mask entirely. It does not queue missed runs and fire them on re-enable.

## Where credentials come from

The example above names a MySQL query but carries no host and no password. Those live on the Collection's Connection. See [Connections](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connections).

---

# Table Commit Triggers

> Configures Table commit triggers via the `trigger_by` decorator option: default, empty-list, and named-Table behavior, cross-Collection `collection/table` references, and returning None to skip commits.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/triggers/table-commit

A Table trigger runs a Function whenever one of the Tables it watches receives a new Version. This is what makes a pipeline cascade: a Publisher commits, the Transformers reading that Table run, they commit in turn, and the chain continues to the Subscribers at the end.

_Video: A new Table Version triggering a Function run_

Configure it with the `trigger_by` list on the decorator.

## The three configurations

**Omitted.** Transformers and Subscribers fire on a commit to any of their input Tables. Publishers have no input Tables, so they get no automatic trigger at all and run manually or on a schedule.

**An empty list.** `trigger_by=[]` disables automatic triggering. Use it when a Transformer or Subscriber should read its input Tables but not wake up when they change.

**A non-empty list.** The Function watches exactly the Tables named and nothing else. This is how you trigger on a subset of the input Tables, or on a Table the Function does not read at all.

```python
@transformer(
    trigger_by=["sales", "inventory/stock"],
    input_tables=["sales"],
    output_tables=["sales_by_rep"],
)
def summarize(sales: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec:
    return sales
```

## Referencing another Collection's Tables

Write a Table outside the Function's own Collection as `collection/table`, as `inventory/stock` does above. Unqualified names resolve inside the Function's own Collection.

Cross-Collection references work only within a single Project. A reference that crosses Projects surfaces as `Dependency table '<x>' does not exist`, because the row is not visible rather than missing.

A Table cannot trigger the Function that writes it.

## A commit is not the same as a change

Every run that returns data commits a new Version, whether or not the rows differ from the previous one. A Publisher writing three Tables commits all three on every run, so a Function watching any of them fires each time, even for the Tables whose contents were identical.

Returning `None` from a slot also commits a new Version, one that keeps the Table's previous data, so downstream Functions watching that Table fire for it too. See [`None` inputs and outputs](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/functions/#none-inputs-and-outputs).

---

# Stream Triggers

> Stream trigger page: when a @stream_publisher batch is due (batch_min_secs, batch_max_secs, batch_max_rows, batch_max_bytes, batch_idle_secs) and the Kafka, MySQL CDC, Postgres CDC, and Db2 CDC stream sources.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/triggers/stream

A stream trigger runs a Function each time a batch of streamed data is due. It is the only trigger a `@stream_publisher` has: that decorator takes no `trigger_by` at all.

_Video: A Kafka stream triggering a Function run when a batch is due_

```python
from tabsdatak.api import stream_publisher, TableFramesSpec, TableFrameSpec
from tabsdatak.conn.kafka import KafkaStreamSrc
from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import concat


@stream_publisher(
    source=KafkaStreamSrc(
        topic="users",
        data_format="avro",
        schema=AVRO_SCHEMA,
    ),
    batch_max_secs=300,
    batch_max_rows=500,
    output_tables=["users"],
)
def ingest(users: TableFramesSpec) -> TableFrameSpec:
    return concat(users)
```

## How a batch becomes a run

A stream worker reads the source continuously. What it reads is buffered in memory and written out to data files as the buffer fills. When a batch is due, the files written so far, and anything still in memory, are staged and handed to the Function as one batch. The Function runs once per batch and commits a new Version of each of its output Tables.

The worker is long-lived and independent of the Function. It keeps reading while the previous batch is being processed, so a slow Function does not drop records. Batches are processed one at a time, in order, and if the Function takes longer than the batch interval, batches queue up and are processed in turn.

## When a batch is due

The `batch_*` parameters of `@stream_publisher` decide when a batch is due:

-   `batch_min_secs` is the shortest time between two batches, and never less than 60 seconds.
-   Once `batch_min_secs` have passed, a batch is due when `batch_max_secs` have passed, or when at least `batch_max_rows` rows or `batch_max_bytes` bytes are waiting. At least one of the three is required.
-   With no data waiting, nothing runs, unless `batch_idle_secs` is set. Once `batch_idle_secs` have passed, the Function runs with an empty batch.

Tabsdata looks for new batches about every 30 seconds, so a batch can start up to that long after it is due. See [Batch parameters](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/functions/stream-publishers#batch-parameters) for the full rules and examples.

The buffer settings in a source's `src_cfg`, such as `tabsdata.kafka.buffer.max_rows`, only decide when the worker writes what it has read to a file. They do not make a batch due.

## Available stream sources

| Source | System | Output Tables |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `KafkaStreamSrc` | Apache Kafka | the Tables named in `output_tables` |
| `MySQLCdcStreamSrc` | MySQL | one per tracked Table |
| `PostgresCdcStreamSrc` | PostgreSQL | one per tracked Table |
| `Db2CdcStreamSrc` | IBM Db2 | one per tracked Table |

All four are registered as stream sources, which `tdk connection types` shows in the **Mode** column as `Stream Source`. Like ordinary sources they belong to a `sources` Collection, and the address and credentials live on that Collection's Connection rather than on the source object.

The CDC sources track a list of qualified Table names and resume from a stored position. Postgres additionally requires a logical replication slot, since the WAL it reads is retained on the server until the consumer confirms it. See [Postgres CDC](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connectors/postgres-cdc), [MySQL CDC](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connectors/mysql-cdc), [Db2 CDC](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connectors/db2-cdc), and [Kafka](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connectors/kafka).

## Constraints on the Function

A `@stream_publisher` differs from the other decorators in three ways:

-   It takes one `TableFramesSpec` parameter per source slot, always in array mode, because a batch is a list of frames rather than a single frame.
-   It returns one `TableFrame` per output Table, the same as a Publisher.
-   It must **not** declare a `ctx` parameter. It runs inside the runtime's stream loop rather than per-transaction, so there is no `TrxCtx` at the call boundary and declaring one fails registration.

See [Stream Publishers](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/functions/stream-publishers) for the decorator's parameters and lifecycle.

---

# Secrets Management

> Explains how to register credentials in Tabsdata Connections via `tdk connection template` and `tdk collection create`/`update`, the dehydration into a secret store, `$secret:<VARIABLE>` environment references, and the security tradeoffs of passing secrets to a coding agent.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/secrets-management/

Credentials used by Publisher and Subscriber Functions are stored in Connections. Connections are credential stores that are indirectly attached to a function and enable the function access to specific credentials.

A Project can also hold secrets that its Functions read directly. See [Project Secrets](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/projects#project-secrets).

To register a credential into Tabsdata, the user must generate a `.yaml` connection document template through the `tdk connection template` cli command and fill in the required credentials. Once the document is completed, it must be attached to a collection through the `tdk collection create` or `tdk collection update` cli command.

During connection registration, Tabsdata **dehydrates** the Connection document by extracting its credentials into a separate secret store and replacing them in the stored Connection with references to those secrets.

Once stored, credentials are only made available to a Function when it runs. In fact, once credentials are in Tabsdata, there is no way to read them out of the system. This is by design, ensuring your secrets are always secure.

When a coding agent builds workflows for you, it can only pass credentials into Tabsdata that you give it. Understand the security implications of providing credentials to your LLM before you do.

There are several ways to pass secrets to an LLM for creating connections.

## Create the Connection Yourself

The most secure option is to create the Connection outside of the agent.

You can ask the agent to generate a Connection template, then add the credentials yourself, and register the Connection with Tabsdata using the `tdk collection create` or `tdk connection update`\` CLI command. The agent can then create or register Functions against the Collection without ever accessing the credentials required.

This keeps the credentials out of the agent's context and session history.

## Provide Credentials Through Environment Variables

Connection templates can reference credentials using `$secret:<VARIABLE>`. When working through an agent, the environment variable must be available to the process running the LLM and the Tabsdata server. This means the variable must be set in the shell environment before both processes are started.

This avoids placing the credential directly in the agent prompt, but still gives the agent process access to it. Environment variables may also be visible to other processes running in the same environment.

For these reasons, environment variables are better suited for development and testing than for long-lived production credentials. Adding or updating secrets also requires restarting both the agent and the Tabsdata server with the updated shell environment.

warning

Storing credentials in environment variables does not prevent the agent from accessing their values. However, it allows the agent to pass the environment variable name as a literal to the Tabsdata server, which can then resolve the value server-side. This reduces the likelihood of the secret being captured in the agent's transcript.

## Provide Credentials Directly to the Agent

You can also provide credentials directly to the agent and have it create the Connection for you.

This is the simplest option, but the credential passes through the agent's context and may be stored in its session history. Credentials provided this way may be at increased risk for exposure.

## Provide Credentials Through a File

In scenarios where the agent is requesting multiple points of data, or in sessions where providing credentials directly inline requires pasting the same content multiple times, you can pass all relevant data into a `.txt` file and pass the path to the agent during your session

warning

Putting credentials in a file and asking an agent to read that file does not prevent the agent from accessing them. Once the agent reads the file, the credentials have passed through the agent just as if they were provided directly.

---

# Service Tokens

> How a service token lets CI jobs, schedulers and scripts call Tabsdata as its owner without a password, and which of the owner's permissions it carries.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/service-tokens

A **service token** is a credential owned by a user that automation such as CI jobs, schedulers and scripts uses to call Tabsdata as that user, without a password. A service token acts with a narrowed subset of its owner's permissions: project development work only.

## How a service token works

Each user account holds at most two service tokens, in slots `1` and `2`. With two slots, you can create a new token while the old one is still in use.

A token starts with `tdst_` and is displayed only once, when it is created. The server stores only a SHA-256 digest of the token and can never show it again.

Every token is created with a lifetime in days. The deployment's `service_tokens.max_days` setting is the ceiling (90 in the shipped configurations). A token that never expires (`-1`) works only where `max_days` is `-1`. If `max_days` is not set, service tokens are disabled on that deployment.

A token stops working when any of the following happens:

-   the token expires
-   the owner or an administrator revokes the token
-   the owner's account is disabled
-   the owner's account is deleted

Changing the owner's password does not affect existing tokens. A session started with a token is never renewed, and lasts until the token expires or is revoked.

Clients send the token in the `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header.

### Rotating a token

To rotate a token without downtime:

1.  Create a token in the free slot.
2.  Move your consumers to the new token.
3.  Wait until **Last used** for the old slot stops changing. **Last used** updates about every ten minutes.
4.  Revoke the old slot.

## Managing tokens in the UI

Open **Account → Service tokens**. The page shows **Slot 1** and **Slot 2**. A filled slot shows the token's prefix (`tdst_v1_<hint>…`), its comment, and when the token was created, when it expires and when it was last used.

1.  To create a token, click **Create token** in an empty slot. Choose **Expires after a number of days** (90 by default) or **Never expires**, add an optional comment of up to 200 characters, then click **Create token**.
2.  Click **Copy** in the **Token created in slot N** panel. The token is shown only on this page. After you click **Dismiss** or leave the page, you can't get the token back. If you lose it, revoke the slot and create a new token.
3.  To revoke a token, click **Revoke** in a filled slot, then **Revoke token**. Every client using that token stops working immediately.

## Managing tokens with the tdk CLI

To manage tokens, log in with your username and password first.

```bash
tdk auth service-token create --slot 1 --expires-in-days 90 --comment "nightly CI"
tdk auth service-token list
tdk auth service-token revoke --slot 1
```

-   `create` prints the token once. `--expires-in-days` has no default: pass a positive number, or `-1` for a token that never expires.
-   `create` is refused if the slot already has a token. Revoke that slot first.
-   `list` shows each slot's hint, comment, creation time, expiry and **Last used** (updated about every ten minutes).

To run commands as a token, export the token and log in. With no value, `--token` reads the `TDK_TOKEN` environment variable, so the token never appears in shell history:

```bash
export TDK_TOKEN=tdst_v1_...
tdk login --server https://tabsdata.example.com --token
```

`--token` cannot be combined with `--user` or `--password`. A token login is never renewed. When the token expires or is revoked, log in again with a new token.

See [tdk auth](https://docs.tabsdata.com/cli/tdk/auth/) for every flag of the `service-token` commands.

## Permissions a token carries

A token carries two of its owner's project permissions, `view_project` and `develop_project`, in the projects where the owner holds them. A token never has more permissions than its owner.

The server reads the owner's current grants every time the token is used. If an administrator removes a project grant from the owner, the token loses that grant immediately.

Higher roles count. If the owner has `manage_project` on a project, the token gets `develop_project` there. A system admin's token can therefore do development work in every project.

| Area | What the token can do |
| --- | --- |
| Projects | List and read the owner's projects; read their groups, metrics, snapshots and in-flight work |
| Collections | Create, update, delete and read collections; read a collection's connection |
| Functions | Register, update, patch, enable, delete and trigger functions; read history, executions and bundles |
| Tables | Read schema, samples, data versions and lineage; download data; delete tables |
| Runs | List plans, transactions and function runs; cancel and recover them; replay function runs |
| Workers | List workers and read or tail their logs |
| Identity | `GET /auth/info` (who am I) and read its own token record |

## Permissions a token does not carry

Every other operation is refused with `403 This operation cannot be performed with a service token`, even when the owner holds the permission. A leaked token therefore can't grant access, create accounts or create another token.

| Not carried | What this blocks for a token |
| --- | --- |
| `manage_access` (system) | Managing users, permission grants and other users' tokens |
| `manage_roles` (system) | Creating, editing and assigning roles |
| `create_projects` (system) | Creating projects |
| `manage_project` (project) | Updating or deleting a project; creating, changing or deleting its groups |
| Token management | Creating, listing or revoking tokens, including its own. A token can't create its own replacement |
| Account self-service | Changing the owner's password; refreshing or extending its own session |

An administrator with `manage_access` can list and revoke any user's tokens through the REST API (`/users/{user}/service-tokens`), using a password session.

---

# User Interface

> Tabsdata web UI pages for the Overview, Projects, Collections, Functions, Tables, Executions, Worker logs, Triggers, Search, Tabby, Security, System, and Account, plus the local URL and demo.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/user-interface

The Tabsdata **User Interface** (UI) is a web interface for inspecting and managing the resources within a Tabsdata Server.

When running Tabsdata locally, the UI is available at `http://localhost:2457`, where `2457` is the Server's default public port. Sign in using the same username and password used with the `tdk` CLI.

The UI demo provides a read-only Tabsdata Server with three Projects and existing execution history. Actions that create, modify, trigger, or delete resources are disabled.

[Explore the UI](https://docs.tabsdata.com/ui-demo/)

## Overview

The **Overview** page summarizes activity across every Project in the Server.

For each Project, the page shows:

-   Tables committed
-   Rows committed
-   Running Executions
-   Warnings
-   Errors

Activity can be viewed across six time ranges.

## Projects

The **Projects** page shows activity for the selected Project, including data that is currently in flight and data that has already been committed.

The page also includes a graph of committed data over time.

From the UI, you can:

-   Create Projects
-   Share Projects
-   Switch the currently selected Project

Most pages in the UI are scoped to the selected Project. Use the Project selector in the side panel to switch between Projects.

## Collections

The **Collections** page lists the Collections within the selected Project.

Opening a Collection shows its:

-   Functions
-   Tables
-   Connection configuration

Sensitive credentials stored in a Connection are hidden from the UI.

From the UI, you can also:

-   Create, edit, and delete Collections
-   Grant a Collection access to Tables in another Collection
-   Remove previously granted access

## Functions

Opening a **Function** shows the code registered with Tabsdata and its version history.

Function versions are retained so you can inspect previous versions, including the version used for a particular Function Run.

From the UI, you can:

-   Trigger a Function
-   Delete a Function

Editing a Function's code is performed using `tdk` rather than through the UI.

## Tables

Opening a **Table** shows its schema, sample rows, and version history.

Each Table version includes the Execution that wrote it, allowing changes in the Table to be traced back to the Execution that produced them.

The Table page also includes **Run SQL query**, which lets you edit and run a SQL query against the Table's sample data.

From the UI, you can also delete a Table.

## Executions

The **Executions** page shows the Execution Plans created within the selected Project.

Execution Plans are separated into:

-   Active
-   Issues
-   Finished

Opening an Execution Plan shows a graph of its execution flow and provides access to the Transactions, Function Runs, and Workers created as part of the Execution.

Transactions, Function Runs, and Workers can each be filtered by status.

### Worker logs

Opening a Worker provides access to the logs produced while it was running.

Worker logs can be:

-   Viewed in the UI
-   Viewed in their raw form
-   Downloaded

When a Function Run fails, its Worker logs contain the output and errors produced during execution.

### Triggers

The Executions area also shows the triggers configured for the Project, including:

-   Cron Triggers
-   Stream Sources

This lets you inspect both what causes Functions to run and the Execution Plans created when they run.

## Search

The **Search** page searches for resources across the Tabsdata Server.

Use Search to locate a resource without navigating through its Project and Collection.

## Tabby

**Tabby** is the built-in Tabsdata agent for interacting with and inspecting a Tabsdata Server. See [Tabby](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/tabby) for setup, commands, and an example chat.

Tabby requires an Anthropic or OpenAI API key to be configured on the Server.

From Tabby, you can:

-   Start a new chat
-   Continue existing chats
-   Stop a response while it is being generated
-   Search previous messages
-   Export a chat as Markdown
-   Use page-specific suggested prompts
-   Run a Server health check

Suggested prompts depend on the page you are viewing. For example, a Collection page may include prompts for listing Functions or creating a Publisher.

The **Run health check** action generates an AI-written report about the current health of the Server.

## Security

The **Security** page manages users, roles, and permissions for the Tabsdata Server.

From the UI, you can:

-   Create, edit, and delete users
-   Create and delete roles
-   Add users to roles
-   Remove users from roles
-   Grant permissions
-   Remove permissions

## System

The **System** page shows the status and runtime information for the Tabsdata Server.

## Account

The **Account** page shows information about the currently signed-in user.

From the UI, you can also:

-   Change your password
-   Log out
-   Switch between light and dark themes
-   Pin resources to the side panel
-   Clear pinned resources

The Server's SSL certificate can also be downloaded from the login page.

# Tabby

> The built-in operational agent, opened from the UI. It answers questions about the server's resources, monitors dataflows, traces failures to root cause and suggests fixes, and, when the server allows it, creates and changes resources on request. It runs in the server's AI agent service (port 2459) and needs an Anthropic or OpenAI key, set with `tdkserver quickstart --config anthropic-key=env:ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/tabby

**Tabby** is the built-in Tabsdata agent, opened from the **Tabby** page of the [User Interface](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/user-interface). Tabby answers questions about the resources on a Tabsdata Server and, when the Server allows it, creates and changes them on request.

Tabby

Did any execution plans fail in customer\_management?

No. The 10 most recent execution plans in customer\_management all finished, and each one committed 5 function runs with no errors. The three latest:

| Execution plan | Triggered by | Status | Duration |

anthropic claude-sonnet-4-6

The UI demo includes the Tabby page. Messages cannot be sent from the demo.

[Open Tabby in the UI demo](https://docs.tabsdata.com/ui-demo/tabby)

## Requirements

Tabby runs in the Server's AI agent service, on port `2459` by default, and requires an Anthropic or OpenAI API key. When no key is configured, the Server starts without the AI agent service and Tabby is unavailable.

The key is set when the instance is created, with `--config anthropic-key=…` or `--config openai-key=…`:

```bash
tdkserver quickstart --config anthropic-key=env:ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
```

To add or change the key on an existing instance, download the instance's config, set `api_key` under `ai_providers.anthropic` or `ai_providers.openai` in `aiagent.yaml`, and apply the change:

```bash
tdkserver config get --with-secrets
tdkserver config put --apply
```

note

Tabby runs in the Server's AI Agent process, on port `2459`. The process starts only when an API key is provided during server initialization, and Tabby needs that key to be valid.

## Starting a chat

Open **Tabby** from the side navigation, or press **⌘K** from any page to ask Tabby about the page you are viewing.

A new chat offers four starting prompts:

-   Set up a data flow
-   Connect to an external system
-   Check executions health
-   Show me what Tabsdata can do

Other pages suggest prompts for what they show. A Collection page, for example, suggests listing its Functions, listing its Tables, and creating a Publisher.

## Commands

Commands are typed into the message box.

| Command | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `/help` | Show available commands |
| `/new` | Start a new conversation |
| `/clear` | Clear the current conversation |
| `/export` | Export the conversation as Markdown |
| `/models` | List available providers and models |
| `/provider <name>` | Switch AI provider |
| `/model <name>` | Switch to a specific model, by full or partial name |
| `/health` | Show agent health and status |
| `/pop [name]` | Open resources from the conversation in new tabs, or one resource by name |

The provider and model can also be switched from the selector above the message box.

## Managing chats

Chats are stored on the Server and can be continued later.

From a chat, you can:

-   Search the chat's messages
-   Export the chat as Markdown
-   Stop a response while it is being generated
-   Retry a response that failed

## Building custom connectors

Tabby can write a custom connector for a system that Tabsdata does not support natively. Tabby's reference includes the connector interface in `tabsdatak.spi`, and every connector installed on the Server, including custom ones, is part of what Tabby knows. Installing the connector remains a manual step. See [Custom Connectors](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/plugins).

## Changes to resources

Whether Tabby can create, change, or delete resources is set by `allow_writes` in the Server's `aiagent.yaml` config.

# Data Quality

> Data quality checks in Tabsdata: DataQuality classifiers (IsNotNull, IsBetween, IsIn, Matches, ScaleCategorizer) and operators (Filter, Select, Summary, Fail, Enrich) passed via on_tables to publishers and transformers.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/data-quality

**Data quality** checks validate the rows of a Table as a Function writes it. A check is a `DataQuality` object passed to a Publisher or Transformer through the `on_tables` argument of its decorator. After the Function succeeds, Tabsdata runs the check against the named output Table, where it can label rows, remove or copy rows that fail, write a summary, or fail the Transaction.

Data quality checks are available on `@publisher`, `@stream_publisher`, and `@transformer`. `@subscriber` does not take `on_tables`.

```python
from tabsdatak.api import transformer, TableFrameSpec
from tabsdatak.dataquality import (
    AnyFailed,
    DataQuality,
    Filter,
    IsBetween,
    IsIn,
    IsNotNull,
    Summary,
)


# transformer that dedupes the raw orders, with a data quality check that moves
# rows failing any rule to orders_rejected and writes a summary of the verdicts
@transformer(
    input_tables=["raw_orders"],
    output_tables=["orders"],
    on_tables=[
        DataQuality(
            table="orders",
            classifiers=[
                IsNotNull(["order_id"]),
                IsBetween(["amount"], min_val=0, max_val=10000),
                IsIn(["status"], values={"open", "shipped", "cancelled"}),
            ],
            operators=[
                Filter(AnyFailed(), to_table="orders_rejected", include_quality_columns="criteria"),
                Summary(),
            ],
        ),
    ],
)
def clean_orders(raw_orders: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec:
    return raw_orders.unique()
```

A `DataQuality` check has three parts:

-   **table**: the output Table the check runs on
-   **classifiers**: the rules that label each row, at least one
-   **operators**: what to do with the labels, at least one

## Classifiers

A classifier evaluates one or more columns and writes a verdict for each row into a new verdict column. Classifiers fall into two kinds: **boolean classifiers** decide whether each value passes a rule, and **categorizers** assign each value to a bin.

### Boolean classifiers

| Checks | Classifiers |
| --- | --- |
| Null and NaN | `IsNull`, `IsNotNull`, `IsNan`, `IsNotNan`, `IsNullOrNan`, `IsNotNullNorNan` |
| Sign of a number | `IsPositive`, `IsNegative`, `IsZero`, `IsNotZero`, `IsPositiveOrZero`, `IsNegativeOrZero` |
| Booleans | `IsTrue`, `IsFalse` |
| Ranges | `IsBetween`, `IsNotBetween` |
| Sets of values | `IsIn`, `IsNotIn` |
| Text | `Matches`, `DoesNotMatch`, `HasLength` |

```python
from tabsdatak.dataquality import HasLength, IsBetween, IsIn, IsNotNull, Matches

IsNotNull(["order_id", "customer_id"])
IsBetween(["amount"], min_val=0, max_val=10000, closed_on="both")
IsIn(["status"], values={"open", "shipped", "cancelled"})
Matches(["email"], pattern=r"^[^@]+@[^@]+$")
HasLength(["country_code"], min_len=2, max_len=2)
```

Classifiers share these settings:

-   **column\_names**: the columns to classify. Each entry is a column name, or a `(column, verdict_column)` tuple that names the verdict column. When omitted, the classifier applies to every user column.
-   **on\_missing\_column**: `"ignore"` (the default) skips a named column that is not in the Table, and `"fail"` fails the check.
-   **on\_wrong\_type**: `"ignore"` (the default) skips a column whose data type the classifier does not support, and `"fail"` fails the check.
-   **on\_wrong\_value**: `"ignore"` (the default) gives a null verdict for a value that cannot be evaluated, and `"fail"` fails the check.
-   **tags**: labels that scope operators to this classifier.
-   **prefix**: text added to the start of every verdict column name. Defaults to `@td.dq.`, and `""` adds no prefix.

### Categorizers

`ScaleCategorizer` assigns each numeric value to a bin of a scale. The verdict column holds the bin number, or a reserved value for a null, a NaN, or a value below or above the scale.

| Scale | Bin edges |
| --- | --- |
| `LinearScale` | Equal-width bins |
| `LogarithmicScale` | Spaced logarithmically |
| `ExponentialScale` | Spaced exponentially |
| `MonomialScale` | Bin widths that grow as a power law |
| `IdentityScale` | One bin per integer |

```python
from tabsdatak.dataquality import InBins, LinearScale, ScaleCategorizer, Select

# splits amount into five equal-width bins between 0 and 10000
ScaleCategorizer([("amount", "amount_bin")], scale=LinearScale(0.0, 10000.0, bins=5), prefix="")

# copies orders in the top bin, or above the scale, to large_orders
Select(InBins(column_name="amount_bin", bins={5, "overflow"}), to_table="large_orders")
```

Bins are numbered from 1. A scale created with `use_bin_zero=True` gives its minimum value a bin 0 of its own.

## Criteria

Criteria select the rows that the `Filter`, `Select`, and `Fail` operators act on.

| Criteria | Selects rows where |
| --- | --- |
| `AllOk()` | Every boolean classifier passes |
| `AnyFailed()` | At least one boolean classifier fails |
| `InBins(column_name, bins)` | A categorizer's bin is one of `bins` |
| `NotInBins(column_name, bins)` | A categorizer's bin is not one of `bins` |

`AllOk` and `AnyFailed` treat a null or NaN verdict as a failure, unless `none_is_ok=True` or `nan_is_ok=True` is set. `InBins` and `NotInBins` accept bin numbers from 0 to 100 and the special bins `"none"`, `"nan"`, `"underflow"`, and `"overflow"`.

## Operators

| Operator | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `Enrich()` | Adds each classifier's verdict column to the Table, or to `to_table`. No rows are removed. |
| `Summary()` | Writes a summary with one row per classifier, holding its verdict counts or bin counts, to a Table named `<table>_dq_summary`, or to `table`. |
| `Filter(criteria)` | Removes the selected rows. They are discarded, or written to `to_table`. |
| `Select(criteria, to_table)` | Copies the selected rows to `to_table`, leaving the Table unchanged. |
| `Fail(criteria, threshold)` | Fails the Transaction when the number of selected rows reaches the threshold. |

`Filter` and `Select` take `include_quality_columns` to choose which verdict columns are carried into `to_table`: `"none"` (the default), `"criteria"`, or `"all"`. The checked Table never carries them.

### Failing a Transaction

`Fail` takes a threshold of rows, as a count or as a percentage of the Table:

```python
from tabsdatak.dataquality import AnyFailed, Fail, PercentThreshold, RowCountThreshold

# fails as soon as one row fails a rule
Fail(criteria=AnyFailed(), threshold=RowCountThreshold(1))

# fails when a twentieth of the table fails a rule
Fail(criteria=AnyFailed(), threshold=PercentThreshold(5))
```

A failed Transaction commits none of its Tables.

## Tags

Tags scope an operator to some of a check's classifiers. An operator with tags applies only to the classifiers that carry a matching tag, and an operator without tags applies to all of them.

```python
from tabsdatak.dataquality import (
    AnyFailed,
    DataQuality,
    Fail,
    Filter,
    IsNotNull,
    Matches,
    RowCountThreshold,
)

DataQuality(
    table="customers",
    classifiers=[
        IsNotNull(["customer_id"], tags=["critical"]),
        Matches(["email"], pattern=r"^[^@]+@[^@]+$", tags=["cleanup"]),
    ],
    operators=[
        # fails the transaction on a missing key
        Fail(criteria=AnyFailed(tags=["critical"]), threshold=RowCountThreshold(1)),
        # moves rows with a malformed email aside without failing
        Filter(AnyFailed(tags=["cleanup"]), to_table="customers_bad_email"),
    ],
)
```

# Data Quality Trends

> How Summary(trends=Trends()) keeps a history of data quality checks in a trend Table, and how the Tabsdata UI charts it.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/data-quality-trends

A `Summary` records how a Table's data quality looked in one Transaction. **Trends** keep that history: every time the check runs, its summary is folded into a trend Table that holds the recent runs one by one, plus weekly and monthly totals that reach further back. Reading the trend Table shows whether a rule fails more or less often over time, without keeping every version of the summary.

Trends are off by default. Turn them on by passing `Trends()` to the `trends` argument of `Summary`:

```python
from tabsdatak.api import transformer, TableFrameSpec
from tabsdatak.dataquality import (
    DataQuality,
    IsBetween,
    IsIn,
    IsNotNull,
    Summary,
    Trends,
)


@transformer(
    input_tables=["raw_orders"],
    output_tables=["orders"],
    on_tables=[
        DataQuality(
            table="orders",
            classifiers=[
                IsNotNull(["order_id"]),
                IsBetween(["amount"], min_val=0, max_val=10000),
                IsIn(["status"], values={"open", "shipped", "cancelled"}),
            ],
            operators=[Summary(trends=Trends())],
        ),
    ],
)
def clean_orders(raw_orders: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec:
    return raw_orders.unique()
```

Each run of `clean_orders` writes `orders_dq_summary` as before, and Tabsdata then folds that summary into `orders_dq_summary_trends`.

The classifiers run while the data is written, in the same execution of the Function. Tabsdata does not read the Table again afterwards to compute the summary or the trend, so there is no separate quality job and no second pass over the data.

The summary and trend Tables are Tabsdata Tables, versioned like any other. Every execution creates a new version of both, so the summary and the trend of any past execution can be read as they were at that point.

See [Data Quality](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/data-quality) for the classifiers and operators a check is built from.

## Data quality in the Tabsdata UI

The Tabsdata UI recognizes data quality Tables and shows them without any setup. A Table that has data quality checks is marked with a **Q** next to its name, in the Table list and in the execution plan graph.

[![Data quality summary of the leads table in the execution plan graph](https://docs.tabsdata.com/assets/images/dq-summary-d7d7d79eb3b60900f76a1d6648dc1d21.jpg)](https://docs.tabsdata.com/assets/images/dq-summary-d7d7d79eb3b60900f76a1d6648dc1d21.jpg)

_The data quality summary of the `leads` Table for one execution, opened from the execution plan graph: 100 rows checked, 10 checks, grouped by column. Each check shows its pass rate and how many rows failed or were null, and the lowest pass rate is called out at the top._

[![Pass rate by classifier for the leads table, run by run](https://docs.tabsdata.com/assets/images/dq-trends-5c9d6994b2a361d85f29a0616b39eeed.jpg)](https://docs.tabsdata.com/assets/images/dq-trends-5c9d6994b2a361d85f29a0616b39eeed.jpg)

_The **Data Quality Trends** tab of the `leads` Table, with its trend chart expanded: the pass rate of every classifier, execution by execution. Hovering over an execution shows all the pass rates at that point._

A Table's data quality shows in two places:

-   **The Table's page.** A Table with a summary has a **Data Quality Summaries** tab, and a Table with a trend has a **Data Quality Trends** tab. Each tab lists the Table's summary or trend Tables; select one to chart it.
-   **The execution plan graph.** Right-click a Table and open **Data Quality** > **Data Quality Summary** or **Data Quality Trend** to see the summary or trend as it was written by that execution.

The trend chart, titled **Pass rate by classifier**, plots `pass_pct` for every classifier:

-   **Runs**, **Weeks**, and **Months** switch between the `run`, `week`, and `month` rows of the trend Table. Buckets are in UTC, and weeks start on Monday.
-   The legend button shows or hides individual classifiers, and the expand button opens a larger chart.
-   On the **Data Quality Trends** tab, a trend Table can be pinned, so that its chart stays on the board while other trend Tables are selected.

## Trends

`Trends` configures the trend Table: its name and how long each tier keeps its rows.

```python
from tabsdatak.dataquality import Summary, Trends

Summary(trends=Trends())
Summary(trends=Trends(table="orders_quality_history", days=14, weeks=26, months=36))
Summary(trends=Trends(days=7, weeks=13, months=0))
```

The first keeps the default retention, the second names the Table and keeps longer history, and the third keeps no month tier.

### Parameters

#### `table`

The Table the trend is written to, as a valid table name. Defaults to `None`, which writes to `<target>_dq_summary_trends`, where `<target>` is the Table the `DataQuality` check runs on. The default name does not follow `Summary(table=...)`: a summary written to `orders_quality` still gets its trend in `orders_dq_summary_trends` unless `table` is set. A name given here is used as is, with no suffix added. The trend Table is created in the same collection as the Function.

#### `days`

How many days a run is kept as its own row, as a non-negative integer. Defaults to `7`. A run counts towards its week and month from its first execution, so expiring its run row does not remove it from the coarser tiers. `0` keeps no run rows.

#### `weeks`

How many weeks a week row is kept, counted from the Monday that starts it, as a non-negative integer. Defaults to `12`, which keeps the current week and the 11 before it. `0` keeps no week rows.

#### `months`

How many months a month row is kept, counted from the 1st of the month, as a non-negative integer. Defaults to `24`, which keeps the current month and the 23 before it. `0` keeps no month rows.

At least one of `days`, `weeks`, and `months` must be greater than zero. To keep no trend, leave `trends` unset.

## How the trend Table is organized

### Tiers

The trend Table holds four kinds of rows, told apart by the `grain` column:

| `grain` | One row per | `bucket` holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `run` | classifier and run | The time of the run |
| `week` | classifier and week | Monday 00:00 UTC of the week |
| `month` | classifier and month | The 1st of the month, 00:00 UTC |
| `folded` | Transaction already counted | The time of the run |

The tiers overlap. A run is added to its week and its month as soon as it happens, not when its run row expires, so the current week row already includes the runs that are still listed one by one, and a month row includes every run of that month. Each tier expires on its own: a week that falls out of the `weeks` window is still counted in its month row.

Weeks and months are bucketed independently, so a week that crosses into a new month is one week row while its runs count towards two month rows. Adding week rows together does not give a month row.

### Retention

Retention is measured against the newest run folded into the Table, not against the wall clock. With the defaults, after a run on a given day the Table holds:

-   a run row for each run in the 7 days before it
-   a week row for that week and each of the 11 weeks before it
-   a month row for that month and each of the 23 months before it

Rows only expire when the trend is updated, so a Table whose check stops running keeps its last rows as they were.

### Folded rows and recovered Transactions

Each `folded` row records one Transaction whose results the week and month rows already include. It carries the Transaction ID and the time of the run, and no counts. When a summary arrives for a Transaction that has a `folded` row, for example because the Transaction was recovered, it is not counted a second time. Summaries that arrive out of order are still counted once each.

A `folded` row is kept for as long as the week or month tier could still be holding that run. When both `weeks` and `months` are `0`, no `folded` rows are kept.

## Trend Table schema

| Column | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `grain` | string | `run`, `week`, `month`, or `folded`. |
| `bucket` | datetime (UTC) | The run time for `run` and `folded` rows, the Monday that starts the week for `week` rows, and the 1st of the month for `month` rows. |
| `classifier` | string | The verdict column the counts belong to, as in the summary, for example `@td.dq.order_id_is_not_null` or the name given in a `(column, verdict_column)` tuple with its prefix. Null on `folded` rows. |
| `runs` | int64 | `1` on a `run` row; the number of runs in the bucket on `week` and `month` rows. Null on `folded` rows. |
| `passed` | int64 | Rows that passed the classifier. |
| `failed` | int64 | Rows that failed the classifier. |
| `nulls` | int64 | Rows with a null verdict. |
| `nans` | int64 | Rows with a NaN verdict. |
| `pass_pct` | float64 | `passed * 100 / (passed + failed)`. Null and NaN verdicts are left out. Null when `passed + failed` is `0`, and on `folded` rows. |
| `txn` | string | The Transaction ID on `run` and `folded` rows. Null on `week` and `month` rows. |
| `folded_through` | datetime (UTC) | The time of the newest run folded so far. Every row of a version holds the same value. |

On `week` and `month` rows, `passed`, `failed`, `nulls`, and `nans` are summed over the runs in the bucket, so `pass_pct` is the share of passing rows across the whole bucket, not an average of the runs' percentages. Like every Tabsdata Table, the trend Table also carries the `$td.` system columns.

Only boolean classifiers are tracked. `ScaleCategorizer` results appear in the summary but not in the trend Table, and a summary with only categorizers adds no rows to its trend Table. Tags on `Summary` apply as usual: the trend tracks the classifiers the summary includes.

## How the trend Table is maintained

Registering a Function that declares `Summary(trends=Trends(...))` also registers a second Function, the trend Function. The trend Function:

-   is named after the trend Table with `_trend` appended, for example `orders_dq_summary_trends_trend`
-   reads the latest summary and the latest version of the trend Table, and writes a new version of the trend Table
-   runs in the same execution as the parent Function, after the summary is written
-   is registered even in a collection that does not otherwise accept transformers

Each run writes a new version of the whole trend Table: the previous version is read back, the new summary is merged in, and the rows that fell out of their tier's window are dropped. Earlier versions of the trend Table stay available like any other Table's.

The trend Table is linked to the Table the check runs on, not to the summary, and its data versions report that Table as their parent.

## Lifecycle

The trend Function belongs to the Function that declares the `Summary`, its parent, and follows it:

-   **Updating** the parent Function with the same declaration keeps the same trend Function. Changing `days`, `weeks`, or `months` keeps its name.
-   **Renaming** the trend Table, through `table`, replaces the trend Function with one named after the new Table.
-   **Adding** `trends` to an existing `Summary` registers a trend Function on the next update.
-   **Removing** `trends`, or the whole `DataQuality` check, deletes the trend Function. The trend Table is kept, frozen, with its history.
-   **Deleting** the parent Function deletes the trend Function, and leaves their Tables frozen. Registering the parent Function again with `tdk fn register --reuse-tables` takes the frozen Tables back, history included.
-   **Disabling** or **enabling** the parent Function does the same to the trend Function.
-   **Moving** the check to another Table of the same Function keeps the summary and trend Tables and links them to the new Table.
-   **No longer producing** the Table the check runs on freezes that Table, its summary, and its trend Table. Deleting the frozen Table also deletes the summary and trend Tables derived from it.

The trend Function cannot be managed directly. Updating, patching, deleting, enabling, disabling, or triggering it by name is refused with:

```text
Function '<name>' is a child function managed by its parent; it cannot be updated, patched, deleted, enabled or triggered directly
```

Make the change on the parent Function instead.

## Examples

### Tracking a source report run by run

A sales operations team publishes the Salesforce _Lead Lifetime_ report once a week and wants to know which data entry problems are getting better. The publisher checks every run and keeps a trend:

```python
from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, publisher
from tabsdatak.conn.salesforce import SalesforceReportSrc
from tabsdatak.dataquality import (
    DataQuality,
    HasLength,
    IsBetween,
    IsIn,
    IsNotIn,
    IsNotNull,
    IsPositive,
    Matches,
    Summary,
    Trends,
)


@publisher(
    source=SalesforceReportSrc(reports=["Lead Lifetime Report"], find_report_by="name"),
    output_tables=["leads"],
    on_tables=[
        DataQuality(
            table="leads",
            classifiers=[
                IsNotNull([("EMAIL", "email_present")]),
                Matches([("EMAIL", "email_valid")], pattern=r"^[^@]+@[^@]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,}$"),
                IsNotNull([("LEAD_SOURCE", "lead_source_present")]),
                IsNotIn([("COMPANY", "company_provided")], values={"[not provided]", "N/A", "Unknown"}),
                IsIn([("RATING", "rating_valid")], values={"Hot", "Warm", "Cold"}),
                IsBetween([("EMPLOYEES", "employees_in_range")], min_val=1, max_val=10_000),
                HasLength([("LAST_NAME", "last_name_valid")], min_len=2, max_len=80),
                IsPositive([("ANNUAL_REVENUE", "revenue_positive")]),
            ],
            operators=[Summary(trends=Trends(days=35))],
        )
    ],
)
def leads_report(leads: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec:
    return leads
```

The report runs once a week, so with the default `days=7` only the latest run would keep a row of its own. `days=35` keeps the last five runs individually. The trend lands in `leads_dq_summary_trends`, with one classifier per verdict column: `@td.dq.email_present`, `@td.dq.email_valid`, and so on.

After a few weeks, the trend separates the problems that are being fixed, such as missing emails once the web form makes the field required, from those that hold steady and those that come and go with list imports. For example, the month row for August 2026 might read:

| grain | bucket | classifier | runs | passed | failed | pass\_pct |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| month | 2026-08-01 00:00:00 UTC | @td.dq.email\_present | 4 | 362 | 38 | 90.5 |

### Inspecting the trend Table

Use `tdk table data` with `--sql` to look at one tier:

```bash
tdk table data --coll sales --name leads_dq_summary_trends --sql "SELECT bucket, classifier, runs, failed, pass_pct FROM leads_dq_summary_trends WHERE grain = 'week' ORDER BY classifier, bucket" --print
```

`folded_through` shows which run the trend has caught up to. The trend Function commits in the same Transaction as the summary, so a committed summary version always has its trend version next to it.

### Reading trends downstream

A transformer can take the trend Table as an input like any other Table, for example to publish a weekly quality scorecard for a dashboard:

```python
from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer
from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import col


@transformer(
    input_tables=["sales/leads_dq_summary_trends"],
    output_tables=["leads_weekly_quality"],
)
def leads_weekly_quality(trends: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec:
    return trends.filter(col("grain") == "week").select(
        "bucket", "classifier", "runs", "passed", "failed", "pass_pct"
    )
```

Each new version of the trend Table triggers the transformer, so the scorecard is refreshed after every run of the report.

### Keeping only recent history

A pipeline that runs every few minutes produces many run rows. Keeping a day of runs and a quarter of weeks, with no month tier, bounds the Table's size:

```python
from tabsdatak.dataquality import Summary, Trends

Summary(trends=Trends(days=1, weeks=13, months=0))
```

## Limitations and validation

-   Trends are only maintained for boolean classifiers. Categorizer results stay in the summary Table.
-   Retention values are whole numbers of days, weeks, or months, `0` or greater. A negative value, a float, a string, or a boolean is refused with error `DQC_32`, as is an invalid `table` name.
-   Setting `days`, `weeks`, and `months` all to `0` is refused with error `DQC_33`. Leave `trends` unset to keep no trend.
-   Every Table a check produces must have a unique name, and that includes trend Tables. Two `Summary` operators with trends on the same check need different `table` names for their trends, or registration fails with error `DQPE_4`.
-   Week and month buckets are always in UTC; weeks start on Monday and months on the 1st. There is no option to bucket in another time zone.
-   A tier that was disabled and is later enabled starts from the runs that follow; it is not filled in from older run rows.
-   The trend Function is managed through the Function that declares the `Summary`. It cannot be triggered, updated, or deleted on its own.

# Lineage

> How Tabsdata records where each table version came from and how to view that lineage in the Tabsdata UI.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/lineage

Any number of factors can evolve over the course of a data pipeline's lifecycle, including the shape of processed data, the logic used to move and transform that data, and when specific data was scheduled to be processed. This is called **Data Lineage**.

Tabsdata's built-in data lineage automatically stores immutable versions of tables and functions as they are modified, preserving a record of how your workflows change over time. This allows users to travel back to historical versions of table data, examine the code that produced them, and see how their workflow logic has evolved.

_Video: In the Tabsdata UI, the trigger time of the newest execution plan is highlighted and the plan is opened from the Executions list, the pub_customers function on its graph is right-clicked to show its code, and the customers table is right-clicked and Go to sample opens the version the plan wrote._

## How Lineage Is Recorded

All Tabsdata functions declare the Tables they read from and write to. This allows Tabsdata to infer dependencies and execution order, a core mechanic that enables Automatic Orchestration and Execution Plans.

Because dependencies are declared ahead of time, Tabsdata automatically links each table version to the function and function code that produced it. These versions are then grouped into an execution plan, along with the other tables and functions affected by the execution.

## Table History

Each time a Function run successfully returns data, Tabsdata creates a new, immutable table version while preserving all previous versions of the table's data and schema.

_Video: In the Tabsdata UI, two older versions of the customers table are selected in turn from the Collections panel, and the Sample tab shows the email and region values that changed between them._

Functions can also read previous Table versions. An input written as `customers@HEAD^` reads the version before the latest, and `customers@HEAD~2..HEAD` reads a range of versions ending at the latest.

Uses the latest version of customers as input.

## Schema History

Each Table version stores its own schema, so a Table's version history records changes to its schema as well as its data. Comparing the schema of one Table version with another shows which columns were added, removed, or changed type.

_Video: In the Tabsdata UI, the customers table version before a schema change is opened, then the table version marked New data with schema changes, and the Schema tab shows region added, signup_date changed from str to date, and fax removed._

## Function History

Functions have their own version history. Whenever a Function is updated, Tabsdata creates a new Function version, retaining a changelog of all previous versions of the function's code.

_Video: In the Tabsdata UI, the two older versions of the pub_customers function are opened in turn from the Collections panel, and the Snippet tab shows the lines of its query that changed between versions._

## Viewing Lineage

In the Tabsdata [User Interface](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/user-interface), lineage can be viewed from Tables, Execution Plans, and Functions.

### Tables

Opening a Table shows three tabs: **Schema**, **Lineage**, and **Sample**. The Lineage tab shows a graph of the Execution Plan that wrote the selected table version. This execution plan is unique to the specific table version, and exploring the lineage of other versions can show the evolution of a particular execution plan.

orders\_clean

Tabsdata›Collections›sales›orders\_clean

### Schema

Table schema defines the structure of a table by listing its columns and their data types.

| Object | Type |
| --- | --- |
| order\_id | i64 |
| customer\_id | i64 |
| amount | f64 |
| ordered\_at | datetime |

# Living Semantic Catalog

> How Tabsdata builds a catalog of what every connected source and destination holds, keeps it current as those systems change, and how agents use it.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/living-semantic-catalog

The **living semantic catalog** is the record the Tabsdata Server keeps of what every connected source and destination holds and how that data can be used. Each source and destination collection has an entry in it: the entities its connection exposes, their fields, and an AI-generated classification of the data.

Tabsdata builds the catalog on its own. Soon after a source or destination collection is created, the server connects to the external system, fetches its metadata, and classifies what it found. The catalog is living because it follows the external systems: when their metadata changes, the connection is classified again, so nobody curates the catalog by hand and it reflects what the systems contain as of the last refresh.

Agents connected to Tabsdata read the catalog when a user asks them to publish from or subscribe to an external system, and use it to tell the user what data is there and how to use it.

_Video: A source collection named crm is created from the CLI with a PostgreSQL connection document, the server probes that connection, reads five tables into the living semantic catalog with a schema fingerprint, and the classifier labels the data as confidential finance data. The next metadata poll finds a new refunds table, the fingerprint changes, and the connection is classified again in full._

## How the Catalog Is Built

Creating a source or destination collection with its connection starts the process. Nothing else is needed from the user.

1.  Soon after the collection is created, the server runs a probe against the external system with the collection's connection. The probe first checks that the system can be reached with the credentials the connection holds.
2.  The probe then reads the system's own metadata: the entities it holds, such as tables, reports, files, objects, or topics, and the fields of each entity. Tabsdata stores the entities with their names and fields, and a fingerprint of the whole schema. Data is not copied into the catalog.
3.  The server's classifier sends the entity list and the collection's description to the configured AI model, together with a few sample rows when the server allows sampling (`catalog.maintenance_samples`). The model's answer is recorded as the connection's [classification](#classification).
4.  The entities and their classification become the connection's entry in the catalog, searchable by keyword and by meaning.

The probe repeats on a schedule, and the classification is redone whenever the metadata the probe finds has changed. See [Keeping It Current](#keeping-it-current).

## What Is Fetched From Each System

The probe reads the metadata the external system already keeps about itself, through the same connector that later moves the data. Each entity is stored with its fully qualified name, its kind, and its fields, plus details that depend on the system.

| System | Entities | Recorded for each entity |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SQL databases: Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server, Oracle, Db2 | tables and views, by database and schema | columns with type, primary key, and column comments |
| Databricks | tables, by Unity Catalog catalog and schema | columns with type and comments |
| Salesforce | reports, by folder, with their report id; SOQL objects | report columns; object fields and whether they are required |
| Object stores and files: Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage, Google Cloud Storage, local files | buckets and prefixes | the file patterns found under each prefix, their format, and the columns read from them |
| MongoDB | collections, by database | collection type (collection, view, time series), indexes, and validators |
| Kafka | topics | partition count |

## Classification

To classify a connection, the server gives the configured AI model a compact description of the whole connection and asks for a structured judgement of the data. The model receives every entity with its fields, grouped the way the system groups them (database and schema, folder, bucket, namespace), the collection's description, and any sample rows the classifier read.

The result is one classification per connection:

| Field | What it says |
| --- | --- |
| Label | a short name for the data, such as "Customer data" or "Market signals" |
| Domain | the business domain: CRM, finance, marketing, engineering, operations, product, HR, supply chain, security, infrastructure, IoT, analytics, ecommerce |
| Contains | what the data holds, one item per subject |
| Use cases | what this data is typically used for |
| Sensitivity | public, internal, confidential, or restricted |
| Freshness | real-time, hourly, daily, weekly, monthly, or static |
| Typical sources | where this kind of data usually comes from |
| Search terms | the synonyms and business words people would search for it by |

Names, comments, and sample values read from the external system are passed to the model as data, never as instructions, and sample values are never copied into the classification.

Each classification records the fingerprint of the schema it was made from. Comparing that fingerprint with the current one tells Tabsdata when the classification is out of date.

## Keeping It Current

Tabsdata re-reads each connection's metadata on a schedule and whenever a user or an agent asks for a refresh. The schedule is set by `catalog.refresh_interval` in the server configuration, which is 24 hours as shipped. On every read, the probe compares the fingerprint of the metadata it found with the stored fingerprint.

If the fingerprints match, the catalog keeps its entities and its classification. If they differ, because of a new table, an altered table, a new report, or a new file pattern, the stored entities are replaced. Because the stored classification was made for the old schema, the connection is then classified again in full. Tabsdata never attempts a partial update: the model sees the whole connection every time, so the label, the subjects, and the search terms stay consistent with everything the connection now holds.

A classification can also be requested by hand, for example after a collection's description was improved, and the connection is classified again on the next sweep. An existing classification can be discarded, and the next sweep then redoes it.

## How Agents Use the Catalog

When a user asks an agent connected to Tabsdata to publish from or subscribe to an external system, the agent reads the catalog before it writes any code.

To find data, the agent searches the catalog across every connection the user can see. A question like "Where do we keep invoices?" becomes a search by keyword and by meaning over collection names and descriptions, entity names, fields, and the classification's search terms, and the agent answers from the hits instead of guessing names.

To describe one source or destination collection, the agent lists the collection's entities and their fields, and says what the classification found the data to be and how sensitive and how fresh it is.

To propose a function, the agent works from the entities in the catalog. For a source, the agent proposes a publisher over the entities that matter, with the real column names and types. For a destination, the agent proposes a subscriber for the tables to deliver, written to the entities the destination exposes.

See [Configure Your AI Agent](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connect-agent) to set up an agent with Tabsdata.

## Working With the Catalog in tdk

The catalog is read and maintained with `tdk`. Every command takes `-P <project>` and names a source or destination collection, because each connection belongs to exactly one collection.

| Task | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Show the connection's catalog status: last check, last refresh, entity count, and whether the entity list was truncated | `tdk connection get -n <collection>` |
| List the entities and, with `--fields`, their fields | `tdk connection entities -n <collection> [--fields] [--filter fqn:lk:<glob>]` |
| Check that the external system can be reached | `tdk connection check -n <collection>` |
| Re-read the metadata now | `tdk connection refresh -n <collection>` |
| Show the classification and whether the schema changed since it was made | `tdk ai catalog show -n <collection>` |
| Classify the connection again on the next sweep | `tdk ai catalog classify -n <collection>` |
| Discard the classification so the next sweep redoes it | `tdk ai catalog unclassify -n <collection>` |
| Search every connection you can see, by keyword and by meaning | `tdk ai search connections --query "<words>"` |

Viewing a connection's catalog status and its classification requires permission to view the project. Listing its entities, checking it, refreshing it, reading sample rows, and requesting a classification require permission to develop in the project. Discarding a classification requires permission to manage the project.

note

Files of different formats in one `paths` list need no extra configuration. `AUTO` reads each file's extension separately, so a `.csv` and a `.parquet` in the same publisher both land correctly.

The case that does need work is objects whose extensions do not say what they are. `format` is one override for the whole source rather than one per path, so setting it reads every path as that format. Files that genuinely differ and cannot be recognised by name have to be split across publishers, one per format.

```python
@publisher(
  source=AzureBlobSrc(
      paths=["departments.csv", "employees_*.csv"],
      file_info="uri",
  ),
  output_tables=["departments", "employees"],
)
def read_hr(
  departments: TableFramesSpec,
  employees: TableFramesSpec,
) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec, TableFrameSpec]:
  return (departments[0], concat(employees))
```

```
┌─────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┬───────┬─────────┐
│    table    │               from               │ rows  │ columns │
├─────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┼───────┼─────────┤
│ departments │ departments.csv                  │ 14    │ 4       │

└─────────────┴──────────────────────────────────┴───────┴─────────┘
```

Paths resolve against the connection's `base_path`, so the publisher names blobs and never the container. `initial_last_modified` limits a run to blobs modified after a timestamp, and the cutoff advances on every later run.

```python
@publisher(
  source=DatabricksSrc(
      queries=[
          "SELECT * FROM {catalog}.{schema}.country",
          "SELECT * FROM {catalog}.{schema}.city",
      ],
      initial_values={"catalog": "main", "schema": "default"},
  ),
  output_tables=["country", "city"],
)
def read_world(
  country: TableFramesSpec,
  city: TableFramesSpec,
) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec, TableFrameSpec]:
  return (country[0], city[0])
```


`warehouse` and `warehouse_id` name the same thing two ways and are mutually exclusive, so the connection carries one or the other. The staging volume has to be a managed Databricks volume the token can write to, since the connector unloads through it rather than streaming rows.

# Publish data from Db2 CDC

> Covers publishing Db2 change data capture with @stream_publisher and Db2CdcStreamSrc: tables, start_from options (tail, full, head), batch_max_secs, and output_tables.

Source: https://docs.tabsdata.com/tutorials/publishers/db2-cdc

Before you begin

[Quickstart a Server](https://docs.tabsdata.com/server-admin/quickstart) or [Start a Server](https://docs.tabsdata.com/server-admin/start)

[Configure Your AI Agent](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/connect-agent)

## Follow the change log instead of re-reading tables

A CDC source uses `@stream_publisher` rather than `@publisher`. A long-lived worker follows the Db2 change log, and each time a batch is due it hands the changes captured since the previous batch to the publisher, which commits them. One output table per tracked table, so `tables` and `output_tables` line up position by position.

warning

There are several ways to pass secrets into Tabsdata. See [Secrets Management](https://docs.tabsdata.com/guide/secrets-management/) for more info if you are planning to have an LLM register secrets into Tabsdata's credential store.

The stream publisher, registered in `sales_cdc`. `start_from="tail"` means the worker begins at the current log position and never backfills, so the first version holds only changes committed after registration:

```python
@stream_publisher(
  source=Db2CdcStreamSrc(
      tables=["SALES.ORDERS", "SALES.CUSTOMERS"],
      start_from="tail",
  ),
  batch_max_secs=120,
  output_tables=["orders_changes", "customers_changes"],
)
def read_sales_changes(
  orders: TableFramesSpec,
  customers: TableFramesSpec,
) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec, TableFrameSpec]:
  return (concat(orders), concat(customers))
```
